api/DBTools.Core.Progress.Overlay.Runtim.title: Class ProgressOverlay | DB Tools
api/DBTools.Core.Progress.Overlay.Runtim.summary: Class ProgressOverlay Namespace DBTools.Core.Progress.Overlay.Runtime Assembly DBTools.Core.dll WPF implementation of IProgressOverlay bound to the overlay host state of one owner Window. Public instance operations marshal their overlay UI changes to the Dispatcher of the owner window: a direct call on the owner thread, Dispatcher.Invoke from any other thread. The static For factory does not marshal; call it on the UI thread of the owner window. CancelRequested is a thread-safe snapshot that workers can read directly. public sealed class ProgressOverlay : IProgressOverlay Inheritance object ProgressOverlay Implements IProgressOverlay Properties CancelRequested Gets a thread-safe cancellation snapshot without dispatcher access. public bool CancelRequested { get; } Property Value bool Methods For(Window, ILogger) Creates a progress overlay bound to the specified owner window. Call it on the UI thread of the owner window: it reads and attaches the overlay host state of the window on the calling thread without dispatcher marshaling, so a call from another thread throws the WPF thread-affinity InvalidOperationException. public static IProgressOverlay For(Window owner, ILogger logger) Parameters owner Window logger ILogger Returns IProgressOverlay Hide() Hides the overlay and clears transient state. public void Hide() RequestCancel() Programmatically triggers CancelRequested. public void RequestCancel() RunAsync(string, Func<CancellationToken, IProgressOverlay, Task>, bool, ProgressOverlayRunOptions?, CancellationToken) Runs work with an overlay lifecycle managed by the overlay implementation. This is the preferred API for long-running operations because it allows the overlay to guarantee first paint (when requested), enforce minimum visible duration, and bridge cancellation consistently across tools. A second run against the same window while one is active is rejected with InvalidOperationException. public Task RunAsync(string title, Func<CancellationToken, IProgressOverlay, Task> work, bool cancelable = false, ProgressOverlayRunOptions? options = null, CancellationToken ct = null) Parameters title string work Func<CancellationToken, IProgressOverlay, Task> cancelable bool options ProgressOverlayRunOptions ct CancellationToken Returns Task Scope(string, bool) Returns a scope that sets the overlay title and tracks elapsed time. Nested scopes are allowed; the parent scope is restored on dispose. public IDisposable Scope(string title, bool cancelable = false) Parameters title string cancelable bool Returns IDisposable Show(string, bool) Shows the overlay with a title. Optional cancel button. public void Show(string title, bool cancelable = false) Parameters title string Overlay title. cancelable bool Whether the overlay shows a Cancel button. Update(string?, double?) Updates overlay status text and/or progress in [0,1]. Null parameters leave the property unchanged. Nonfinite progress throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException before status or progress changes. public void Update(string? status = null, double? progress01 = null) Parameters status string? progress01 double? UpdateStep(int, int, string, double?) Updates overlay with step information for multi-step operations. Automatically formats status as "Step X/Y: {stepDescription}". public void UpdateStep(int currentStep, int totalSteps, string stepDescription, double? progress01 = null) Parameters currentStep int Current step number (1-based). totalSteps int Total number of steps. stepDescription string Description of current step. progress01 double? Optional overall progress in [0,1].

api/DBTools.Core.Settings.Persistence.IS.summary: Interface ISettingsProvider Namespace DBTools.Core.Settings.Persistence Assembly DBTools.Core.dll Get re-reads the defaults and per-year settings files on every call (synchronous, no cache). A missing file or section, or a missing value whose member is not [JsonRequired], gives the default. A value of the wrong JSON kind at an object or collection position reads as empty, an object, array or null at a string property reads as "", and a later file's null or scalar keeps an earlier object or array. Malformed JSON, a missing [JsonRequired] member (also in an object that reads as empty), a value that does not convert at a bool or number property (null, an object or an array included) and any other I/O error throw. CommitAsync rejects an empty batch, a null entry or a repeated section, locks across processes (IOException after 10 s), re-reads the per-year file, replaces the written sections and swaps it atomically; on failure it is unchanged. public interface ISettingsProvider Methods CommitAsync(IReadOnlyCollection<SettingsSectionWrite>, CancellationToken) System.Threading.Tasks.Task CommitAsync(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyCollection<SettingsSectionWrite> writes, System.Threading.CancellationToken ct = null) Parameters writes IReadOnlyCollection<SettingsSectionWrite> ct CancellationToken Returns Task Get<TSettings>(SettingsSection<TSettings>) TSettings Get<TSettings>(SettingsSection<TSettings> section) where TSettings : class, new() Parameters section SettingsSection<TSettings> Returns TSettings Type Parameters TSettings

api/DBTools.Core.Settings.Persistence.Se.summary: Class SettingsSectionWriter Namespace DBTools.Core.Settings.Persistence Assembly DBTools.Core.dll Persists a validated batch of named sections into the per-year settings file (settings.{YEAR}.json) with one atomic swap and no silent fallbacks. public sealed class SettingsSectionWriter : IDisposable Inheritance object SettingsSectionWriter Remarks Same-year Revit processes share one settings file. api/DBTools.Core.Settings.Persistence.ht.summary: Namespace DBTools.Core.Settings.Persistence Classes SettingsPostCommitException SettingsSectionReader Reads the optional application defaults and per-year overrides using each section's generated metadata. SettingsSectionWrite SettingsSectionWriter Persists a validated batch of named sections into the per-year settings file (settings.{YEAR}.json) with one atomic swap and no silent fallbacks. SettingsSection<TSettings> Interfaces ISettingsProvider Get re-reads the defaults and per-year settings files on every call (synchronous, no cache). A missing file or section, or a missing value whose member is not [JsonRequired], gives the default. A value of the wrong JSON kind at an object or collection position reads as empty, an object, array or null at a string property reads as "", and a later file's null or scalar keeps an earlier object or array. Malformed JSON, a missing [JsonRequired] member (also in an object that reads as empty), a value that does not convert at a bool or number property (null, an object or an array included) and any other I/O error throw. CommitAsync rejects an empty batch, a null entry or a repeated section, locks across processes (IOException after 10 s), re-reads the per-year file, replaces the written sections and swaps it atomically; on failure it is unchanged.

api/DBTools.Core.Tools.Commands.ToolComm.summary: Class ToolCommand Namespace DBTools.Core.Tools.Commands Assembly DBTools.Core.dll Base class for Revit commands to enforce ISafeExecutor, run-scope creation, and centralized error notification. public abstract class ToolCommand : IExternalCommand, IExternalCommandAvailability Inheritance object ToolCommand Implements IExternalCommandAvailability Derived AnalyticalSnapToLevelCommand ErftNewCommand ElevationTagsCommand MoveCombinedFoundationTagsCommand UpdateCombinedFoundationTagsCommand AllowJoinSelectedCommand DisallowJoinSelectedCommand UpdateJoistGirderWeightsCommand OrganizeFoundationTypesCommand RecordSetCommand SgtCommand SettingsCommand TdvExportCommand TdvImportCommand VtcCommand Remarks The parameterless constructor stays inert to satisfy Revit's IExternalCommand contract. Runtime services are resolved during Execute(ExternalCommandData, ref string, ElementSet). Sync-over-Async Pattern: The Execute(ExternalCommandData, ref string, ElementSet) method uses .GetAwaiter().GetResult() because Revit's IExternalCommand.Execute method must return synchronously. The async pattern in RunAsync(ICommandContext) is for composability within the command implementation. Constructors ToolCommand() Creates a command that defers runtime service resolution until execute time. This is required by Revit's IExternalCommand contract (parameterless constructor). protected ToolCommand() Properties RequiresActiveDocument Whether the command works on the active document. A command that changes only application state returns false: its context captures no document, so it also runs when no model is open. protected virtual bool RequiresActiveDocument { get; } Property Value bool Methods Execute(ExternalCommandData, ref string, ElementSet) public Result Execute(ExternalCommandData commandData, ref string message, ElementSet elements) Parameters commandData ExternalCommandData message string elements ElementSet Returns Result IsCommandAvailable(UIApplication, CategorySet) public bool IsCommandAvailable(UIApplication applicationData, CategorySet selectedCategories) Parameters applicationData UIApplication selectedCategories CategorySet Returns bool IsCommandAvailableCore(UIApplication, CategorySet) Evaluates the command's Revit context predicate without resolving application runtime services. protected virtual bool IsCommandAvailableCore(UIApplication applicationData, CategorySet selectedCategories) Parameters applicationData UIApplication selectedCategories CategorySet Returns bool RunAsync(ICommandContext) protected abstract Task RunAsync(ICommandContext context) Parameters context ICommandContext Returns Task

api/DBTools.Presentation.Behaviors.html.summary: Namespace DBTools.Presentation.Behaviors Classes BehaviorState Keeps attached behavior state weakly keyed by its element and releases all state for an element during tool-window retirement. The table is stable; its values must be cleared by Release(DependencyObject) before a payload generation is unloaded. ContextMenuOnClickBehavior Opens a button's context menu from its click, placing it below the button. A toggle button keeps its checked state synchronized with the menu's open state. FocusRequestBehavior Focuses the attached control when a bound request value changes. The request is a plain counter or token owned by the view model; the behavior owns and aborts its posted operation. PreviewZoomBehavior Fits an image inside a named viewport when its binding target updates. It also supports a button click for an explicit zoom request, using names so no payload control type is stored. SelectOnRightClickBehavior Selects and focuses an items-control container before its context menu opens. TreePathNavigationBehavior Expands a tree path, selects its final item, and brings that item into view. Paths contain item values, so payload types do not enter the stable behavior assembly. TreePathRequest Plain path request consumed by TreePathNavigationBehavior. Interfaces IReleasable Releasable state owned by one stable attached behavior.

api/DBTools.Presentation.ToolWindows.ITo.title: Interface IToolWindowSession | DB Tools
api/DBTools.Presentation.ToolWindows.ITo.summary: Interface IToolWindowSession Namespace DBTools.Presentation.ToolWindows Assembly DBTools.Presentation.dll Owns a raw-XAML view and its stable shell. Register payload event handlers and teardown through this session. Retire synchronously on the shell's UI thread before unloading a payload generation. Window and View are unavailable after retirement. ShowDialog returns null after retirement. Host-owned creation, lifecycle, root layout and dispatcher callbacks temporarily clear contextual reflection and restore the caller's scope on return. Raw templates resolve through the stable schema. The close gate, subscribed handlers and AddCleanup callbacks re-enter the creation context with ExecutionContext flow suppressed, which retirement releases on every exit. Suppression prevents captures; clearing contextual reflection controls synchronous resolution. A command must suppress flow for its entire payload reflection scope, including tool-triggered layout outside shell overrides. WPF can measure an invalidated subtree directly; that work can see the command context, but cannot capture it while flow is suppressed. Async callback continuations do not inherit that context; name resolution after an await must explicitly re-enter it under suppression for synchronous work. Binding getters/setters, edit cancellation, collection notifications and a custom shell initializer execute in the host's neutral reflection context; they must not depend on ambient name resolution. public interface IToolWindowSession Properties Closed Completes after an accepted user close, once every AddCleanup callback has run. Task Closed { get; } Property Value Task Remarks Forced retirement leaves this task pending, and it never completes. Callers must not await or block on it during shutdown or reload. Register retirement-time work through AddCleanup, never through a continuation of this task. IsRetired bool IsRetired { get; } Property Value bool Outcome Open until retirement starts. Retire records Closed for an accepted user close or Retired for a forced retirement, including native window destruction, once and before any AddCleanup callback runs. ToolWindowOutcome Outcome { get; } Property Value ToolWindowOutcome View FrameworkElement View { get; } Property Value FrameworkElement Window Window Window { get; } Property Value Window Methods AddCleanup(Action) void AddCleanup(Action cleanup) Parameters cleanup Action Close(bool?, bool) void Close(bool? dialogResult = null, bool bypassGate = false) Parameters dialogResult bool? bypassGate bool HideForPick() void HideForPick() RequestClose() void RequestClose() Require<T>(string) T Require<T>(string name) where T : class Parameters name string Returns T Type Parameters T Retire() Synchronously retires the owned stable graph through the same path after either close kind. Writers are quiesced before behavior release, LIFO cleanup and edit cancellation. Final discovery and severing include disconnected containers and owned popup roots. UI Automation may retain the stable tree; its bindings, resources, inputs and values must no longer retain the payload. Shared stable definitions are not mutated. Forced retirement suppresses payload close notifications. Accepted user close preserves pending form edits and Explicit bindings through Closed and cleanup. Neither path pumps. Register payload event unsubscriptions and other owned work through AddCleanup. Returns null when forced retirement ends the loop; a normal close preserves its dialog result. bool? ShowDialog() Returns bool? api/DBTools.Presentation.Tools.GM.GmComb.summary: Class GmComboBoxDropDownCommandBehavior Namespace DBTools.Presentation.Tools.GM Assembly DBTools.Presentation.dll Attached behavior that executes a command when the user commits a ComboBox selection. Members without an XML comment appear without a description. Writing documentation comments Document each public type and member with /// comments. Give a <summary> for every member, a <param> for every parameter, <returns> for non-void methods and <exception> for exceptions that callers handle: /// <summary> /// Runs an action inside a Revit transaction. /// </summary> /// <param name="action">The action to run in the transaction.</param> /// <returns><see langword="true"/> if the transaction committed; otherwise <see langword="false"/>.</returns> /// <exception cref="InvalidOperationException">No document is active.</exception> public bool Execute(Action action) Use <remarks> only for constraints that a caller must know.

developer-guide/architecture/assembly-lo.title: Assembly Loading Contract | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/assembly-lo.summary: Assembly Loading Contract The installed add-in loads in Revit's default AssemblyLoadContext. Hosted tests and Dev Mode load the product into a context that the dbtools-daemon creates. In every host, App loads each tool assembly by explicit path into the context that holds DBTools.dll. DBTools creates no load context, embeds no runtime payload, generates no command bridges and ships no runtime manifest. Installed layout Each supported year has one directory of ordinary files: <year>/ ├── DBTools.addin ├── DBTools.dll ├── DBTools.Core.dll ├── DBTools.Presentation.dll ├── DBTools.HandyControl.dll └── Tools/ ├── DBTools.AnalyticalSnapToLevel.dll ├── DBTools.DialogSuppression.dll ├── DBTools.ElevationTags.dll ├── DBTools.ERFT.dll ├── DBTools.FoundationTags.dll ├── DBTools.FramingJoins.dll ├── DBTools.GM.dll ├── DBTools.JoistGirderWeight.dll ├── DBTools.OrganizeFoundationTypes.dll ├── DBTools.RecordSet.dll ├── DBTools.SGT.dll ├── DBTools.Settings.dll ├── DBTools.TDV.dll └── DBTools.VTC.dll DBTools.addin names DBTools.dll and the class DBTools.App.Addin.AddinEntry. DBTools.dll contains the entry point and host infrastructure and no tool code. WPF needs the physical location of Presentation and HandyControl, so they stay at the top level. Merged libraries Every third-party runtime library is merged into one owner assembly; no third-party DLL is staged. build/Merging/AssemblyMerges.props declares the merges: App owns ricaun.Revit.UI.0.9.0. Core owns the manifest and YAML parser, MVVM, functional, tessellation, dependency injection, logging, options and primitives libraries, and Serilog.Extensions.Logging. Presentation owns the Helix and SharpDX closure, Serilog, and the public dependency injection and logging abstractions. Serilog is in Presentation, which is never reloaded, because its thread-static state must not enter a collectible load context (dotnet/runtime#134928). A declaration's Include is the assembly name. The optional PackageId names a NuGet package whose name differs; ricaun uses PackageId="ricaun.Revit.UI" because its assembly name contains a version. MSBuild passes each merge its inputs as items: the resolved runtime asset of a package, or the output of a project. The merge copies its evaluated reference files into a temporary reference directory. ILRepack searches only that directory and resolves framework identities only from those files, so other package or compiler-output files and the runtimes installed on the build host cannot change the result. MSBuild Inputs and Outputs, including the owner's project.assets.json, decide when a merge reruns. The task deletes its temporary files afterwards. App host references The pinned ricaun.Revit.UI.0.9.0 assembly references Revit 27.0.4, also when App is compiled for Revit 2026. The App merge therefore binds these host references to the exact identities of the selected year during the final Cecil normalization: RevitAPI;RevitAPIUI;AdWindows;UIFramework Only App does this. MergeReferenceGuard then resolves every TypeRef, MemberRef and attribute type name with Cecil against the selected year's evaluated references. It rejects a missing type or member, a referenced version higher than the evaluated one, and any reference to an assembly that a merge removed. The Nice3point UIFramework reference is part of the Revit reference metadata used for this check; it is not shipped. Entry and idle acknowledgement AddinEntry has a public parameterless constructor for Revit. OnStartup first calls AddinIdle.TryAcknowledge. If DBTOOLS_DAEMON_REVIT_ROLE is set to any nonempty value and the entry assembly is in exactly AssemblyLoadContext.Default, it sets the AppContext data DBToolsDaemon.IdleAddin:DBTools to the entry assembly's file location and returns Succeeded before any runtime, ribbon, logging or tool work. OnShutdown returns Succeeded immediately for that instance. Otherwise startup enters AppStartupBoundary, a non-inlined method, which starts the App lifecycle inside ToolWindowCallbackScope. Startup, shutdown and ribbon failures that cannot reach the normal log are written to %APPDATA%\DBTools\Logs\DBTools.Fallback.log with BCL APIs only. Tool resolution ToolAssemblyResolver.LoadAssembly(rootAssembly, assemblyName) loads a manifest-declared assembly. The name must be a simple name without .dll or path characters. If it equals the root assembly's name, the root is returned. Otherwise the resolver: requires a file-backed root assembly; resolves <root directory>/Tools/<assemblyName>.dll and requires the file; reads the file's assembly name and requires the declared simple name; returns an assembly of that name already loaded in the root's context, if its full identity and location match the file; a different identity or location is an error; otherwise loads the file with that context's LoadFromAssemblyPath. The resolver does not search other contexts, install an AppDomain resolver or create a load context. The ribbon registers each command by its assembly location, full class name and availability type name. Availability is implemented by the command's own assembly. Command and availability callbacks enter ToolWindowCallbackScope, which suppresses ExecutionContext flow and sets contextual reflection to the command's load context. Hosted tests and Dev Mode The daemon creates ProductLoadContext for hosted tests and DevModeLoadContext for Dev Mode. App loads each declared tool from Tools/ into that context; Dev Mode does not probe other subfolders. Presentation and HandyControl stay loaded for the life of the process. App, Core and the tool assemblies can be reloaded, as the host decides. Sandbox Sandbox runs one new process in the default context for each candidate year. Its entry point uses only BCL types: it validates the candidate, loads the top-level product files and the Tools/ assemblies from their paths, and then starts WPF through a non-inlined method. The process exits after validation, so no candidate assembly remains loaded for the next year. See Sandbox Validator. Distribution hashes Distribution validation checks the exact relative file set, PE identities, source-derived versions, first-party reference identities, file lengths and SHA-256 hashes. The hashes identify the staged candidate. Nothing checks them when an assembly loads. See Build Pipeline, Project References and Installation.

developer-guide/architecture/build-pipel.title: Build Pipeline | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/build-pipel.summary: Build Pipeline build.sh (Linux, WSL) and build.ps1 (Windows, PowerShell 7) are the build entry points. Both run dotnet build build/Build.proj -t:<Target> with the pinned SDK; a plain dotnet build build/Build.proj -t:<Target> runs the same graph. The default target is BuildAll, which builds, validates and publishes the complete distribution for Revit 2026 and 2027. BuildAll compiles no test projects. Synopsis ./build.sh [Target] [parameters] pwsh -NoProfile -File build.ps1 [Target] [parameters] Both entries print build/Usage.txt for --help. Option names ignore dashes and case. Option Short form Description --Configuration <Release\|Debug> -d, --debug Build configuration; -d selects Debug --Years <years> -y, --year Revit years, for example 2026 or "2026 2027" --SkipClean <true\|false> --clean --clean sets SkipClean to false and deletes build output first --Verbose [true\|false] -v, --verbose; -q, --quiet Terminal verbosity; quiet is the default --DryRun [true\|false] BuildBundle and BuildInstaller skip the bundle and print the ISCC command instead of running it --CandidateDistributionPath <dir> --candidate-dist Package an existing promoted tree --InnoSetupExe <path> Inno Setup compiler for BuildInstaller --Revit2026Dir <dir>, --Revit2027Dir <dir> Installed Revit, used only for validation --TestProjects <a,b> Projects for the selected-test targets An unknown option exits with status 2 before any SDK work. This includes the former NUKE options --target, --skip and --verbosity. build.sh exits with status 3 in a Windows shell (Git Bash, Cygwin) and names build.ps1. Build.proj validates the option values in its Initialize step: a boolean other than true or false fails before any target runs. Targets Target Result BuildAll Complete 2026/2027 build, validation and promotion to .artifacts/dist/Release BuildApp [-y <year>] App, Core, Presentation, HandyControl and the tool assemblies ValidatePrePush BuildApp plus manifest type validation BuildTests [-y <year>] Every test project and the hosted product inputs; all years by default BuildSelectedLocalTests, BuildSelectedPureTests, BuildSelectedDesignAutomationTests The projects named by --TestProjects in one test lane AssembleDistributionCandidate [-y <year>] A candidate year tree for checks that consume one; it is not published StagePortableAcceptanceInput Stage the candidate and Revit references for portable validation ValidateDistributionCandidate Portable validation and Dev Mode preflight of the candidate PackageSandboxValidationInput A content-addressed zip of the candidate and Sandbox for Windows validation PromoteToDist Replace the published distribution with the validated candidate BuildBundle Package the promoted tree into .artifacts/bundle/DBTools.bundle, one year tree per Revit year, under the Version.props product version BuildInstaller Build the bundle, then the installer with Inno Setup ValidateManifestTypes, VerifyArtifacts, BuildSandbox, BuildValidationRunner, Restore, Clean, Info Individual steps BuildAll, StagePortableAcceptanceInput, ValidateDistributionCandidate, PackageSandboxValidationInput, PromoteToDist, BuildBundle and BuildInstaller build the complete distribution. They require the Release configuration and the complete supported year set, which is the default; a -y that omits a supported year fails. ValidateDistributionCandidate and PromoteToDist also require a clean Git worktree. BuildBundle and BuildInstaller with --candidate-dist PATH package an existing promoted tree without building. --clean deletes build output; without it, an incremental BuildAll reuses the existing artifacts. No target switches to another SDK or output root. BuildAll depends on PromoteToDist, so it runs, in order: Restore, BuildValidationRunner (the Dev Mode policy runner), BuildApp for each year with ValidateProductVersions, VerifyArtifacts, StageDistributionCandidate, WriteCandidateMetadata, StagePortableAcceptanceInput, ValidateDistributionCandidate, ValidateManifestTypes and PromoteToDist. Examples ./build.sh BuildAll ./build.sh BuildAll --clean ./build.sh BuildApp --Configuration Debug --Years 2026 ./build.sh BuildTests ./build.sh BuildSelectedLocalTests --TestProjects DBTools.App.Local.Tests -y 2026 pwsh -NoProfile -File build.ps1 BuildAll Individual projects also build with plain dotnet build. Their MSBuild graph computes content versions and stages runtime prerequisites, but does not validate or publish a distribution. Implementation Each entry maps its options to MSBuild properties, acquires the pinned SDK, initializes the HandyControl submodule when needed, and runs Build.proj. A BUILD test checks that both entries produce the same dotnet build command line. No Build.proj target runs bash or Python, so BuildAll and BuildTests behave the same on Windows. Test execution is done by test.sh. Build.proj owns the target graph and starts each child dotnet build with its own binary log. The C# code of each target is a BuildPipelineStep in build/Tasks (DBTools.Build.Tasks, net8.0, loaded by the SDK's MSBuild on .NET 10). It owns option validation, Revit reference checks, Inno Setup discovery and the distribution steps. The task assembly is written to .artifacts/build-tasks/<Configuration>/ and recompiles only when its inputs change. Compilation on every operating system uses the centrally pinned Nice3point Revit API metadata packages with runtime assets excluded. An installed Revit is never a build prerequisite. --Revit2026Dir and --Revit2027Dir name an installation, native or mounted under WSL, for validation only. The staged Revit API files are reference metadata, not an executable runtime. APS Design Automation builds the separate Revit 2026 net8.0 Sentinel test project with its own API provider. Product output build/MSBuild/ProductOutput.proj and ProductOutput.targets stage this tree for each year in .artifacts/bin/Release/<year>/net10.0-windows/: <year>/ ├── DBTools.addin ├── DBTools.dll ├── DBTools.Core.dll ├── DBTools.Presentation.dll ├── DBTools.HandyControl.dll └── Tools/ └── DBTools.<Tool>.dll StageProductOutputTask keeps the Tools/ directory and validates each declared owner image. DBTools.addin names DBTools.dll and the class DBTools.App.Addin.AddinEntry. Intermediate runtime inputs can be year-keyed under .artifacts/bin/Release/<year>-runtime-input/. Local test staging copies the year tree recursively into the test output and removes stale top-level tool images. The installer receives the file list from DistributionContract.ProductFiles as the ISCC define ProductFiles and checks each year against it. Assembly merges build/Merging/AssemblyMerges.props declares one owner for each merged library; AssemblyMerge.targets runs the merge. Every merged library is private to its owner and absent from the year tree, including Tools/. Each owner is merged once per build; MSBuild Inputs and Outputs skip the merge when nothing changed. The merger writes a deterministic MVID and PDB, and version validation requires each stable assembly (Presentation, HandyControl) to have the same version and SHA-256 in every year. Owner Merged libraries DBTools.dll (App) ricaun.Revit.UI DBTools.Core DBTools.Manifest, YamlDotNet, CommunityToolkit.Mvvm, CSharpFunctionalExtensions, LibTessDotNet, Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection, .Logging, .Options, .Primitives, Serilog.Extensions.Logging DBTools.Presentation HelixToolkit and SharpDX assemblies, Cyotek.Drawing.BitmapFont, CommunityToolkit.Diagnostics, Serilog, Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions, Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Abstractions Serilog is in Presentation, which is never reloaded, because its thread-static state must not enter a collectible load context (dotnet/runtime#134928). The merge details are in Assembly Loading Contract. Content versions WPF resolves compiled resource URIs by assembly name and version, and Dev Mode identifies Presentation and HandyControl by full identity and SHA-256 hash. A content version therefore changes exactly when an assembly image can change. build/MSBuild/ContentVersion.targets computes it inside each ordinary compilation from these inputs: source, XAML and resource bytes, with the metadata that names, types and exposes each resource (Link, LogicalName, ManifestResourceName, Access, culture and generator metadata); resolved references: a package by its immutable coordinates, a project or local reference by its bytes, resolved before WPF markup compilation; source generators and the properties visible to them; the emitted assembly attributes, rendered as the SDK generates them, and the framework attribute; the signing key, Win32 manifest and resources, and the effective PathMap; the compiler options that change emitted code or metadata; for a merge owner, the merged project images and the merger code and binaries; for HandyControl, its vendor URI rewrite rules and the rewrite task's source (DBT_ContentVersionRule and DBT_ContentVersionInput). The content hash keys the rewrite, and a missing rewritten file reruns it. These are not inputs: build scripts and targets, .editorconfig and other analyzer configuration, diagnostic-only analyzers and warning options. Editing them changes no version. No Git commit or tree enters assembly attributes, content inputs or debug metadata. The computation runs inside the project's own compilation: it starts no second MSBuild evaluation and loads no other project. Because the inputs are hashed, resetting a source timestamp cannot hide changed bytes. A referenced content version is part of the referencing image, so consumers change version with it. An implementation-only change behind an unchanged version does not propagate through compiler references. The input list is written one entry per line to: .artifacts/obj/content-version/<Configuration>/<year|shared>-<flavor>/<project>/<framework>/inputs.txt The SHA-256 of the list is the input hash. Its first six bytes give the four-part assembly version: 4.<u16(bytes 0..1) % 65535>.<u16(bytes 2..3) % 65535>.<u16(bytes 4..5) % 65535> AssemblyInformationalVersion is <version>+inputs.<hash>. Compare two input lists to see why a version changed. Identical inputs keep the same identity and output timestamps. Content versions apply to Presentation, HandyControl, Core, App and projects that set DBT_IsToolAssembly=true. Other product metadata uses the release version from Version.props. Checked-in files are named relative to the repository root and artifacts relative to a relocatable root, so a fresh clone gives the same versions. Repository source and intermediate PDB documents use the path prefix /_/dbtools/; transformed vendor documents use /_/dbtools/vendor-build/. SourceLink revision stamping is off. A WPF temporary project hashes its parent's input list, so local-type identities in BAML carry the final version. The staged year trees carry the version evidence: each first-party image has its content version and input hash, the version must derive from that hash, and a stable image must be byte-identical in every year. The staging step reads them before it validates the compiled resource URIs. Candidate validation and promotion Distribution validation walks each year tree recursively. It requires the exact relative file set with Tools/ as the only directory, and checks PE identities, source-derived versions, first-party reference identities, framework references, and the length and SHA-256 of every file. It also checks the add-in entry, commands, availability types, manifests, resources and ownership. A missing, extra, misnamed, misplaced or stale file fails the candidate. Manifest validation scans every manifest.yml under src/ and resolves module, command, availability and design-time ViewModel type names against the compiled images of each year. Every declared owner must resolve to Tools/<owner>.dll. BuildAll and ValidatePrePush run it. ValidateDistributionCandidate prints one Dev Mode preflight line per year: Revit <year> Dev Mode preflight: <n> failures, <m> warnings; outcome=<x> Promotion requires a clean Git worktree (tracked and untracked files) with a resolved HEAD. Three records describe a distribution: The build metadata (build.json) records the years, frameworks, the distribution fingerprint, the Git commit and tree IDs, the source versions, the hash of each product file and the Protocol package pin. The portable acceptance receipt, written by ValidateDistributionCandidate, records for each year the validated files, the Revit reference descriptors and the Dev Mode preflight result. The promotion receipt, .artifacts/dist/Release/promotion-receipt.json, embeds the acceptance receipt with the source snapshot and the distribution fingerprint. It contains no temporary staging paths; consumers validate it against the published tree. Promotion validates the staged candidate, its fingerprint, the exact year trees and the receipt. It then deletes the published .artifacts/build.json, replaces .artifacts/dist/Release with the validated tree, and writes build.json last. Read the distribution only after the build command exits successfully. When promotion prepares the new tree, each declared file whose SHA-256 equals the file at the same path in the current .artifacts/dist/Release becomes a hard link to that file; new and changed files are copied. An unchanged file therefore stays the same file across promotions, and a virus scanner that has scanned it (Windows Defender on a Dev Mode host) does not scan it again. If the platform refuses a link (different file system, no hard-link support, permission error), promotion logs the reason once at low importance and copies that file and all remaining files. No step writes into a published file. Point Dev Mode at .artifacts/dist/Release/<year> directly; a copy is a set of new files that the scanner scans again. Hosted test inputs Hosted staging builds one complete product tree for the selected year and includes it with relative paths unchanged, including the 14 tool assemblies in Tools/. Test assemblies, NUnit and adapter files, and companions are separate inputs. The input cache checks relative path, identity, length and hash before the daemon request is written. Test restore roots are per year: Local years restore separately, and Design Automation shares the 2026 root. The Pure root restores every Pure project against $(DBT_PureRevitYear) owners through static graph restore. NuGet keys package specifications by project path, so one root never mixes owner variants. See Test Pipeline. Pinned SDK build/DotNet/sdk.sh selects the SDK version from global.json. If no installed dotnet has that SDK, it uses the private root ~/.dotnet/pinned-sdk-<version>. A system dotnet with the pinned SDK is used as is. A build needs only the SDK. A net8.0 test host (the APS Design Automation Sentinel) also needs the .NET 8 runtime. sdk.sh pins that runtime version, because global.json cannot, and installs it only when such a host runs: test.sh requests it, or run bash build/DotNet/sdk.sh --test-host-runtime. On a system dotnet without the .NET 8 runtime, a net8.0 test host uses the private root. A package in the private root is valid only when its marker file, .dbt-complete-<package>-<version>, names its archive. To install a package, sdk.sh: checks the archive against the SHA-512 in Microsoft's release metadata; extracts it into a staging directory beside the root; renames the version directories into place; writes the marker. A version directory without a valid marker is replaced from the verified archive; one that already matches stays. The lock <root>.lock serializes installs across builds and worktrees, and a build that waited for the lock checks the markers again before it installs anything. The Linux installer requires Python 3.10 or later. build.ps1 uses the same root, SHA-512 check, marker and lock for the SDK without Python. It downloads the release metadata's dotnet-sdk-win-<arch>.zip and replaces a root without a valid marker as a whole. It installs no test-host runtime. Build servers DBT_BUILD_SERVERS sets the server mode for every wrapper invocation (build.sh, test.sh, the lane helpers and their child builds). DBT_MSBUILD_MAX_CPU_COUNT sets the graph build parallelism (default 2); the wrappers validate it and Build.proj passes it to its child builds. build.sh runs Build.proj itself without the MSBuild server; each child dotnet build uses the selected mode. 1 (default): the invocation owns one compiler server and one MSBuild server. Its scope ID, dbtools-scope-<owner pid>-<run id>, is the compiler pipe name, and <scope id>-msbuild is the MSBuild handshake salt. On every trapped exit, each server gets a shutdown request with a 30 s timeout; then every process the invocation still owns is terminated, the compiler by its exact -pipename: argument and MSBuild nodes by the exact salt in their environment. No process is matched by name. A starting invocation stops dbtools-scope servers whose owner process no longer exists; servers of a live owner are never touched. In one measurement on an 8 GB host, a clean two-year BuildApp took 229 s with the servers and 547 s without them, and used about 1.4 GB more peak memory. 0: no compiler server and no MSBuild server (UseSharedCompilation=false). Use this on hosts that admit builds by free memory. build.ps1 always uses mode 0, because the ownership checks read Linux /proc. Node reuse is off in both modes. Outside a wrapper, Directory.Build.props keeps the compiler server off. UseSharedCompilation is not a content-version input. build/Testing/check-build-server-lifecycle.sh <second-checkout> is a manual test with the real SDK. It covers a normal exit, a failed build, SIGTERM, SIGKILL followed by the next build's sweep, and a concurrent owner in another checkout. Logs Each run writes to .artifacts/build/<YYYYMMDD-HHmmssfff>-<pid>/, named by build.sh or build.ps1 (by Build.proj for a plain dotnet build). The folder holds the full plain-text console.log at detailed verbosity and one binary log per child build. When the build ends, successfully or not, the entry writes a completed marker and copies the log to .artifacts/build/console.log. Each run first prunes old folders. It keeps the ten newest completed folders, deletes folders that contain only a marker, deletes unmarked folders after 24 hours without activity, and skips folders whose process is still running. Test builds write .artifacts/build/test-matrix.binlog, replacing the previous one. The terminal shows per-step progress, errors, warnings, the Dev Mode preflight lines and the MSBuild summary. --verbose adds the child build output. The file log is always detailed. Directory layout Path Contents .artifacts/bin/<Configuration>/<Year>/<TFM>/ Compiler output; the shared bucket when no year is selected .artifacts/obj/ Intermediate output and content-version input lists .artifacts/vendor/<Configuration>/handycontrol/net10.0-windows/ HandyControl build output .artifacts/sandbox/<Configuration>/<year>/<TFM>/ Sandbox build output .artifacts/.staging/<build id>/distribution-candidate/Release/ Candidate distribution .artifacts/dist/Release/<year>/ Published distribution, with promotion-receipt.json in .artifacts/dist/Release/ .artifacts/build.json Build metadata of the published distribution .artifacts/bundle/, .artifacts/installer/ Bundle and installer .artifacts/build/ Run logs Directory.Build.props defines the output and object roots. WPF temporary projects (_wpftmp) get a separate intermediate path. The standard target framework is net10.0-windows; Design Automation uses net8.0-windows. Directory.Build.targets adds host warnings, project-reference routing, WPF designer fixes and product and test staging hooks. HandyControl HandyControl is built from the vendor/HandyControl submodule through build/HandyControl/DBTools.HandyControl.csproj. The project imports the four upstream shared .projitems files and the upstream resources, writes transformed intermediate copies that use the DBTools assembly name and versioned pack URIs, and compiles Shared/Themes/Theme.xaml as the theme. The upstream project-root Theme.xaml generated by its PreBuild step is not an input. A missing submodule, resource or transform input fails with its path. Concurrency Run one build or test command per worktree at a time. Concurrent builds need separate BaseArtifactsDir roots; sharing compiler or WPF output between roots is not supported. A nested test command reuses the build-server scope of its parent. build.sh, build.ps1 and test.sh take no lock and do not check free memory. Continuous integration The CI and Documentation workflows run only on manual dispatch, not on pushes or pull requests. CI mode build runs BuildAll; mode build-test also builds and runs the selected tests. The release workflow, triggered by a published release, builds and promotes the distribution and bundle on Linux, then runs only the Inno Setup compiler on Windows. The self-hosted Windows test runner consumes compiled test artifacts through test.sh and does not build the product. Source maps and CANON These checks are run by the pre-push hook and CI, not by any build target: python3 .agents/work/canon_source_maps.py writes one MAP.md beside each manifest. A map lists the current source tree, including untracked files that are not ignored, and labels test folders as test mirrors. --check recomputes the maps byte for byte (UTF-8, LF) and fails if one is stale. python3 .agents/work/canon_source_fidelity.py --gate checks folder and namespace agreement, type and file identity, repeated declarations, vocabulary and unresolved rulings for the declared source roots. Troubleshooting Problem Action dotnet or the pinned SDK is missing Run bash build/DotNet/sdk.sh. The .NET 8 runtime for the Design Automation Sentinel is missing Run bash build/DotNet/sdk.sh --test-host-runtime. HandyControl output is missing Run the build from a Git checkout with network access, so the entry can initialize the submodule. WPF designer output collides Build through the repository targets, so _wpftmp gets its own intermediate path. MSBuild task DLLs stay locked A wrapper killed past its exit trap leaves its servers running until the next wrapper invocation stops them. Run the command again. A focused build is slow Build the project or use BuildApp; keep BuildAll for the full distribution. See Project References, Test Pipeline, Assembly Loading Contract and Sandbox Validator.

developer-guide/architecture/immutable-c.title: GM Production Contracts | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/immutable-c.summary: GM Production Contracts These Global Mapper (GM) behaviors are performance or correctness requirements. Do not change them to make a test pass; a test that conflicts with one of them is usually out of date. Change a contract only as a deliberate product decision, and update this page with it. Paths are relative to src/Tools/Common/GM/. Usage index sampling cap Features/Usage/Revit/Operations/Indexing/UsageIndexSource.Families.cs, QuerySampleInstanceIdsBySymbol The usage index samples one family instance per family type (symbol), at most 2500 instances (MaxSampleInstances in UsageIndexSource.cs). It streams view-independent (model) instances first and returns as soon as it has 2250 samples. Only when the model instances give fewer than 2250 samples does it add view-owned instances of the active view, up to the cap. Unbounded iteration scales with views times instances: a project with 200 views and 50,000 instances stalls for minutes. One geometry pass per usage kind Features/Usage/Revit/Operations/Indexing/StyleMaterial/UsageStyleMaterialCollector.cs, QueryStyleMaterialUsageChunk Style and material usage are captured from the same sample. Instance geometry is requested once for styles and once for materials, both with IncludeNonVisibleObjects = true. Symbol geometry is requested only when the instance has no geometry. Style geometry uses the owning or active view; material geometry uses view-independent Fine detail. Sharing one geometry result between them changes coverage. The combined chunk shares element lookup and the traversal of family-dependent styles. One instance for parameter discovery Features/Families/Revit/FamilyScanner.ParameterNames.cs, QueryMappableParamNamesForFamily Parameter-name discovery reads the parameters of every type of the family and of one instance. Parameter definitions are family-level, so every instance has the same definitions; scanning more instances adds cost and no data. Deep scan runs only on request Features/DeepScan/Workflow/DeepScanWorkflow.cs A deep scan opens family documents with EditFamily, which takes seconds per family. It runs only from a user action: Scan Family on a family row, deep scan of all visible families, or deep scan of unscanned families with zero instances (after a confirmation). Background prewarm only reads the deep scan cache; it never starts a scan. See GM specification. Parameter discovery filter Revit/ParameterDiscovery/ParameterDiscoveryEligibility.cs Discovery excludes read-only parameters, built-in parameters (InternalDefinition with a valid BuiltInParameter) and blank definition names. It does not filter on UserModifiable, because Revit can report a parameter that the API can write as not user-modifiable. Removing the read-only or built-in filter offers parameters that cannot be written or should not be mapped. Adding a UserModifiable filter hides valid mapping targets. Simple style canonicalization UsageStyleMaterialCollector.RecordStyle; Features/Usage/Revit/Operations/Indexing/UsageIndexSource.StyleMaterial.cs, BuildStyleCanonicalizationMap Style usage records the raw style ID and its canonical projection ID only. Recording every equivalent alias multiplies dictionary insertions per geometry object without improving the result. Style maps built once per usage build UsageIndexSource.StyleMaterial.cs, BuildStyleMaterialUsageAsync Style canonicalization, category projection and object-style classification run once per usage build, and their results are passed to each chunk of 25 instances (UsageChunkSize). Rebuilding them per chunk repeats a full FilteredElementCollector scan for every chunk.

developer-guide/architecture/overview.ht.title: Architecture Overview | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/overview.ht.summary: Architecture Overview DBTools is a suite of Revit add-in tools. Revit loads one entry assembly, DBTools.dll, built from src/DBTools.App. App loads shared infrastructure from DBTools.Core.dll, stable WPF types from DBTools.Presentation.dll, and each tool from its own assembly in the Tools/ directory. flowchart TB Revit[Revit Host] -->|DBTools.addin| App[DBTools.dll / App] App --> Core[DBTools.Core.dll] App --> Presentation[DBTools.Presentation.dll] Presentation --> Handy[DBTools.HandyControl.dll] App -->|explicit path: Tools/| Tools[Tool assemblies] Core --> RevitAPI[Revit API] Components Project Assembly Responsibility src/DBTools.App DBTools.dll Revit entry point, startup and shutdown, service composition, ribbon, embedded tool manifests src/DBTools.Core DBTools.Core.dll Shared execution (call gate, transactions, safe execution), settings, logging, tool registry, manifest loading, tool assembly resolution src/DBTools.Presentation DBTools.Presentation.dll WPF resources, themes, controls and window shells that live for the whole Revit process build/HandyControl DBTools.HandyControl.dll Renamed build of the vendored HandyControl library src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool> DBTools.<Tool>.dll One tool: its module, commands, features and views src/DBTools.Sandbox Sandbox executable Candidate validator and UI development host that runs without Revit Presentation references only WPF and HandyControl. App, Core and the tools may reference Presentation. See Project References. Product tree Each supported Revit year has one directory: <year>/ ├── DBTools.addin ├── DBTools.dll ├── DBTools.Core.dll ├── DBTools.Presentation.dll ├── DBTools.HandyControl.dll └── Tools/ └── DBTools.<Tool>.dll (14 tool assemblies) The build merges every third-party runtime library into one owner assembly, so the directory contains no other DLLs. The same tree is used by the installer, hosted test staging, Sandbox and Dev Mode. See Assembly Loading Contract and Build Pipeline. Load contexts The installed add-in runs in Revit's default AssemblyLoadContext. For hosted tests and Dev Mode, the dbtools-daemon loads the product into its own context (ProductLoadContext or DevModeLoadContext). DBTools creates no load context of its own. App loads each tool assembly into the context that already holds DBTools.dll. Startup DBTools.App.Addin.AddinEntry implements IExternalApplication. OnStartup runs these steps in order: Idle check. If DBTOOLS_DAEMON_REVIT_ROLE is set and the entry assembly is in the default load context, the add-in sets the AppContext key DBToolsDaemon.IdleAddin:DBTools to the entry assembly's location and returns Succeeded without further work. OnShutdown then also returns immediately. This lets the daemon run a Revit that has the installed add-in while it tests its own copy. Callback scope. AppStartupBoundary (not inlined) enters ToolWindowCallbackScope, which suppresses ExecutionContext flow and sets contextual reflection to the entry assembly's load context. Runtime. App reads the Revit year from VersionNumber, creates the logging host and the service provider, and publishes them through AppRuntimeAccessor. Theme validation. ThemeValidator.ValidateOrThrow loads and freezes the theme dictionaries and lays out a probe control tree. Ribbon. App composes the ribbon from the embedded manifests. Background startup. App starts the local Revit task host and an asynchronous startup task that installs the Revit main-window owner provider and attaches tool hooks. Publication. App registers an Idling handler for failed-startup cleanup, then the deferred startup handlers (ApplicationInitialized and Idling), and publishes the started state. A failure in steps 3 to 6 cleans up what was created and returns Failed. A failure of the background task is cleaned up on the next Idling event. Failures that cannot reach the normal log are written to %APPDATA%\DBTools\Logs\DBTools.Fallback.log with BCL APIs only, so this log works before Core loads. Tools and commands Each tool has a manifest.yml that names its assembly, module type, commands and availability types. App embeds all manifests. At startup: ToolModuleCatalog loads and validates the embedded manifests once. The App registrar loads each declared assembly with ToolAssemblyResolver.LoadAssembly, which loads only <entry directory>/Tools/<name>.dll. The registrar creates each module, collects its settings, services, settings packs and hooks, checks ownership, and merges them into the App service collection. Manifests without a module register only ribbon items. ToolRegistry.MergeFrom validates every incoming tool and hook against the existing registrations before it changes anything, so a conflict leaves the registry unchanged. Duplicate internal names are rejected. The ribbon refers to each command by its assembly location and full type name. When a command runs, CommandPreflight checks, before any run scope exists, that its ribbon panel is enabled in Settings, that its availability type allows it, and that no active feature warning disables it. Only then does CommandContextFactory create the run scope with the command's execution profile. Settings-only and hook-only tools still have a manifest and a module. Services and scopes The App service provider holds application-lifetime services: logging, settings, hooks, ISafeExecutor, the tool registry and ribbon state. Each command run, modeless session or test opens a scope that holds the Revit run scope (IRevitRunScope), its IRevitCallGate, ITransactionRunner and ITransactionGroupService. Command, availability and window callbacks enter ToolWindowCallbackScope. Source layout Tool source is under src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool>/ with namespace root DBTools.<Tool>. Folders are named for what they own, for example App/, Features/, Domain/, Revit/, Settings/, Assets/ and Tests/. A tool has only the folders it needs. Generic folders such as Helpers, Models or Infrastructure are not used for production code. Supported years Desktop Revit 2026.5 and later, and Revit 2027, both target net10.0-windows. build/Distribution/RevitYearContract.cs defines the supported years. APS Design Automation tests use a separate Revit 2026 net8.0-windows profile. Build and validation build.sh (Linux, WSL) and build.ps1 (Windows) run build/Build.proj. BuildAll builds, validates and publishes the complete two-year distribution. BuildApp, BuildTests and test.sh build smaller graphs. See Build Pipeline and Test Pipeline. Distribution validation records the length and SHA-256 of every file in the candidate. These hashes identify what was built and tested. They do not authenticate assemblies at load time.

developer-guide/architecture/project-ref.title: Project References | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/project-ref.summary: Project References Desktop Revit 2026.5 and later, and Revit 2027, use one target framework, net10.0-windows. build/Distribution/RevitYearContract.cs and build/MSBuild/RevitTargetFrameworks.props define the supported years and their framework. Projects use $(DBT_RevitTargetFramework) and contain no year-specific framework conditions. Assemblies Project Assembly Role src/DBTools.App DBTools.dll Revit entry point, App lifecycle and host infrastructure, embedded tool manifests src/DBTools.Core DBTools.Core.dll Shared execution, settings, logging, tool registry, manifest loading, tool assembly resolution src/DBTools.Presentation DBTools.Presentation.dll Stable WPF resources, controls and window shells build/HandyControl DBTools.HandyControl.dll Renamed HandyControl build src/DBTools.Manifest merged into Core Portable manifest.yml parser (net8.0) for build tooling and validation src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool> DBTools.<Tool>.dll One tool: commands, features and tool services src/DBTools.Sandbox Sandbox executable Candidate validation and UI development without Revit Reference direction App references Core and Presentation. It embeds every src/Tools/**/manifest.yml as a resource and compiles no tool source. Core references Presentation and DBTools.Manifest. It references the Revit API where a shared capability needs it. Tools reference Core, and Presentation for their UI. Presentation references only WPF and HandyControl. It does not reference App, Core, tool types or the Revit API. Sandbox compiles against Core, Presentation and HandyControl without copying their runtime files, and loads them from the candidate year directory at run time. App owns the ricaun.Revit.UI compile reference; the merge folds its runtime into DBTools.dll. Add a third-party runtime dependency through a declared merge in build/Merging/AssemblyMerges.props, not through a copy step. See Assembly Loading Contract. Tool assemblies Set DBT_IsToolAssembly=true in a project that produces a shipped tool assembly. The build stages its output in the year's Tools/ directory and gives it a content-derived version. At run time App resolves the tool through ToolAssemblyResolver, which loads into the context of the App and Core root assembly. The same rule applies in the default context, in the daemon's ProductLoadContext and in DevModeLoadContext. Every manifest under src/Tools/ has its own assembly, including Settings, SGT and DialogSuppression. A tool assembly must not contain a copy of Core or of Presentation. Test references Pure projects use the ordinary compile and runtime graph of their lane. Revit-hosted Local projects receive the selected year's host references and the staged product tree with Tools/ intact. Hosted input generation keeps the product root separate from test assemblies and adapter dependencies. A project reference must not place product assemblies flat beside a test assembly: the product requires the year root and its Tools/ subdirectory. Keep a dependency's host or resource constraint in the project that owns it, and validate the resulting candidate tree. Do not add projects for unsupported frameworks or a second DBTools load context. See Assembly Loading Contract, Build Pipeline and Test Pipeline.

developer-guide/architecture/revit-execu.title: Revit Execution and Progress Overlay | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/revit-execu.summary: Revit Execution and Progress Overlay This guide captures the required execution flow for Revit API access and the progress overlay system used by DBTools tools. It summarizes the current contracts in code and shows practical do/don’t examples. Centralized runner responsibilities ToolCommand Owns the top-level Revit command entrypoint: public Execute validates Autodesk inputs and passes the non-null UIApplication to the package-visible ExecuteCore seam. ExecuteCore runs through ISafeExecutor, resolves CommandContextFactory from the live runtime, and invokes the protected RunAsync implementation hook with the one owning CommandContext. Keeps command helpers narrow: command subclasses resolve services from ICommandContext, whose inherited IAppRunScope exposes the scope's RevitRunScope and Resolve<T>() directly. Window-owning features compose ToolWindowFactory and invoke IToolWindowSession.ShowDialog() or Show() so the session owns reflection scope and retirement. Expected refusals throw Core's SafeExecutionRefusedException with a user-facing reason. SafeExecutor returns SafeExecutionStatus.Refused without failure surfacing or exception diagnostics. The Warning banner owns the single Warning log; executions without a banner log [Refused] {Name}: {Message}. ToolCommand still returns Revit Result.Cancelled. Unexpected exceptions retain the existing Error diagnostics and Error banner. IAppRunScopeFactory Composes the concrete App scope: App composition registers IAppRunScopeFactory after Core Revit services. CommandContextFactory consumes it and calls Create(...); the factory selects the profile-specific call gate, constructs RevitRunScope, and returns IAppRunScope, which owns scoped resolution and disposal. Profiles are the switch: InlineUi uses InlineRevitCallGate; QueuedModeless uses QueuedRevitCallGate. The profile determines whether Revit API calls run inline (modal) or are queued through the App-owned ExternalEvent host (modeless). Active-document verification Consumers that retain a launch document call GetVerifiedActiveDocument(...). The run scope rejects invalid expected or active documents and requires matching DocumentSessionKey values before it returns the active document. IRevitCallGate profiles Modal inline (InlineUi): InlineRevitCallGate checks every Action invocation-list member for an async state machine and rejects statically awaitable result types before validating context, then runs admitted callbacks immediately on the Revit UI thread. Use for modal commands and daemon-hosted Revit automation where Revit already owns the thread. Queued modeless (QueuedModeless): QueuedRevitCallGate applies the same admission before scheduling through the owned ExternalEvent host. Use for modeless windows or long-running flows that must be queued to the UI thread. Reference-typed results: Reference-typed multicast result delegates are rejected before invocation because ordinary multicast dispatch exposes only the final return value. After invocation, reference-typed results receive a runtime Task/ValueTask guard, including values erased behind interfaces. Nullable ValueTask result types are rejected statically; custom awaiter structs are not detected. When to use InlineUi vs QueuedModeless InlineUi: modal Revit commands or daemon-hosted Revit automation contexts that already run on the UI thread and do not require ExternalEvent/Idling pumping. QueuedModeless: modeless tool windows or long-running workflows that must marshal Revit API work onto the UI thread via the queued host. ITransactionRunner / ITransactionGroupService Resolve scoped transaction services from the App/command scope (context.Resolve<ITransactionRunner>() / context.Resolve<ITransactionGroupService>()) to ensure Revit API access is routed through the call gate and wrapped in proper transactions. IRevitRunScope owns only UIApplication, the call gate, document access, and disposal. TransactionRunner is explicitly built on top of IRevitCallGate and applies synchronous delegate/result-type admission before entering the gate or opening a transaction. Its reference-result awaitable guard executes inside the transaction body, before commit. This keeps transactions and UI-thread access consistent with Revit’s rules. ITransactionRunner exposes named active-document and explicit-document methods. Delegates receive RevitTransactionContext, which carries both UIApplication and Document without multiplying overloads by delegate shape. ITransactionGroupService exposes only the manual active-document lifecycle: BeginAsync(...), FinalizeAsync(...), IsActive, and IsGroupHealthyAsync(...). Callers that need guaranteed cleanup must own the try/catch/finally around FinalizeAsync(...) in the workflow that knows whether the group should commit or roll back. Trimmed surface: The old no-context RunAsync(...), UIApplication-specific transaction overloads, RunAtomicAsync*, BeginAsync(Document, ...), RunAsync(string, Document, ...), and RunAsync(Document, string, ...) overloads were removed as dead public contract or avoidable Revit API type exposure. Source: src/DBTools.Core/Revit/Execution/CallGate/CallGateDelegateValidator.cs:14-55 Source: src/DBTools.Core/Revit/Execution/CallGate/InlineRevitCallGate.cs:26-64 Source: src/DBTools.Core/Revit/Execution/CallGate/QueuedRevitCallGate.cs:38-100 Source: src/DBTools.Core/Revit/Transactions/TransactionRunner.cs:26-101 Prohibition: Revit API outside IRevitCallGate IRevitCallGate is the unified entry point for all Revit API access and enforces synchronous callbacks on the UI thread. Any direct Revit API usage outside the call gate risks invalid context exceptions or UI-thread violations. Execution context best practices (external refs) These are contextual practices aligned with Revit’s external API requirements and the current call-gate implementation. Modeless UI uses the owned ExternalEvent host. The queued gate marshals work to the Revit UI thread through one generation-owned native event and enters an explicit main-thread API scope inside its Execute callback. Use task-based wrappers to schedule synchronous Revit work (e.g., Revit.Async-style wrappers). The call gate rejects async-state-machine Actions and Task/ValueTask result shapes before scheduling, so keep asynchronous workflows outside the gate and in-gate delegates synchronous. Validate API context before inline execution. Inline execution uses the same API authority as queued execution. RevitHost supplies application data; the product determines authority, including after an awaited continuation in the driver callback. API-context admission and ExternalEvent probes RevitCallGateApiContext.IsActive is the product's API-context authority. Known native entry points use its internal synchronous Enter scope as a fast path. Untracked calls first check the Revit dispatcher, then create and immediately dispose an unraised ExternalEvent with a stateless no-op handler. Workers return false before the probe. Every untracked call probes again; no success or failure is cached across turns. Current exposes a known UIApplication only while the context is active. An ambient application reference is data, not authority. The public UIApplication constructor requires ApplicationServices.Application. There is no public conversion from UIControlledApplication.ControlledApplication. If startup has not received any UIApplication, queued work obtains it from the real ExternalEvent callback. No private-field reflection is used. The probe uses a fresh event rather than adding/removing a handler on a Revit event. It neither modifies the current event's subscriber collection nor writes a document, so it avoids the same-event subscription restriction and document-write restrictions in Idling, ViewActivated, DocumentChanged and updater callbacks. API admission still does not grant permission to use an API forbidden in a particular callback; callers must respect read-only and dynamic-update restrictions. The 2026 and 2027 API references list the Create signature and null-handler exception, but omit its outside-context exception. An Autodesk support discussion records that runtime check and distinguishes UI-thread access from API authority. The choice of allocation over subscription follows these API boundaries; the references do not separately certify every callback combination. The probe does not distinguish add-in ownership. When it succeeds inside another add-in's main-thread API callback, it returns true and DBTools runs inline without an explicit DBTools scope, matching ricaun's routing. DBTools-owned callback entries use an explicit synchronous UIApplication scope, and later continuations must probe or queue again. The scope is a ref struct, so a caller cannot hold it across an await. Its shared lifetime lets even an unsafe wrong-thread disposal revoke the original authority before reporting the misuse. Enter stays internal: App's linked native callbacks and FoundationTags' standalone Idling owner need access. GM's existing friendship supports synchronous-delegate validation, and GM does not enter scopes. The hosted certification fixture (RevitCallGateApiContextHostedCertificationTests) exercises real ViewActivated, DocumentChanged, FailuresProcessing, and IUpdater.Execute callbacks through real transactions and view activation. It always opens and activates the staged GM model, restores the original view, and rolls back the temporary view. The host retains the staged active document until Revit closes. It cannot certify OnShutdown while the daemon keeps the whole NUnit run inside one Revit callback; the RevitHostedTurns lane certifies modeless false results (RevitCallGateModelessHostedTurnCertificationTests) and native Idling delivery to App's deferred-startup subscription (AppDeferredStartupSubscriptionHostedTurnTests). Only an untracked main-thread admission allocates and disposes an unraised ExternalEvent per authority check; explicit scopes avoid that probe cost, and workers return false before probing. Each native Execute turn runs, in FIFO order, every queued item that was waiting when the turn started, so N waiting calls cost one Revit round trip instead of N. Items queued during the turn wait for the next turn, and after the first item a turn starts no new item once its 50 ms budget is used, so an expanding queue cannot monopolize that turn. A failed or canceled item completes its own task and the turn continues with the next item. An item that leaves a transaction open in any document ends the turn: Revit discards what a callback leaves open only when the callback returns, so the next item waits for a later turn instead of running inside it. A transaction group without an open transaction is invisible to that check, so every production member that creates a TransactionGroup also calls RevitCallGateTurnBoundary.EndAfterCurrentCall(), which ends the turn after its call. TransactionGroupTurnBoundaryContractTests (Build tests) fails when a construction lacks it. Nested Auto calls stay inline while ForceQueue explicitly defers to a future turn. The probe never raises its event and therefore does not claim that Revit dispatched a later native turn. The owned scheduler posts every raise to the Revit dispatcher at Normal priority, also when the caller is already on the dispatcher thread. A caller therefore never waits on native Raise, a burst of calls shares one raise, and the raise for work left after a turn runs after Execute returns instead of inside Revit's own handler. Denied and TimedOut responses retain the queue and retry with 50–500 ms backoff for at most five seconds. Expiry faults that waiting batch; the scheduler accepts new work. Each turn feeds a throttled Debug summary ([CallGate/Turns]): turns and calls, maximum queue depth, the Raise-to-Execute gap, Execute duration, native Raise duration and results, and refused-raise retries. It is written when a turn leaves the queue empty, at most once per second, or after 10 s of a queue that stays busy; turns inside the one-second interval are reported with the next activity. Retirement aborts its posted raise, stops and detaches its retry timer, releases queued delegates, and disposes its native event. Dropped tasks never complete; a worker synchronously waiting on one would hang. Failed-startup cleanup uses cancellation instead because Revit and its callers remain alive. Progress overlay usage Host requirements Host tool views through ToolWindowFactory and IToolWindowSession. The stable modal/modeless shells expose the WPF owner contract. Core installs WindowInitializer before raw XAML loads and retires its lifecycle state with the session. For tool-specific windows, bind overlay ownership explicitly with ProgressOverlay.For(this, logger) so state, dispatcher affinity, and diagnostics remain tied to that host window. The logger is required at this runtime boundary; composition supplies the owner logger rather than routing through a fallback. Scope and dispatcher rules Always use Scope(...) for long operations. Nested scopes are state-local to the owner-bound overlay and clean up in LIFO order. Show/Update/Hide are UI-dispatched. ProgressOverlay marshals public calls to its owner's WPF dispatcher, so callers should use the overlay API and avoid touching overlay state directly from background threads. Status transitions force a render pump. Update(...) delegates state mutation to OverlayState.ApplyUpdate(...), where status-string changes call RequestRender(force: true) and progress-only updates remain throttled (force: false). This keeps short phase changes visible under Revit dispatcher starvation without removing global throttles. Overlay render flushing is guarded and throttled. RequestRender still schedules a render callback, and uses a single-frame pump helper (TryPumpSingleFrame) with a depth guard and short time budget to restore incremental visual updates without unbounded re-entrancy. Under Revit-hosted dispatcher starvation, the queued callback that clears the pending-render flag can be delayed; forced renders (step transitions) bypass the pending guard, and a stuck-pending timeout allows recovery when the dispatcher is slow. Overlay responsibilities are owner-bound. ProgressOverlay.Hosts.cs is the single Window-to-OverlayState lifecycle and visual-host registry; ProgressOverlay.Operations.cs exposes the public lifecycle API; Runtime/ProgressOverlayRunWorkflow.cs owns RunAsync(...) show policy, linked CTS lifecycle, cancel polling, watcher observation, and hide sequencing. There is no ambient or process-global host selection. Coverage expectation: cheap IProgressOverlay doubles can stay in pure/view-model tests, but production overlay behavior belongs in a local WPF/Revit-hosted lane. GM's local shell fixture directly exercises ProgressOverlay.For(...) visual-host injection and RunAsync(...) cancellation bridging with a real WPF dispatcher instead of RecordingOverlay. Cancel handling Prefer RunAsync(...) so the overlay owns cancellation bridging. ProgressOverlayRunWorkflow polls CancelRequested, cancels a linked CTS, and hands the work delegate a token that fires on cancel — so long-running operations should run their work through RunAsync(...) rather than hand-rolling a watcher. SGT placement (PlacementCommandService) and GM commit-review both use this API. Poll CancelRequested and bridge to your CTS only when not using RunAsync(...). The overlay exposes a thread-safe CancelRequested property; workflows that still drive their own Scope(...) (for example SGT analysis) bridge it into operation cancellation manually. Do/Don’t examples (from current code) Call gate usage Do: queue modeless work with synchronous delegates. await _gate.RunAsync(app => { // Revit API work here (sync only) return true; }); This aligns with QueuedRevitCallGate.RunAsync(...), which admits only synchronous result shapes before marshalling to the Revit UI thread. Don’t: use an async-void Action or return Task, Task<T>, ValueTask, or ValueTask<T> from a call-gate delegate. These shapes are rejected before the delegate can start. Progress overlay scope Do (SGT): create a scope and poll cancel status. using var scope = _overlay.Scope(ProgressScopeAnalyze, cancelable: true); _overlay.Update(ProgressCalibratingFamilies, 0.0); if (_overlay.CancelRequested) { linkedCts.Cancel(); } SGT’s analysis workflow creates a scope, updates it, and bridges cancel requests into the analysis CTS. Do (GM): use Scope(...) and CancelRequested while applying mappings. using var scope = _overlay.Scope("Applying mappings...", true); if (_overlay.CancelRequested) { _cts.Cancel(); } GM's commit review view model follows this pattern to keep UI cancel actions responsive during long operations. Don’t: manipulate overlay state directly or bypass the dispatcher. Use Show/Update/Hide/Scope so the overlay stays UI-thread safe. Nested Scope(...) calls restore the parent state held by the same owner-bound overlay in LIFO order when the inner scope ends. After Show(...) resets the previous cancellation state, the cancel watcher starts its delay before the operation body begins, so normal cleanup observes one already-started watcher rather than a scheduling race. Source: src/DBTools.Core/Progress/Overlay/Runtime/ProgressOverlay.Operations.cs Source: src/DBTools.Core/Progress/Overlay/Runtime/ProgressOverlayRunWorkflow.cs Phase 2: Granular progress primitives Tuple progress payload Phase 2 migrated tool-level progress from IProgress<string> to IProgress<(string message, double? progress01)>. This allows tools to emit both a status message and a numeric 0..1 progress fraction in a single report, enabling smoother overlay bar updates. Affected interfaces: IMappingService.ApplyPlanAsync — GM mapping engine IOrchestrator.PlaceAsync / UpdateAsync — SGT orchestrator IPlacementWriter.PlaceAsync / UpdateAsync — SGT domain writer MonotonicProgressAdapter Wraps an IProgress<(string, double?)> and enforces monotonic non-decreasing progress01 values. Status-only updates (null progress01) are forwarded without affecting tracking. Create one instance per logical run. Both the adapter and overlay reject NaN and infinities before publishing an update. Finite values still clamp to [0,1]. A rejected adapter report does not change its monotonic tracking. Overlay admission occurs before either status or progress changes. var adapter = new MonotonicProgressAdapter( new Progress<(string message, double? progress01)>(update => _overlay.Update(update.message, update.progress01))); await _mapping.ApplyPlanAsync(plan, adapter, ct); MappingChangeContext helper updates (GM) MappingChangeContext.ReportProgress(message) now accepts an optional double? progress01 parameter. The 3-arg ReportProgress(stageName, current, total) overload has been renamed to ReportProgressStage(stageName, current, total, progress01?) for clarity. Per-tool overlay integration Tool Progress source Overlay mapping GM MappingPlanExecutor emits writer-level (writerIndex/totalActiveWriters) MonotonicProgressAdapter in CommitReviewViewModel TDV Transfer executor reports per-view stage percents (0, 10, 25, 35, 60, 85, 100) TdvWindowViewModel.UpdateTransferOverlayProgress maps them through six weighted stages SGT PlacementExecutionService.PlaceAsync / UpdateAsync emit wall-level + sub-step progress MonotonicProgressAdapter in ShellWindowViewModel RecordSet PlanExecutor emits per-item status + int percent VM combines status and percent in overlay update Note: RecordSet intentionally uses IProgress<int> (percentage) rather than the tuple pattern. This is because RecordSet's PlanExecutor uses a weight-based percentage calculation internally, and the VM combines the separate status log stream with the integer percentage for overlay updates. This approach avoids additional refactoring of the executor's internal progress model while still achieving the same overlay UX. Common failure modes Dispatcher errors or missing host: calling overlay APIs without a window initialized by Core WindowInitializer, or bypassing the overlay API, can lead to dispatcher errors or missing state. Always use Scope/Show/Update/Hide on a supported Presentation window host. Revit context leaks: direct Revit API access outside IRevitCallGate or attempting async delegates inside the gate can lead to invalid context errors. Stick to the call gate + transaction runner, and keep delegates synchronous. Re-entrant UI pumping risk during active Revit execution: progress overlay updates now use a bounded single-frame pump with depth guards; avoid introducing additional custom pump loops or unguarded dispatcher-frame usage outside this shared helper.

developer-guide/architecture/sandbox-val.title: Sandbox Validator | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/sandbox-val.summary: Sandbox Validator DBTools.Sandbox validates one staged product year without Revit.
