In headless mode it checks the candidate files, metadata and manifests. On Windows it also builds the real tool windows and checks themes, layout, bindings and Dispatcher cleanup. It is also a host for developing tool UI with design-time view models. Synopsis DBTools.Sandbox [--headless] [--dist-dir DIR] [--revit-reference-dir DIR] Option Description --headless Run static and metadata validation without creating windows. Requires --revit-reference-dir. --dist-dir DIR A year directory (for example .artifacts/dist/Release/2026) or a distribution root that contains year directories. Default: .artifacts/dist/Release of the repository that contains the executable, else of the current directory. --revit-reference-dir DIR Revit reference metadata for the year, checked against the installed runtime. Valid only with --headless. Both --option VALUE and --option=VALUE are accepted. An empty value, an unknown argument or a missing value is an error. Without --headless, Sandbox runs interactively against the installed Revit runtime. WSL paths of the form /mnt/<drive>/... are converted to Windows paths. Example, after ./build.sh BuildAll: dotnet run --project src/DBTools.Sandbox/DBTools.Sandbox.csproj -- \ --headless --dist-dir .artifacts/dist/Release/2026 \ --revit-reference-dir /path/to/Revit2026 The exit status is 1 when validation fails before WPF starts; the error is written to standard error. Process model Each year runs in a new process in the default load context: SandboxEntry uses only BCL types. It parses the options, resolves the year directory and runs SandboxCandidate.Validate. A non-inlined method prepares the Revit runtime resolver and loads HandyControl, Presentation, Core, App and the manifest-declared tools from their candidate paths. A second non-inlined method starts the WPF application. The JIT compiles this call only after the candidate assemblies are loaded, so Core and WPF cannot resolve from anywhere else first. The process exits after validation, so no assembly of one candidate stays loaded for another year. Sandbox creates no load context, does not run App's Revit startup, does not load Revit reference files as product assemblies and does not probe subfolders other than Tools/. Candidate contract Relative path Content DBTools.addin Add-in manifest naming DBTools.dll and DBTools.App.Addin.AddinEntry DBTools.dll App entry DBTools.Core.dll Core DBTools.Presentation.dll Stable WPF assembly DBTools.HandyControl.dll Renamed HandyControl Tools/DBTools.<Tool>.dll The 14 tool assemblies SandboxCandidate checks the add-in file, the top-level files, the flat Tools/ directory, the PE simple names, and conflicts with assemblies already loaded in the process. No third-party DLL may be present. Validation sequence Resolve the year directory and the optional Revit reference directory. Check DBTools.addin, the exact top-level files, the recursive Tools/ files, the supported year and framework, and the PE simple names. Read the App, Core, Presentation, HandyControl and tool references and their source-derived versions from PE metadata, without loading Revit API assemblies. Discover the embedded manifests and validate module, command, availability, icon, raw XAML and design-time view model ownership. On Windows (not --headless), load the resources and themes, build each window, run layout and interaction checks, capture binding errors, close every window and verify Dispatcher cleanup. Portable validation of a distribution archive checks the same file set and also file lengths and SHA-256 hashes. Components Component Responsibility SandboxEntry BCL-only option parsing, year selection, candidate check and the non-inlined WPF start SandboxCandidate Candidate files, direct image loading, PE identity and loaded-image path checks SandboxDistributionContext References to the candidate's App, Core, Presentation, HandyControl and tool assemblies and manifests ManifestValidator Manifest owners, commands, availability types, raw resources and design-time view models AssemblyMetadataInspector PE metadata and reference identities, read from bytes without running Revit code HeadlessValidationWorkflow The headless sequence and its structured result ToolWindowValidator Window construction, layout, interaction, binding errors and cleanup The portable manifest rules are in testing/DBTools.Distribution.Validation/Manifest/PortableToolManifestValidator.cs. Tool window registration A tool lists its Sandbox windows in manifest.yml: sandboxWindows: - id: DBTools.MyTool.Main displayName: "My Tool" group: "Common" xamlResource: "DBTools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolView.xaml" windowKind: Modal designTimeViewModelType: "DBTools.MyTool.App.DesignTime.MyToolDesignTimeViewModel" designTimeViewModelAssembly: "DBTools.MyTool" designTimeViewModelVisibility: Public windowKind is Modal or Modeless. SandboxCatalog (Core) reads these entries into window specifications, and Sandbox hosts each raw view in the stable Presentation ToolWindowHost. No candidate Window type crosses between assemblies. Validation requires, for each entry: a nonempty id, displayName, group, xamlResource, designTimeViewModelType and designTimeViewModelAssembly; an EmbeddedResource in the owning project with exactly that LogicalName; a root element that derives from FrameworkElement and is not a Window; the host supplies the window shell; no x:Class, x:ClassModifier or x:FieldModifier, no code-behind event attributes, no CLR namespaces of the tool assembly, no implicit templates for tool types, no inferred DataGrid columns and no pack URIs into the tool assembly; a concrete design-time view model whose visibility matches designTimeViewModelVisibility (Public or Internal) and that has a parameterless constructor (public for Public); Sandbox invokes it. It should hold fixed display data and use no Revit, network or settings services. Tool code can check DBTools.Core.Sandbox.SandboxMode.IsActive to avoid services that do not exist in Sandbox. Every manifest command type must implement IExternalCommand and every availability type IExternalCommandAvailability, in the declared owner assembly under Tools/. Window checks ToolWindowValidator opens each raw view through ToolWindowHost with its design-time view model and then: measures and arranges the window at a fixed size and at infinite size; selects every tab of each TabControl and restores the original tab; shows the row details of the first three rows of each nonempty DataGrid, except grids whose details are VisibleWhenSelected; records WPF binding errors; closes the window and waits for a bounded ApplicationIdle Dispatcher barrier. It fails when the Dispatcher is missing, shutting down or aborted, or when a cleanup operation is still pending after the barrier. Build output and archives Sandbox is built once per year, although both years use the same framework: .artifacts/sandbox/<Configuration>/<year>/<TFM>/ build output sandbox/<year>/<sanitized-tfm>/ path inside the validation archive ./build.sh PackageSandboxValidationInput writes a content-addressed validate-dist-<sha256>.zip with the candidate and Sandbox. The DIST suite consumes that archive and writes a structured result JSON (see Test Pipeline). The archive and the result keep normalized relative paths. A passing headless or Linux result covers files and metadata only; native WPF behavior requires the Windows run. Daemon Dev Mode injection and reload are tested separately. Troubleshooting Failure Where to look Candidate file missing or extra ProductOutput staging and DistributionContract .addin entry mismatch build/Installer/DBTools.addin and the App output Tool assembly missing The manifest assembly name and Tools/ staging Raw XAML resource missing EmbeddedResource LogicalName in the owning project Design-time view model cannot be created Its visibility, designTimeViewModelVisibility and parameterless constructor Binding errors Explicit bindings and the stable Presentation templates Layout failure ToolWindowValidator measure and arrange messages Cleanup timeout Dispatcher and window owner lifetime A window failure reports both the primary exception and any cleanup exception. See Sandbox Integration, Assembly Loading Contract and Test Pipeline.

developer-guide/architecture/structural-.title: Structural Preview | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/structural-.summary: Structural Preview DBTools.Presentation.StructuralPreview is the stable WPF host for the structural 3D preview shared by ERFT and SGT. A tool adapter supplies immutable scene data and receives pointer events. The host owns the Helix viewport, effects manager, camera, navigation, materials, hit testing, tooltip, overlay markers and cleanup. Helix and SharpDX are merged into Presentation as internal types; no tool assembly or raw view names them. ERFT and SGT register the presenter's disposal with their tool-window sessions. The component has no Core, App or tool-assembly dependency. Its public scene records contain only immutable arrays, System.Numerics values, strings, integers and scalar values. Attach and dispose Call StructuralPreview3DFactory.Attach on the viewport host dispatcher. The ContentControl must be empty. The optional overlay canvas must use the same dispatcher. The returned IStructuralPreview3D owns one viewport and one effects manager. All presenter methods and disposal are synchronous UI-thread operations. Attach returns a disabled presenter without loading or creating Helix objects when StructuralPreview3DOptions.Disabled is true, and returns one with the load error as its reason when the Helix libraries cannot be loaded. The disabled presenter still validates and copies supplied scene and emphasis data, reports its status reason, returns false from projection, and can be disposed repeatedly. For an available presenter, Dispose removes viewport, camera, owner-window, timer and input handlers; closes the tooltip; removes only the overlay children created by this presenter; disposes owned scene elements, viewport and effects manager; clears scene data and subscriber events; and clears the host content only when that content is still the viewport owned by this presenter. Cleanup is synchronous and does not post a dispatcher frame. Disposal clears subscriptions before cleanup, so it publishes zero presenter events during or after disposal. Repeated disposal is safe. Scene data and picks SetScene validates and deep-copies the supplied records and arrays. The caller may then release or reuse its own objects. Equal mesh geometry keeps existing Helix models; geometry or appearance changes update the rendered decorations and materials, while bounds or exterior-normal changes update camera state. Mesh Opacity supplies the material alpha and overrides the alpha byte in Argb. Line sets multiply their ARGB alpha by Opacity. Selection and hover colors preserve the mesh opacity. Mesh picking is independent of emphasis. A mesh is eligible for a hit only when its supplied IsPickable value is true; context meshes can therefore be pickable or non-pickable independently of their material role. A floor is supplied as scene geometry, normally a context mesh with IsPickable: false. Line sets and non-pickable meshes do not produce mesh hits. A missed hit has null mesh ID, null context ID and null world point. A hit's mesh and context hits are resolved independently: each is the nearest eligible hit for its role. MeshId is the nearest member ID, or null when there is no member hit; ContextId is the nearest context ID independently. WorldPoint is the nearest member hit point when one exists, otherwise the context hit point, so a context-only hit has a null mesh ID and a context world point. The event also carries WPF screen coordinates relative to the viewport and keyboard modifiers. SetEmphasis accepts one emphasis state per mesh ID. The presenter applies selection, segment-selection, sibling, dimmed and hover material policies from the selected StructuralPreviewPalette. StructuralPreviewPalette.Sgt and .Erft are the adapter presets. They differ in member color boost, surfaces, selection and hover colors, and edge and outline settings, and use the same renderer. The presenter adds a pivot marker to the supplied overlay canvas while orbiting. The marker and all generated WPF objects have their data context cleared or blocked so tool data contexts do not flow into the stable visual tree. Home views and camera movement The ExteriorThreeQuarter strategy is the SGT home view. When bounds or the exterior normal changes, the session recomputes and stores a raw Home camera. Its exact formula is: distance = max(2.2 * boundsDiagonal, 8) yaw = 28 degrees pitch = 0.22 downward along the configured up axis The exterior normal is projected onto the up plane. A missing horizontal normal uses negative Y as the stable fallback. The stored Home keeps this exact distance. Clamping applies to the displayed camera only. If the user has moved the camera, a changed scene clamps the current camera and retains the new raw Home for a later reset. Reset clears the moved flag, applies Home, and clamps the displayed camera. ERFT uses the PreserveAngle strategy. When bounds change, the session fits the current view angle and captures that result as Home. The fit formula is: halfV = radians(fieldOfView) / 2 halfH = atan(tan(halfV) * aspect) distance = max(boundsDiagonal / 2 / sin(min(halfV, halfH)), 2) * 1.2 Helix FieldOfView is the vertical angle. The fit keeps the bounds' bounding sphere inside both the vertical and the horizontal field of view, so the whole scene is visible at the viewport aspect when the fit runs; the distance clamp still applies. Scene constraints use the Core bounds-only constants: diagonal = actualDiagonal, or 10 when actualDiagonal <= 1e-6 min = clamp(diagonal * 0.0005, 0.005, 0.75) max = clamp(diagonal * 40, min * 2, 50000) targetPad = max(2, diagonal * 6) near = max(0.0005, min * 0.05) far = max(100, max * 2) When a scene changes mesh geometry without changing these bounds, the presenter keeps the stored Home object and only updates its owned render models. Adapters must compute bounds from every mesh vertex so a real extent change is reported as a bounds change; a bounds change is an intentional Home refit under PreserveAngle. ZoomToFit performs the exact fit. When FitRedefinesHome is enabled, the fitted camera becomes Home and the viewport default camera is updated to the same pose; otherwise the fit marks the camera as user-moved while preserving Home. ResetView restores stored Home. Pan uses screen-space camera axes, orbit uses the configured arbitrary up axis around the selected or picked pivot, and wheel zoom moves toward the picked world anchor. Gesture cancellation occurs on lost capture, window deactivation, unload and disabled interaction. The viewport's native view cube handles its own preview input before scene picking. The presenter keeps the default camera synchronized with stored scene Home when a scene is attached; an explicit fit also updates it when FitRedefinesHome is enabled. Input and hover StructuralPreview3DOptions.ShowTooltips defaults to true. It enables the stable presenter's mesh tooltips. When disabled, pointer updates keep the tooltip closed. Materials and lighting Adapters choose StructuralPreviewPalette.Sgt or .Erft and can copy the record to adjust individual values. A palette supplies member and context surfaces, key/fill/rim/ambient light colors, sibling and dimmed policies, selection and hover colors, emissive scaling, edge colors and thickness, outline mode and pivot colors. IsPickable controls hit testing. A non-pickable context mesh remains rendered with its base context material but bypasses selection, segment-selection, sibling, dimmed and hover emphasis; pickable context meshes can receive context hover, sibling and dimmed states but never member selection states. The SGT preset uses these alpha rules. Sibling emphasis scales diffuse alpha by 0.70 and retains the source ambient, specular and emissive alpha. Dimmed emphasis sets every channel's alpha to max(0.05, sourceAlpha * 0.45). Hovering a sibling restores the base material and adds emissive brightness while preserving its source alpha. Hovering a dimmed mesh adds emissive brightness and retains the dimmed alpha. The default options select the SGT palette and exterior home strategy. ERFT selects both its palette and its camera strategy: var options = new StructuralPreview3DOptions { Palette = StructuralPreviewPalette.Erft, HomeView = StructuralPreviewHomeView.PreserveAngle }; Diagnostics and projection Diagnostic reports debug, warning and error messages as plain strings with an optional exception. Repeated identical diagnostic messages are suppressed for two seconds. An initialization or disabled-path diagnostic is delivered once to the first diagnostic subscriber; the reason is also available in Status. Event publication takes an invocation-list snapshot and stops when a callback disposes the presenter. No presenter event is raised after Dispose clears subscriptions. On the first render failure, the presenter changes to Unavailable, disables interaction, cancels navigation, clears hover state, stops its clamp timer and collapses the viewport. It reports that failure as an error diagnostic, subject to the two-second diagnostic de-duplication; later render failures are ignored while the presenter is unavailable. TryProjectToViewport returns false when the presenter is unavailable, disposed, unloaded, has no render context, receives a non-finite point, has an invalid camera or the point is behind the camera. It returns WPF device- independent coordinates relative to the viewport on success. Projection failures are reported as debug diagnostics and never escape as exceptions. Public API The following declarations are the public API. Rendering records remain in DBTools.Presentation.StructuralPreview.Rendering; configuration and events remain in DBTools.Presentation.StructuralPreview. public static class StructuralPreview3DFactory { public static IStructuralPreview3D Attach( ContentControl viewportHost, Canvas? overlay, StructuralPreview3DOptions options); } public interface IStructuralPreview3D : IDisposable { bool IsAvailable { get; } StructuralPreview3DStatus Status { get; } event EventHandler? StatusChanged; event EventHandler<StructuralPreviewPointerEventArgs>? Clicked; event EventHandler<StructuralPreviewPointerEventArgs>? HoverChanged; event EventHandler<StructuralPreviewDiagnosticEventArgs>? Diagnostic; void SetScene(StructuralScene3D? scene); void SetEmphasis(StructuralEmphasis emphasis); void SetInteractive(bool active); void ResetView(); void ZoomToFit(); bool TryProjectToViewport(Vector3 world, out Point viewportPoint); } public sealed record StructuralPreview3DOptions { public Vector3 UpAxis { get; init; } = Vector3.UnitZ; public double FieldOfView { get; init; } = 45; public int Msaa { get; init; } = 4; public bool EnableSsao { get; init; } = true; public bool ShowViewCube { get; init; } = true; public bool ShowTooltips { get; init; } = true; public StructuralPreviewHomeView HomeView { get; init; } = StructuralPreviewHomeView.ExteriorThreeQuarter; public bool FitRedefinesHome { get; init; } public StructuralPreviewPalette Palette { get; init; } = StructuralPreviewPalette.Sgt; public bool Disabled { get; init; } public string? DisabledReason { get; init; } } public enum StructuralPreviewHomeView { ExteriorThreeQuarter, PreserveAngle } public sealed record StructuralPreview3DStatus( StructuralPreview3DState State, string? Reason = null); public enum StructuralPreview3DState { Ready, Unavailable, Disposed } public enum StructuralPreviewDiagnosticLevel { Debug, Warning, Error } public sealed class StructuralPreviewDiagnosticEventArgs( StructuralPreviewDiagnosticLevel level, string message, Exception? exception = null) : EventArgs { public StructuralPreviewDiagnosticLevel Level { get; } = level; public string Message { get; } = message; public Exception? Exception { get; } = exception; } public sealed class StructuralPreviewPointerEventArgs( string? meshId, string? contextId, Point screenPoint, Vector3? worldPoint, ModifierKeys modifiers) : EventArgs { public string? MeshId { get; } = meshId; public string? ContextId { get; } = contextId; public Point ScreenPoint { get; } = screenPoint; public Vector3? WorldPoint { get; } = worldPoint; public ModifierKeys Modifiers { get; } = modifiers; } public enum StructuralPreviewOutlineMode { CreaseEdges, AllEdges } public sealed record StructuralPreviewSurface( Vector3 Ambient, Vector3 Specular, float EmissiveFactor, float Shininess = 30); The palette declaration exposes the following complete public surface: public sealed record StructuralPreviewPalette { public static StructuralPreviewPalette Sgt { get; } public static StructuralPreviewPalette Erft { get; } public float MemberColorBoost { get; init; } = 0.18f; public uint BackgroundArgb { get; init; } = 0xFF1E1E28; public Vector4 KeyLightColor { get; init; } = Vector4.One; public Vector4 FillLightColor { get; init; } = new(0.9f, 0.9f, 1f, 1f); public Vector4 RimLightColor { get; init; } = new(0.4f, 0.4f, 0.5f, 1f); public Vector4 AmbientLightColor { get; init; } = new(0.3f, 0.3f, 0.35f, 1f); public StructuralPreviewSurface MemberSurface { get; developer-guide/architecture/test-pipeli.title: Test Pipeline | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/test-pipeli.summary: Test Pipeline DBTools tests run through one of two routes: ./test.sh resolves the selected projects, builds them, freezes their inputs and runs them locally or submits them to the dbtools-daemon fleet. It accepts the shared --tool, --scope, --year, --fixture and filter options and writes the receipts that --no-build and CI consume. Plain dotnet test on an entry project in testing/Daemon/ uses the pinned daemon VSTest adapter (DbToolsDaemon.RevitTest.TestAdapter). MSBuild builds the selected assemblies, models, includes and per-year sources, and the adapter submits them in one request. Use one route per invocation. Both read the relay URL from DBTOOLS_DAEMON_RELAY_URL; the daemon owns relay credentials, and neither route accepts or stores them. Lanes Lane Marker Where it runs Pure plain [Test] Without Revit. Locally when possible; otherwise as a daemon PureSuite job on a hidden Windows desktop Local [RevitLocal] Inside Revit on a daemon worker, for one selected year DA [RevitDA] On the invoking host, as an HTTP client of APS Design Automation; never through the daemon DIST The Windows distribution acceptance suite, always a daemon PureSuite job BUILD Linux-native build and distribution contract suites Local tests exercise the real ribbon, WPF and add-in lifecycle in Revit. The DA lane builds the Revit 2026 Sentinel WorkItem test project and runs it with dotnet test. A run takes 5 to 12 minutes and spends APS cloud credits. It requires APS_CLIENT_ID and APS_CLIENT_SECRET and fails, rather than skips, when either is missing. APS_BUCKET selects the OSS bucket (default dbtools-tests). Run the network-free tests of that project with -f 'TestCategory!=RevitDA'. See APS Design Automation Sentinel. test.sh Synopsis ./test.sh <verb> [options] Verb Action test Build the selected tests and run or submit them list List the statically discovered tests for the selection validate-request Resolve selectors and projects without building or submitting submit Build and submit a Local daemon job; rejects the pure and da scopes rerun --request <id> Rerun the failures of an accepted daemon request from its submitted bytes, without building build Run build.sh Without --scope, the scope is pure. rerun replays the recorded request and rejects --scope. test.sh passes nothing through to dotnet: -- is rejected; use --filter, --fqn, --fixture or --compile-only. An unknown option is an error. Run ./test.sh --help for the complete option list. Selection Option Description --tool TOOL[,TOOL] BUILD, APP, CORE, DA-SENTINEL, DIST, or a tool key such as GM --scope SCOPE[,SCOPE] pure, local, da or all -y, --year YEAR; --years 2026,2027 Revit years for hosted execution --project PATH[,PATH] Repository-relative .csproj paths with forward slashes; narrows the tool and scope selection and cannot bypass it --fixture NAME Fixture class; repeatable -f, --filter FILTER VSTest filter for Pure tests; exact or prefix FQN form for daemon jobs --fqn FQN Exact test name; repeatable; exclusive with --filter and --fixture --changed-since REV Select test owners affected since a revision; unknown inputs select all test.sh list --projects prints the sorted scope<TAB>project rows and is the source of truth for what a request selects. It evaluates project membership, explicit Compile Include, Exclude and Remove items, disabled default items, NUnit fixture attributes and the selected tool, scope and year. The same index resolves fixtures and exact FQNs. A fixture must resolve to one compiled owner class. An unknown fixture or project, an unreadable project or source file, a project the selected tool and scope cannot reach, or an explicit scope with no resolved project exits with status 2 before any build or submission. An exact FullyQualifiedName=<FQN> filter becomes an exact daemon selector, and a prefix filter becomes a prefix selector. A hosted filter that cannot be mapped exits with status 2 instead of selecting the whole assembly. Years Pure requests have no year. They reject --year, --years, --keep-open and --isolation. Local requests take -y or --year; --scope all applies the year only to the hosted part. DA always builds Revit 2026: a DA-only request rejects other years, and a combined request must include 2026. A two-year Local selection makes one daemon request per year, each with its own product tree and report. Daemon options Option Description --machine MACHINE Pin a worker. DBTOOLS_DAEMON_MACHINE_ID sets a default pin. Without a pin the daemon chooses (Auto) --relay URL Relay URL; default DBTOOLS_DAEMON_RELAY_URL --queue-timeout HH:MM:SS Maximum wait for a claim, including the Revit lease for hosted runs --execution-timeout HH:MM:SS Maximum execution time after the lease --isolation MODE, --keep-open Hosted isolation mode; leave Revit open --result-json PATH Write the validated daemon terminal report by atomic replacement --include PATH Add a file or directory to the submitted bundle; repeatable --compile-only (--build-only) Build and write the receipt; run nothing --no-build Consume a matching receipt; reject stale or missing outputs Environment Variable Description DBT_PURE_CONCURRENCY Maximum concurrent Pure daemon submissions (default 2) DBT_MSBUILD_MAX_CPU_COUNT Maximum graph build parallelism (default 2) DBT_BUILD_SERVERS 1 (default): scoped compiler and MSBuild servers; 0: none DBT_TEST_INPUT_CACHE_ROOT Root of the frozen test input cache DBTOOLS_DAEMON_CLI Daemon CLI command (default dbtools-daemon-cli) Examples ./test.sh list --tool GM --scope all ./test.sh test --tool APP --scope pure ./test.sh test --tool GM,RecordSet --scope pure ./test.sh test --tool GM --scope pure --fixture DuplicateDetectionEngineTests ./test.sh test --filter 'FullyQualifiedName=DBTools.GM.Tests.AdapterTests.SomeTest' ./test.sh test --tool BUILD --scope pure ./test.sh test --tool APP --scope local -y 2026 --fixture RibbonCompositionTests ./test.sh validate-request --tool GM --scope local -y 2026 \ --queue-timeout 00:05:00 --execution-timeout 00:30:00 ./test.sh test --scope pure --compile-only ./test.sh test --scope pure --no-build ./test.sh rerun --request REQUEST_ID Execution Pure routing test.sh checks each selected Pure assembly for its .deps.json, .runtimeconfig.json and the output-local NUnit3.TestAdapter.dll, then routes it: to the daemon if it is the DIST suite or a machine is pinned; to the daemon if it targets Windows and the host is not Windows; to the daemon if the host lacks Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App; a missing other framework is an error; otherwise to local VSTest. Local projects, including the Linux BUILD and Distribution suites, run one after another; daemon submissions run concurrently. A local project that runs zero tests fails. With a filter expression, the run fails only when no selected project runs a test. Linux-native BUILD projects and *.Portable.Pure.Tests projects are skipped on Windows with a notice. Inputs and receipts For a selected lane and year, the MSBuild graph returns the test assembly, target framework, model items and product-tree includes in one pass. Before any submission, test.sh freezes the assemblies, runtime closure, product-tree includes, models and companions into the content-addressed test input cache, so a later build cannot change the submitted files. A normal exit removes the per-run directory. --compile-only writes a receipt bound to the source identity, the selected projects, the graph inputs and the output hashes. --no-build verifies all of these and refuses stale or missing files. CI resolves the selectors once with ./test.sh list --projects, compiles each selected scope with --compile-only, transfers the receipt and the recorded input closure, and runs them with --no-build. The consumer never rebuilds. Linux BUILD and DIST jobs do not depend on the Windows transfer. Results The daemon terminal JSON is the result. A successful run must report a positive executed count; a report of zero tests fails. A distinctive nonzero daemon exit status is kept even when the terminal JSON is missing or malformed. Independent scopes in one request continue after a failure, but test.sh returns the first nonzero status and never reports a failed run as passed. DIST DIST is a closed surface. It requires --tool DIST alone, --scope pure, --filter FullyQualifiedName=DBTools.Distribution.Windows.Tests.WindowsAcceptanceTests.ValidatesTheStagedCandidate, --result-json PATH, and exactly one --include that names a validate-dist-<sha256>.zip archive (see PackageSandboxValidationInput in Build Pipeline). It rejects --fixture and --machine. dotnet test with the daemon adapter : "${DBTOOLS_DAEMON_RELAY_URL:?Set the daemon relay URL}" # One hosted test for Revit 2026; the entry builds the per-year sources. DBTOOLS_DAEMON_REVIT_YEARS=2026 dotnet test testing/Daemon/Hosted/GM.Hosted.Entry.csproj \ --filter "FullyQualifiedName~FamilyDeepScanTests.GM_DeepScan_Smoke" # Pure tests on a hidden daemon desktop. dotnet test testing/Daemon/Pure/GM.Pure.Entry.csproj \ --filter "FullyQualifiedName~UIStateCacheTests.SetAsync_WritesTheStableCamelCaseGoldenFormat" testing/Daemon/Hosted/<Tool>.Hosted.Entry.csproj builds the Local tests of that owner for both years (Hosted2026.proj, Hosted2027.proj). testing/Daemon/Pure/<Tool>.Pure.Entry.csproj selects every DBTools.<Tool>.*Pure.Tests.csproj beside its owner. After the build, the entry writes dbtools-daemon.runsettings from Hosted.runsettings or Pure.runsettings with the literal sources, models and includes. The hosted settings default to years 2026,2027, isolated execution and a 30-minute timeout, and treat a run with no tests as an error. Product staging Each Local or hosted test for a year receives the same product tree that the installer uses: product/<year>/ ├── DBTools.addin ├── DBTools.dll ├── DBTools.Core.dll ├── DBTools.Presentation.dll ├── DBTools.HandyControl.dll └── Tools/DBTools.<Tool>.dll The tree keeps its relative paths. Test assemblies and NUnit and adapter dependencies are separate inputs. App loads tools from Tools/ by explicit path into the context that holds it, so ProductLoadContext and DevModeLoadContext receive the same identities as the staged tree. Test support installs no resolver for product assemblies. Test projects Test projects are next to their production owners: src/DBTools.App/Tests/DBTools.App.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj src/DBTools.Core/Tests/DBTools.Core.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj src/DBTools.Sandbox/Tests/DBTools.Sandbox.Pure.Tests.csproj src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool>/Tests/DBTools.<Tool>.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj testing/DBTools.Build.Tests/ build and distribution contracts (Linux) testing/DBTools.Distribution.Tests/ portable archive contracts (Linux) testing/DBTools.Distribution.Windows.Tests/ DIST suite testing/RevitTestModels/ test models by year and tool A project has both a .Pure.Tests and a .Local.Tests project only when both kinds of test exist. Pure projects list their source files explicitly and reference their normal production owners. Shared props give every Pure project $(DBT_PureRevitYear) (2026) and static graph restore, and pass that year on owner references, so a plain dotnet build or dotnet test of one project needs no properties. Revit is compile-only in Pure tests: a test must not load Revit-typed members or scan owner types outside the loadable set. Local projects disable default compile items and include only hosted fixtures. Presentation behavior tests are under Presentation; the Core Pure projects link the fixtures they can run without Revit. Tests that need a real WPF window run in a Windows-capable lane. Portable Pure projects Core and SGT define an optional $(DBT_PortableTargetFramework). Their *.Portable.Pure.Tests projects build against that framework and run on Linux; CI and Windows test.sh route them to Linux. To make a project portable: declare desktop and portable TargetFrameworks; condition DBT_RevitHostIdentity, UseWPF and the Presentation ProjectReference on the desktop framework, and keep Revit references under the desktop host identity condition; set DBT_UsesMergedAssemblies=false in portable consumers. build/MSBuild/Portable.targets excludes App, Revit, Views, DesignTime and XAML inputs. Portable images use ordinary NuGet dependencies, have no content version and add no staged runtime files. Core uses an explicit list of source files for its portable build. Test models Hosted projects declare RevitTestModel items relative to testing/RevitTestModels: testing/RevitTestModels/ ├── 2026/GM/gm_test_model.rvt ├── 2026/SGT/sgt_test_model.rvt ├── 2026/SGT/_LinkedModels/sgt_test_linked_model.rvt ├── 2026/Regression/realtest_model.rvt ├── 2027/... (same layout) ├── GM/SharedParameters/shared_parameters.txt └── VTC/vtc_import_layers.dxf Model files and explicit non-RVT inputs keep their relative paths in the daemon stage. Hosted fixtures find them under DBTOOLS_DAEMON_REVIT_MODELS_DIR; Pure fixtures use the repository root in DBT_TEST_REPO_ROOT. TestPathResolver reads the root on every call, so a hosted job never sees the model root of a previous job. A fixture may open a temporary copy of a model, but the daemon owns the active document and the worker lifecycle. Do not resolve models from a worker checkout or an %APPDATA% cache; there is no dbtools.testparams.json. Test support testing/TestSupport holds shared test infrastructure and doubles for true externals. Tool-specific doubles are under testing/TestSupport/<Tool> and are linked as source by the matching test projects; they are not a separate assembly. Revit/RevitHost.cs initializes the year, the App runtime and the product Revit call gate before the test body, and supplies the real UIApplication through an ambient scope that does not carry API access across an await. It owns the scheduler unless a fixture holds a longer lease. Forced-queue tests call the real external-event handler synchronously to model a later API turn; one daemon NUnit callback contains no second native turn. Wpf/WpfTestRuntimeBootstrap.cs registers pack URI support, installs the shared window owner, validates themes in the runtime assembly's contextual reflection scope, and releases only its own provider at teardown. It adds no Resolving handlers and does not force Presentation or HandyControl into the default context. Logging/TestLoggingBridge.cs uses production logging when Revit provides it and a console and file host otherwise. Hosted fixtures release only their own runtime, Revit task, owner handle and window resources. Cleanup reports both the primary failure and any cleanup failure. Writing tests When a test fails, investigate the production code first. Use test doubles only for true external boundaries such as Revit, the file system, the network and the clock; do not replace DBTools services or orchestration to make an assertion pass. Each behavior test asserts a real outcome. Keep a fixture in its owner project and lane. A fixture with several independent checks records each failure, attempts safe cleanup and reports them together. The build and distribution suites read already-built product metadata and reject a stale source snapshot. Source, build and test changes alter the snapshot; documentation and transient artifacts do not. See Build Pipeline, Assembly Loading Contract and Sandbox Validator.

developer-guide/architecture/theme-syste.title: Theme System | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/theme-syste.summary: Theme System DBTools.Presentation.dll holds every compiled WPF resource of the product: the theme dictionaries, stable controls and window shells. It stays loaded for the life of the Revit process. Tool views are raw XAML that Presentation parses at run time, so App, Core and the tool assemblies contain no BAML and no .g.resources. Each window merges the theme into its own resources, never into Application.Resources, so DBTools does not change the appearance of other add-ins. Assembly roles Assembly Compiled WPF content DBTools.Presentation Theme dictionaries, stable windows and controls, tool behaviors and converters under Tools/<TOOL>/, the merged Helix theme, and the settings views of DialogSuppression, ElevationTags, FoundationTags and JoistGirderWeight (linked from those tool folders) DBTools.HandyControl The HandyControl skins and themes DBTools.Core None. Window lifecycle, error boundaries, registry, commands and runtime hosts can be reloaded Tool assemblies None. Tool views are embedded as raw XAML Presentation keeps explicit Page, Compile and EmbeddedResource items (EnableDefaultPageItems=false). The linked tool settings views keep their tool namespaces, for example DBTools.DialogSuppression.Settings.Views; the tool projects remove them from their own Page items. Tool views A tool embeds each view as an EmbeddedResource with the logical name DBTools.ToolViews.<TOOL>.<View>.xaml. ToolWindowFactory.Create (Core) opens a view in these steps: ToolWindowHost.Create (Presentation) creates a stable shell, ToolWindowModalShell or ToolWindowModelessShell. The shell initializer runs before the view is parsed. The default is WindowInitializer.Initialize or InitializeModeless, which applies the theme, binds the owner window, registers the progress overlay and installs the error boundary and logging. ToolWindowXaml.LoadElement parses the raw view inside ToolWindowReflectionScope, and the view and shell receive the tool's view model as DataContext. The factory registers the session in ToolWindowRegistry. The caller shows the window with session.ShowDialog() or session.Show() and gets named controls with session.Require<T>(name). The Settings, Alert, Logger and notification banner windows are raw resources in Presentation and use the same loader; so do tool template dictionaries such as the VTC diff templates and the SGT opening view. For these windows Core keeps the state, commands and lifecycle and event handling; the controls need no typed constructor from a reloadable assembly and do no type discovery at run time. Retirement tears down bindings, automation roots, resources and callbacks. Core lifecycle handlers are released through BehaviorState and session cleanup before the shell closes. A custom shell initializer releases its own handles. Raw views name only framework types or public stable Presentation types and merge the theme through Presentation's ResourceUri markup extension before they use static theme keys. Tool content uses explicit keyed templates. SGT's opening and girt grids use stable behaviors over tool row state. ERFT and SGT pass immutable scene data to the stable 3D viewport, which owns camera, material, picking and device state (see Structural Preview). Theme dictionaries The root dictionary is: /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Theme.xaml <PresentationVersion> is the content version of the Presentation assembly (see Build Pipeline). The root merges, in this order: /DBTools.HandyControl;V<HandyControlVersion>;component/Themes/SkinDark.xaml /DBTools.HandyControl;V<HandyControlVersion>;component/Themes/Theme.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Tokens.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Brushes.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Converters.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Controls.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/DataGrid.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Menus.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Components.xaml ThemeResourceLoader (Core) checks this order. At startup ThemeValidator.ValidateOrThrow registers the pack URI scheme, loads each dictionary separately and freezes its freezables, loads the root and checks its merged dictionaries, and then measures and arranges a probe tree of standard controls. A failure stops startup; see Troubleshooting. Resource URIs Every compiled resource URI contains the assembly's version. A changed stable assembly therefore has a new identity, and WPF cannot select an older copy of Presentation or HandyControl that an earlier DBTools version has already loaded. Presentation URIs use the Presentation version and HandyControl URIs use the HandyControl version. The component URI is relative, so Application.LoadComponent does not need the pack scheme to be registered. Use ResourceUri.CreateResourceUri for Application.LoadComponent, dictionary sources and the dictionary markup extensions. Use ResourceUri.CreateAbsoluteResourceUri for images and icons created in code without a WPF base URI. It registers the pack scheme and returns pack://application:,,,/<assembly>;V<version>;component/<path>. WindowInitializer loads the window icon with BitmapCacheOption.OnLoad inside its warning boundary; otherwise WPF can defer the file lookup until it creates the window handle. XAML namespaces XAML outside Presentation refers to stable types with clr-namespace:...;assembly=DBTools.Presentation. XAML compiled by Presentation uses the namespace form without assembly=. This keeps the BAML compiler from resolving Presentation types through a reloadable assembly. BAML assembly versions The BAML assembly table must contain the final assembly version, because WPF resolves local markup extensions through that table separately from the outer pack URI. Keep SDK assembly-info generation on in WPF temporary projects. With it off, BAML references Version=0.0.0.0; if an older Presentation is already loaded in the default context, the CLR can satisfy that request with the older copy. That copy lacks HandyControlResourceUriExtension, and WPF throws NotImplementedException before it opens the HandyControl dictionaries. WPF's local-assembly fallback runs only when loading throws, so a successful bind to the older copy bypasses it. See .NET 10 WPF assembly and type resolution and CoreCLR version compatibility. The hosted version probe (src/DBTools.Core/Tests/Fixtures/PresentationVersionProbe) tests two orders: an older Presentation loaded first, and the current HandyControl loaded before the older UI. In both, it resolves the older resources before it loads the current Presentation, then checks the current theme, overlay and alert resources. It prints the theme's BAML assembly reference and the loaded UI identities and contexts before theme resolution. Linux build tests inspect the emitted BAML identities and the generated InitializeComponent URIs. developer-guide/developing/feature-warni.title: Feature Warnings | DB Tools
developer-guide/developing/feature-warni.summary: Feature Warnings Feature warnings provide a mechanism to notify users of configuration issues and automatically disable affected tools until the problem is resolved. Warning state is runtime/session-only and is never persisted to disk. Overview Feature warnings serve two purposes: User Notification: Display prominent warnings in the Settings window when configuration issues exist Tool Protection: Automatically disable ribbon buttons for tools that depend on valid configuration Warnings are declarative (defined in manifest.yml) but activated programmatically based on validation logic. When a warning is active: The warning card appears in the Settings window Associated ribbon buttons become disabled The Settings button icon shows a warning indicator The DB Tools tab gets a highlight marker Warning Lifecycle 1. DEFINITION (manifest.yml) Warning metadata declared: id, title, message, disableTools | v 2. REGISTRATION (ToolModule.RegisterSettingsPacks) SettingsPackRegistration.Warning supplies warning metadata and validation logic | v 3. VALIDATION (Settings window load / Save; the Validate button only diagnoses) Pack context validates settings and computes warning state | v 4. ACTIVATION (ISettingsWarningService.SetWarning) Warning state stored in-session, ribbon buttons disabled | v 5. DISPLAY (SettingsWarningCardView) Warning card shown with Clear button | v 6. CLEARING (User clicks Clear / conditions change) Warning state cleared, ribbon buttons re-enabled Defining Warnings in manifest.yml Warnings are declared within settingsPacks in your tool's manifest.yml: Complete Schema tool: settingsPacks: - key: structural.foundation_tags # Unique pack identifier title: "Combined Foundation Tags" # Display title in Settings warnings: - id: core.structural.combined_tags # Unique warning identifier title: "Combined Foundation Tags Disabled" # Warning card title message: "Combined foundation tag updates are disabled due to a warning. Clear the warning to re-enable." disableTools: # Tools to disable when active - DBTools.UpdateCombinedFoundationTags - DBTools.MoveCombinedFoundationTags - DBTools.OrganizeFoundationTypes Warning Properties Reference Property Required Description id Yes Globally unique warning identifier (e.g., core.structural.combined_tags) title Yes Title shown in the warning card header message Yes Detailed message explaining the issue and resolution disableTools No List of ribbon tool internalName values to disable ID Naming Convention Use a hierarchical naming scheme: core.{domain}.{feature} - For core/shared functionality tools.{toolname}.{warning} - For tool-specific warnings Examples: core.library.invalid - Library paths are invalid core.structural.elevation_tags - Elevation tag alignment warning core.structural.joist_girder - Joist girder weight warning Warning Properties in Code The ToolWarningManifest class represents the YAML definition: public sealed class ToolWarningManifest { public string Id { get; set; } = string.Empty; public string Title { get; set; } = string.Empty; public string Message { get; set; } = string.Empty; public List<string>? DisableTools { get; set; } } Registering Warning Definitions Warnings must be registered in your ToolModule.RegisterSettingsPacks() method. This connects the declarative manifest to the runtime validation logic. Complete Registration Pattern public override void RegisterSettingsPacks(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { Guard.NotNull(services, nameof(services)); Guard.NotNull(manifest, nameof(manifest)); var configSection = manifest.GetRequiredConfigSection(); var pack = manifest.GetSingleSettingsPack(); var warning = pack.GetSingleWarning(manifest.Id); var panel = manifest.GetRequiredPanel(); services.AddDbtSettingsPackDefinition<MyToolSettings, MySettingsPackContext>( new SettingsPackRegistration<MyToolSettings, MySettingsPackContext> { ConfigSection = configSection, PackKey = pack.Key, PackTitle = pack.Title, RibbonPanel = panel, ContextFactory = (sp, input) => new MySettingsPackContext(), ViewFactory = context => new MySettingsPackView { DataContext = context }, Warning = new SettingsPackWarningRegistration<MySettingsPackContext> { Id = warning.Id, Title = warning.Title, Message = warning.Message, ToolInternalNamesToDisable = warning.DisableTools?.ToArray(), FlagGetter = context => context.HasWarning, FlagSetter = (context, active) => context.HasWarning = active } }); } The registration extension constructs the internal warning definition and validates all required strings and delegates at the DI admission boundary. Source: src/DBTools.Core/Settings/Composition/SettingsPackServiceCollectionExtensions.cs SettingsPackWarningRegistration Properties Property Type Description Id string Warning identifier from manifest Title string Display title Message string Display message FlagGetter Func<TContext, bool> Gets warning state from context FlagSetter Action<TContext, bool> Sets warning state on context ToolInternalNamesToDisable IReadOnlyCollection<string>? Tools to disable Settings Model Requirements Warning state is session-only. Settings models should persist user preferences (for example AutoUpdateEnabled) but should not persist warning flags. using DBTools.Core.Settings; namespace DBTools.MyTool.Settings; public sealed class MyToolSettings : IAutoUpdateSettings { public bool AutoUpdateEnabled { get; set; } // Other settings... } The IAutoUpdateSettings interface requires only persisted auto-update preference: public interface IAutoUpdateSettings { bool AutoUpdateEnabled { get; set; } } Triggering Warnings Warnings are triggered through the ISettingsWarningService: Service Interface public interface ISettingsWarningService { IReadOnlyCollection<ISettingsWarningDefinition> Definitions { get; } bool IsWarningActive(string warningId); SettingsWarningStateChange SetWarning(string warningId, bool active); } SettingsWarningService owns definition lookup, the narrow tool-facing state API, and session-only publication state. Active-id enumeration and full-state/change publication remain internal operations used only by settings orchestration. It does not accept or mutate an erased settings context. Each ISettingsPackRuntimeWarning is already bound to the exact context created by its pack runtime; settings rows update that bound warning and then publish the state through the service. SettingsWarningPublicationPolicy owns per-warning event publication, full warning replay, and aggregate HasWarnings publication over the service-provided warning state. Setting a Warning Active // In your validation logic var warningService = serviceProvider.GetRequiredService<ISettingsWarningService>(); warningService.SetWarning("core.my_tool.warning", true); Clearing a Warning warningService.SetWarning("core.my_tool.warning", false); Validation in Settings Pack Context Typically, warnings are validated when the settings pack loads or saves. Implement validation in your context's ValidateAsync method: public async Task<SettingsValidationResult> ValidateAsync(CancellationToken ct) { var errors = new List<string>(); // Validate configuration if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(LibraryPath) || !Directory.Exists(LibraryPath)) { errors.Add($"Library path '{LibraryPath}' does not exist."); HasWarnings = true; // Set context warning flag } else { HasWarnings = false; } return errors.Count > 0 ? SettingsValidationResult.Failed(errors) : SettingsValidationResult.Success(); } Warning UI in Settings Window When warnings are active, they appear as prominent cards in the Settings window: SettingsWarningCardView <Border Style="{DynamicResource WarningBar}" Visibility="{Binding IsActive, Converter={StaticResource Converter.BoolToVisibility}}"> <Grid> <Grid.ColumnDefinitions> <ColumnDefinition Width="*" /> <ColumnDefinition Width="Auto" /> </Grid.ColumnDefinitions> <StackPanel> <TextBlock FontWeight="SemiBold" Foreground="{DynamicResource {x:Static theme:BrushKeys.Warning}}" Text="{Binding Title}" /> <TextBlock Margin="{DynamicResource TGap6}" Style="{DynamicResource DescriptionText}" Text="{Binding Message}" /> </StackPanel> <Button Grid.Column="1" MinWidth="70" MinHeight="28" Padding="{DynamicResource Pad8x4}" Command="{Binding ClearCommand}" Content="Clear" Style="{DynamicResource SecondaryButton}" /> </Grid> </Border> Warning Card ViewModel SettingsWarningViewModel receives an ISettingsPackRuntimeWarning whose getter/setter are already bound to its owning pack context. It owns the Clear/Fix commands, warning-service interaction, remediation dispatch, and logged/bannered action failures: public sealed partial class SettingsWarningViewModel : ObservableObject, IDisposable { public string WarningId => _warning.Id; public string Title => _warning.Title; public string Message => _warning.Message; public bool IsActive => _warning.IsActive; public IAsyncRelayCommand ClearCommand { get; } public IAsyncRelayCommand FixCommand { get; } public bool HasFix => _actionPolicy.HasFix; private async Task ClearAsync() { if (await _actionPolicy.ClearAsync().ConfigureAwait(true)) OnPropertyChanged(nameof(IsActive)); } } disableTools Mechanism When a warning is active, the specified ribbon tools are automatically disabled. Event Flow Warning Activated: ISettingsWarningService.SetWarning() is called Event Published: ISettingsChangePublisher.PublishWarningChanged() fires Listener Receives: RibbonSettingsSubscriber handles the settings change event Warning Policy Applies: RibbonSettingsUpdater dispatches the registry update Buttons Disabled: RibbonControlRegistryUpdater updates created controls // RibbonSettingsSubscriber.cs private void OnWarningChanged(object? sender, WarningChangedEventArgs e) { RibbonSettingsUpdater.ApplyToolWarningState(e, _logger); } RibbonSettingsSubscriber remains the settings-event adapter. RibbonSettingsUpdater owns both aggregate warning visuals and per-tool warning enablement dispatch. Ribbon Registry Update RibbonControlRegistryUpdater.RegisterToolButton(...); RibbonSettingsUpdater.ApplyToolWarningState(...); The ribbon registry state is initialized by RibbonComposer before observers publish any state, so warning handlers operate against an explicit registry snapshot rather than startup-time property mutation. Visual Indicators When warnings exist: Settings Button Icon: Changes to show warning indicator Tab Highlight: DB Tools tab shows a "New" highlight private void OnWarningsChanged(object? sender, WarningSetChangedEventArgs e) { RibbonSettingsUpdater.ApplyVisualState(e.HasWarnings, _logger); } RibbonSettingsUpdater owns warning visual policy/dispatch, per-tool warning enablement dispatch, and current warning-state publication/reset. RibbonSettingsSubscriber stays as the settings event adapter, and the registry updater exposes only internal low-level settings icon/tab-highlight/tool-enabled mutation. Conditional Warnings Warnings can be conditional based on settings or environment. Implement the condition in your validation logic: Based on Settings Value public async Task<SettingsValidationResult> ValidateAsync(CancellationToken ct) { // Only validate if feature is enabled if (!AutoUpdateEnabled) { HasWarning = false; return SettingsValidationResult.Success(); } // Validate when enabled if (!IsConfigurationValid()) { HasWarning = true; return SettingsValidationResult.Failed("Configuration is invalid."); } HasWarning = false; return SettingsValidationResult.Success(); } Based on Environment public async Task<SettingsValidationResult> ValidateAsync(CancellationToken ct) { var errors = new List<string>(); foreach (var path in LibraryPaths) { if (!Directory.Exists(path)) { errors.Add($"Path '{path}' does not exist."); } } HasWarnings = errors.Count > 0; return HasWarnings ? SettingsValidationResult.Failed(errors) : SettingsValidationResult.Success(); } Auto-Update Task Integration For tools with auto-update functionality (triggered on view activation), ViewActivationTask<TSettings> checks warning state before execution: public async Task<ViewActivationAdmission?> AdmitAsync(UIApplication uiapp, ViewActivatedEventArgs args, CancellationToken ct) { var settings = _settingsProvider.Get(_settingsSection); if (!settings.AutoUpdateEnabled) { LogSkip("auto-update disabled"); return null; } foreach (var warningId in _warningIds) { if (_warnings.IsWarningActive(warningId)) { LogSkip("warning active"); return null; } } if (!await ShouldRunInternalAsync(uiapp, args, settings, ct).ConfigureAwait(false)) return null; // The admission executes with this attempt's settings snapshot and never reads settings again. return new ViewActivationAdmission(executionCt => ExecuteInternalAsync(uiapp, args, settings, executionCt)); } This ensures auto-update tasks don't run when warnings are active, protecting against potential failures. Clearing Warnings Warnings can be cleared in several ways: 1. User Clicks Clear Button The Settings window warning card has a "Clear" button. The view model clears the warning via ISettingsWarningService and reports failures through the Core logging/banner path: private async Task ClearAsync() { if (await _actionPolicy.ClearAsync().ConfigureAwait(true)) OnPropertyChanged(nameof(IsActive)); } 2. Programmatically When Conditions Change // After user fixes configuration if (IsConfigurationNowValid()) { warningService.SetWarning("core.my_tool.warning", false); } 3. Through Settings Pack Context Reset public void ResetToDefaults() { AutoUpdateEnabled = true; HasWarning = false; // Clear warning flag // Reset other settings... } Real Examples Example 1: Foundation Tags Warning Disables multiple related tools when foundation tag configuration has issues: # manifest.yml settingsPacks: - key: structural.foundation_tags title: "Combined Foundation Tags" warnings: - id: core.structural.combined_tags title: "Combined Foundation Tags Disabled" message: "Combined foundation tag updates are disabled due to a warning. Clear the warning to re-enable." disableTools: - DBTools.UpdateCombinedFoundationTags - DBTools.MoveCombinedFoundationTags - DBTools.OrganizeFoundationTypes Example 2: Library Paths Warning Disables import/export when library paths are invalid: # manifest.yml settingsPacks: - key: core.library title: "Library Files" warnings: - id: core.library.invalid title: "Library Paths Invalid" message: "One or more saved library file paths are invalid. Fix the paths and save the settings to re-enable import/export." disableTools: - DBTools.ExportToLibrary - DBTools.ImportFromLibrary Example 3: Simple Single-Tool Warning # manifest.yml settingsPacks: - key: structural.joist_girder_weight title: "Joist Girder Weights" warnings: - id: core.structural.joist_girder title: "Joist Girder Weights Disabled" message: "Joist girder weight updates are disabled due to a warning. Clear the warning to re-enable." disableTools: - DBTools.UpdateJoistGirderWeights Warning Event Args The warning system uses specific event args for state changes: WarningChangedEventArgs Fired when a specific warning's state changes: public sealed class WarningChangedEventArgs : EventArgs { public string WarningId { get; } public string PackKey { get; } public bool IsActive { get; } public IReadOnlyCollection<string> ToolInternalNamesToDisable { get; } } WarningSetChangedEventArgs Fired when the overall warning state changes (any warnings -> no warnings, or vice versa): public sealed class WarningSetChangedEventArgs : EventArgs { public bool HasWarnings { get; } } Best Practices 1. Clear Warning Messages Write messages that explain: What is wrong Why it matters How to fix it # Good message: "One or more saved library file paths are invalid. Fix the paths and save the settings to re-enable import/export." # Bad message: "Warning active." 2. Disable Only Affected Tools Only list tools that actually depend on the valid configuration: # Good - only disables tools that use foundation tags disableTools: - DBTools.UpdateCombinedFoundationTags - DBTools.MoveCombinedFoundationTags # Bad - disables unrelated tools disableTools: - DBTools.UpdateCombinedFoundationTags - DBTools.SomeUnrelatedTool 3. Auto-Disable Auto-Update When setting a warning active, also disable auto-update to prevent background failures: // Context flag setter (for auto-update packs) (context, active) => { context.HasWarning = active; if (active) context.AutoUpdateEnabled = false; // Optional: keep background hooks quiet } 4. Test Warning Scenarios Ensure your tool handles: Warning active on startup (validate-aware packs are evaluated by the startup warning publisher before the initial warning publish) Warning cleared mid-session Multiple warnings in same pack Runtime exceptions in hooks (banner + session-disable; do not activate feature warnings) Validation exceptions in validate-aware packs (exceptions are runtime errors; log and do not activate feature warnings) Cross-References Creating New Tools - Tool module registration Settings Packs - Settings pack configuration Modularity - Tool module architecture

developer-guide/developing/hooks.html.summary: Hooks Hooks are the extensibility mechanism that allows DBTools modules to respond to Revit application events without coupling directly to the Revit API event system. They provide a clean, testable abstraction for behaviors like auto-updating elements when views change or injecting contextual ribbon UI. Overview What Are Hooks? Hooks are interfaces that define contracts for responding to specific application-level events. Rather than subscribing directly to Revit's UIControlledApplication events, tools register hook handlers that the central HookHost dispatches to when events occur. Why Use Hooks? Direct Revit Events DBTools Hooks Scattered subscriptions across tools Centralized event management Manual exception handling Automatic error handling via ISafeExecutor Tight coupling to Revit API Testable abstractions Risk of blocking UI thread Async-first design Complex lifecycle management Automatic attach/detach Key Benefits Centralized Dispatch: All event handling flows through HookHost, ensuring consistent error handling and logging Async Support: Hook handlers can perform async work without blocking Revit's UI thread Automatic Lifecycle: Hooks are attached/detached during app startup/shutdown Settings Integration: View-activated tasks integrate with the settings system for enable/disable control Warning System: Hooks can set warnings when they fail, disabling auto-update until the user resolves them Hook Architecture Component Overview flowchart TB subgraph Revit["Revit Application"] Events["UIControlledApplication Events"] end subgraph Core["DBTools.Core"] HookHost["HookHost"] Registry["ToolRegistry"] Executor["ISafeExecutor"] end subgraph Handlers["Hook Handlers"] VAH["ViewActivationHook"] LCH["IHookLifecycle"] end subgraph Tasks["View Activated Tasks"] ET["ViewActivatedTask (Elevation Tags)"] FT["FoundationTagsViewActivatedTask"] JGT["AutoUpdateTask"] end Events -->|ViewActivated| HookHost Events -->|SelectionChanged/DialogBoxShowing| LCH HookHost --> Executor Executor --> VAH Executor --> LCH VAH --> ET VAH --> FT VAH --> JGT Registry -.->|"GetHookImplementations<T>()"| HookHost Registration Flow sequenceDiagram participant Boot as AppRuntimeFactory participant Module as ToolModule participant Registry as ToolRegistry participant Host as HookHost participant DI as IServiceProvider Boot->>Module: RegisterHooks(registry, manifest) Module->>Registry: RegisterHook<THook, TImpl>() Note over Registry: Stores Type mapping Boot->>DI: BuildServiceProvider() Boot->>Host: AttachAsync(application, ct) Host->>Registry: GetHookImplementations<T>() Host->>DI: GetService(implType) Host->>Host: Subscribe to Revit events The HookHost HookHost is the central attach/detach coordinator that: Delegates handler resolution to HookCatalog, which reads hook types from ToolRegistry Subscribes/unsubscribes Revit events it owns directly (e.g., ViewActivated) Delegates ViewActivated safe-executor policy to ViewActivatedHookDispatcher Delegates initialization, queued rollback, and synchronous shutdown aggregation to HookLifecycleCoordinator Records each attach owner before initialization starts, so shutdown can detach a subscription while its initialization task is incomplete var initializedActions = await _lifecycleCoordinator .InitializeAsync(attachActions, ct, RecordAttachAction) .ConfigureAwait(false); Available Hook Types ViewActivationHook Responds to Revit's ViewActivated event, which fires whenever the user switches views. DBTools keeps a single core-owned hook that dispatches registered IViewActivationTask instances. public sealed class ViewActivationHook { Task OnViewActivatedAsync( UIControlledApplication application, ViewActivatedEventArgs args, CancellationToken ct); } Use Cases: Auto-updating elevation tags when entering floor plans Refreshing parameter values on view change Updating cached view-specific data Important Considerations: Handler runs on the Revit UI thread context Must not block; use async patterns Errors are caught by ISafeExecutor and logged Automation-host suppression is startup-owned: AddinEntry skips HookHost.AttachAsync(...) when startup detects an externally managed call-gate host, so the handler does not perform its own host check. IHookLifecycle Manages module-owned lifecycle hooks. Use this for service modules that need application-wide event subscription, such as dialog interception, and for contextual ribbon injectors that manage their own Revit event subscriptions. public interface IHookLifecycle { Task InitializeAsync(UIControlledApplication application, CancellationToken ct); Task RollbackAsync(UIControlledApplication application, CancellationToken ct); void Shutdown(UIControlledApplication application); } Use Cases: Cross-tool dialog suppression services Application-wide dialog telemetry or warning hooks that must subscribe once per Revit session Contextual ribbon injectors that add and refresh tool-owned UI from Revit events Lifecycle: InitializeAsync is called by HookHost.AttachAsync(...). The handler owns hook lifecycle while a tool-local adapter subscribes to UIControlledApplication.DialogBoxShowing or equivalent reflected event metadata. RollbackAsync reverses a completed attach when later initialization fails; it may queue work back into the valid initialization context. Shutdown completes synchronously inside HookHost.Detach() while Revit's application-shutdown callback is still valid. Implementations own partial initialization before InitializeAsync returns. Dialog Suppression records ownership immediately after the adapter subscribes and invokes its existing unsubscribe path if later logging fails, preserving both the initialization and cleanup failures. Core's ViewActivated event subscription follows the same transaction as module lifecycles. Its attach and rollback operations are force-queued, and host state is not published until the subscription succeeds. ContextualRibbonInjector Base class for dynamic ribbon UI that appears based on application state (typically selection). It implements IHookLifecycle; tool modules register the concrete injector against that lifecycle contract. public abstract partial class ContextualRibbonInjector : IHookLifecycle, IDisposable Use Cases: Adding "Edit" buttons to contextual tabs when tool-specific elements are selected Showing/hiding ribbon controls based on selection state Injecting panels into Revit's contextual "Modify" tabs Lifecycle: InitializeAsync called during HookHost.AttachAsync(...) Injector creates its edit event and subscribes to SelectionChanged transactionally. If post-subscription callbacks or initial evaluation fail, it immediately runs its own cleanup in the queued initialization context, attempts event detach, contextual UI removal, and edit-event disposal, and preserves both initialization and cleanup failures. Contextual edit ExternalEvent handlers validate the tool's registered command type through CommandPreflight before running the edit flow, so ribbon-panel settings warnings and command registration policy are shared with normal ToolCommand execution. Attach rollback uses the queued RollbackAsync path; normal App shutdown calls synchronous Shutdown to unsubscribe and remove contextual UI before HookHost.Detach() returns. The selection controller retains the exact detach action captured at successful subscription, so shutdown does not need to manufacture or queue a new UIApplication. ExternalEvent Rule: Create ExternalEvent instances only from standard Revit API execution contexts (for example, inside InitializeAsync/RefreshAsync work that runs through ModelessQueuedCallGate). Do not call ExternalEvent.Create(...) directly from Autodesk ribbon command callbacks. Shutdown Completion Contract Revit's IExternalApplication.OnShutdown boundary is synchronous. AppShutdownLifecycle.Shutdown calls AppShutdownWorkflow.RunSynchronously directly in that API turn. It cancels startup and disposes its cancellation source only when startup is already complete or absent, detaches hooks, and disposes runtime hosts before returning. It does not queue Revit work or pump the dispatcher. Unfinished startup or deferred observation produces Result.Failed after every owned teardown action is attempted. IHookLifecycle defines three operations: initialization calls asynchronous InitializeAsync; attach rollback calls asynchronous RollbackAsync, retaining the queued Revit call-gate path because rollback may resume away from the UI callback; application shutdown calls synchronous Shutdown on Revit's callback thread. This method has no cancellation token because it cannot publish or await background work; HookShutdownAction owns only the resulting plain Action. HookCatalog consumes only this lifecycle contract; it has no concrete Contextual Ribbon type check and no task-completion adapter. The coordinator retains successfully initialized owners for reverse-order attach rollback. HookHost also retains each attempted owner before its initializer runs. Normal shutdown therefore reaches subscriptions created during partial attach or an unfinished rollback. HookAttachAction cancels pending work, prevents later initialization and rollback dispatch, and makes completed shutdown idempotent. Cancellation failure does not prevent its shutdown callback. Failed callbacks remain available for retry. Late attachment completion does not invoke Revit shutdown callbacks from a background thread. Core owns pending WPF DispatcherOperation handles. Posting registers its owner before BeginInvoke, attaches the returned handle, and rechecks retirement so a late handle is aborted even if shutdown drained the registry while posting was in progress. At the end of synchronous shutdown, DispatcherOperationRegistry.Retire closes posting, releases callbacks and cancellation registrations, and aborts pending operations. It invokes no payload callbacks and leaves their completion tasks pending. Posts refused before queueing return canceled tasks. Ordinary WindowStaticRuntime.Reset does not retire the queue. Logger, ribbon, notification and progress posts share WpfDispatcher.Post. Callback failures are observed and reported; a failing error reporter remains on the completion task and cannot escape into Dispatcher.UnhandledException. Cancellation of an active operation keeps normal installed behavior. Retirement does not pump WPF to finish tasks. View-activated task runtime failures are the exception to generic banner suppression: Core's ViewActivatedTaskRunner presents one canonical auto-update failure banner, then lets the safe executor capture the failed task outcome without presenting a second generic banner. The IViewActivationTask System For the common pattern of "do something when a view activates," DBTools provides a higher-level abstraction: IViewActivationTask. The single ViewActivationHook dispatches to all registered tasks. IViewActivationTask Interface public interface IViewActivationTask { string TaskId { get; } string DisplayName { get; } IReadOnlyCollection<string> WarningIdsToSetOnFailure { get; } // Returns this attempt's admission, or null to skip it Task<ViewActivationAdmission?> AdmitAsync(UIApplication uiapp, ViewActivatedEventArgs args, CancellationToken ct); } // One admitted attempt; the task captures exactly the state its execution uses public sealed class ViewActivationAdmission { public ViewActivationAdmission(Func<CancellationToken, Task> execute); public Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken ct); } IViewActivationTask has no execution method. The hook executes the admission that this attempt's AdmitAsync returned, once. No admission is stored on the task or reaches another attempt. Each admission captures typed state: ViewActivationTask<TSettings> captures its settings snapshot, and the Foundation Tags prerequisite monitor captures the admitted document and its key. ViewActivationTask A base class that provides settings integration and common checks: public abstract class ViewActivationTask<TSettings> : IViewActivationTask where TSettings : class, IAutoUpdateSettings, new() { public async Task<ViewActivationAdmission?> AdmitAsync(...) { var settings = _settingsProvider.Get(_settingsSection); // Built-in checks if (!settings.AutoUpdateEnabled) return null; if (_warnings.IsWarningActive(...)) return null; // Delegate to subclass if (!await ShouldRunInternalAsync(uiapp, args, settings, ct)) return null; // The admission executes with this attempt's settings snapshot; settings are never read again return new ViewActivationAdmission(executionCt => ExecuteInternalAsync(uiapp, args, settings, executionCt)); } protected virtual Task<bool> ShouldRunInternalAsync(...) => Task.FromResult(true); protected abstract Task ExecuteInternalAsync(UIApplication uiapp, ViewActivatedEventArgs args, TSettings settings, CancellationToken ct); } A settings-read failure can therefore occur only in AdmitAsync, where Core sets the task's warnings. Execution Flow sequenceDiagram participant Revit participant Host as HookHost participant Exec as ISafeExecutor participant Handler as ViewActivationHook participant Task as IViewActivationTask participant Settings as ISettingsProvider Revit->>Host: ViewActivated event Host->>Exec: RunWithoutThrowingAsync(handler dispatch) Exec->>Handler: OnViewActivatedAsync() loop For each registered task Handler->>Task: AdmitAsync() Task->>Settings: Get(settingsSection) alt AutoUpdateEnabled && no active warning Task-->>Handler: admission (captures the settings snapshot) Handler->>Exec: RunWithoutThrowingAsync(admission.ExecuteAsync) Exec->>Task: admission.ExecuteAsync() alt Success Task-->>Exec: Complete else Failure Note over Exec,Task: Core runner shows the canonical auto-update failure banner; executor records the failed outcome and suppresses propagation to protect the Revit event loop Note over Task,Settings: Core's ViewActivationHook skips the task for this document session. Warning ids are set only by AdmitAsync failures and by task-owned prerequisite or configuration checks end else Disabled or warning active Task-->>Handler: null (skip) end end Registering Hooks In ToolModule.RegisterHooks() Override RegisterHooks in your ToolModule to register hook handlers: public sealed class MyToolModule : ToolModule { public override void RegisterServices(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { // Register the handler as a service services.AddSingleton<MyContextualInjector>(); } public override void RegisterHooks(ToolRegistry registry, ToolManifest manifest) { Guard.NotNull(registry, nameof(registry)); Guard.NotNull(manifest, nameof(manifest)); registry.RegisterHook<IHookLifecycle, MyContextualInjector>(); } } Registering View Activated Tasks View-activated tasks use a different pattern. Instead of registering directly as hooks, they're registered as IViewActivationTask services that the single ViewActivationHook collects: public override void RegisterServices(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { var warningIds = GetWarningIdsOrThrow(manifest); services.AddSingleton<IViewActivationTask>(sp => new ViewActivatedTask( sp.GetRequiredService<ISettingsProvider>(), sp.GetRequiredService<SettingsSection<ElevationTagsSettings>>(), sp.GetRequiredService<ISettingsWarningService>(), sp.GetRequiredService<ElevationTagsUpdater>(), sp.GetRequiredService<IErrorNotifier>(), sp.GetRequiredService<ILogger<ViewActivatedTask>>(), warningIds)); } Registration in AppHooksToolModule The manifest type DBTools.App.Composition.AppHooksToolModule registers the single ViewActivationHook that dispatches to all tasks: public sealed class AppHooksToolModule : ToolModule { public override void RegisterServices(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { services.AddSingleton<ViewActivationHook>(); } public override void RegisterHooks(ToolRegistry registry, ToolManifest manifest) { registry.RegisterHook<ViewActivationHook, ViewActivationHook>(); } } Implementing Hook Handlers Step 1: Define Your Handler Class public sealed class MyViewActivatedTask : ViewActivationTask<MyToolSettings> { public MyViewActivatedTask( ISettingsProvider settings, SettingsSection<MyToolSettings> settingsSection, ISettingsWarningService warnings, IErrorNotifier notifier, ILogger<MyViewActivatedTask> logger, IReadOnlyCollection<string> warningIds) : base(settings, settingsSection, warnings, notifier, logger, "mytool.updater", "My Tool Auto-Update", warningIds) { } } Step 2: Implement ShouldRunInternalAsync (Optional) Filter when your task should run based on view type, document state, etc.: protected override Task<bool> ShouldRunInternalAsync( UIApplication uiapp, ViewActivatedEventArgs args, MyToolSettings settings, CancellationToken ct) { var view = uiapp.ActiveUIDocument?.Document?.ActiveView; if (view == null) return Task.FromResult(false); // Only run in floor plans return Task.FromResult( view.ViewType == ViewType.FloorPlan || view.ViewType == ViewType.CeilingPlan); } Step 3: Implement ExecuteInternalAsync Perform the actual work with the settings that admitted this attempt: protected override Task ExecuteInternalAsync( UIApplication uiapp, ViewActivatedEventArgs args, MyToolSettings settings, CancellationToken ct) { var doc = uiapp.ActiveUIDocument?.Document ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("No active document."); var view = doc.ActiveView ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("No active view."); var gate = new InlineCallGate(uiapp); var tx = new TransactionRunner(gate); var updater = new MyAutoUpdater(tx, doc, view, Logger, settings); updater.Run(); return Task.CompletedTask; } Step 4: Register in Your ToolModule public override void RegisterServices(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { var warningIds = new[] { "mytool.auto_update.warning" }; services.AddSingleton<IViewActivationTask>(sp => new MyViewActivatedTask( sp.GetRequiredService<ISettingsProvider>(), sp.GetRequiredService<SettingsSection<MyToolSettings>>(), sp.GetRequiredService<ISettingsWarningService>(), sp.GetRequiredService<IErrorNotifier>(), sp.GetRequiredService<ILogger<MyViewActivatedTask>>(), warningIds)); } Implementing Contextual Ribbon Injectors For tools that need dynamic ribbon UI (like SGT's "Edit" button on selected girts): Step 1: Implement IHookLifecycle public sealed class MyContextualInjector : IHookLifecycle { private readonly ILogger<MyContextualInjector> _logger; private readonly ISafeExecutor _executor; private Action? _detach; public Task InitializeAsync(UIControlledApplication application, CancellationToken ct) { if (_detach != null) return Task.CompletedTask; // Subscribe to selection changes // Use ModelessQueuedCallGate for safe async access return _gate.RunAsync(app => { app.SelectionChanged += OnSelectionChanged; _detach = () => app.SelectionChanged -= OnSelectionChanged;
