}, ct); } public Task RollbackAsync(UIControlledApplication application, CancellationToken ct) { if (_detach == null) return Task.CompletedTask; return _gate.RunAsync(_ => Detach(), ct); } public void Shutdown(UIControlledApplication application) => Detach(); private void Detach() { _detach?.Invoke(); _detach = null; RemoveInjectedUI(); } } Step 2: Handle Selection Changes private async void OnSelectionChanged(object? sender, SelectionChangedEventArgs e) { if (sender is not UIApplication uiapp) return; await _executor.RunWithoutThrowingAsync( () => RefreshAsync(uiapp, CancellationToken.None), _logger, notifier: null, opts: new SafeExecuteOptions { Name = "My Contextual Selection Hook", BannerMode = SafeExecuteOptions.Mode.SuppressAlways }, ct: CancellationToken.None); } Step 3: Inject UI into Contextual Tabs private void EnsureInjected(UIApplication uiapp) { var ribbon = ComponentManager.Ribbon; if (ribbon == null) return; var targetTab = TryGetContextualTab(ribbon); if (targetTab == null) return; var panel = EnsurePanel(targetTab); var btn = BuildButton(); btn.CommandHandler = new RibbonButtonCommand(OnButtonClick); panel.Source.Items.Add(btn); } Hook Execution Order Registration Order Hooks are resolved in the order they were registered: AppHooksToolModule registers ViewActivationHook (core) Tool modules register their IViewActivationTask implementations Tool modules register IHookLifecycle implementations for contextual ribbon lifecycle work Dispatch Order flowchart LR subgraph Startup["App Startup"] A1[Attach Hook Host] A2[Initialize lifecycle actions] A3[Queue ViewActivated subscription] A4[Publish attached state] end subgraph Runtime["Runtime Events"] R1[ViewActivated fires] R2[For each handler in order] R3[For each task in order] end subgraph Shutdown["App Shutdown"] S1[Detach Hook Host] S2[Unsubscribe ViewActivated] S3[Shutdown lifecycle actions] end A1 --> A2 --> A3 --> A4 A4 -.->|"User navigates"| R1 R1 --> R2 --> R3 R3 -.->|"App closes"| S1 S1 --> S2 --> S3 Priority Considerations Currently, hooks execute in registration order without explicit priority. If you need guaranteed ordering: Register in a specific order through AppToolModuleRegistrar Or coordinate within a single handler that manages multiple sub-tasks Common Patterns Auto-Update on View Change The most common pattern for tools like Elevation Tags: // 1. Define settings with IAutoUpdateSettings public class MySettings : IAutoUpdateSettings { public bool AutoUpdateEnabled { get; set; } = true; public bool HasWarning { get; set; } } // 2. Create a task extending ViewActivationTask<TSettings> public class MyAutoUpdateTask : ViewActivationTask<MySettings> { protected override Task<bool> ShouldRunInternalAsync(...) { // Filter by view type return Task.FromResult(view.ViewType == ViewType.FloorPlan); } protected override Task ExecuteInternalAsync(...) { // Perform update logic with the admitted settings } } // 3. Register in ToolModule services.AddSingleton<IViewActivationTask>(...); Contextual Ribbon Button For tools that need UI when specific elements are selected: // 1. Implement IHookLifecycle or derive from ContextualRibbonInjector public class MyInjector : ContextualRibbonInjector { // Track subscribed state private bool _subscribed; // Track injected buttons for visibility control private readonly Dictionary<string, RibbonButton> _buttons = new(); // Evaluate selection and show/hide button private void OnSelectionChanged(...) { bool hasMyElements = EvaluateSelection(uiapp); ToggleButtons(visible: hasMyElements); } } // 2. Register hook registry.RegisterHook<IHookLifecycle, MyInjector>(); Warning Integration Feature warnings are for actionable prerequisite/configuration failures (e.g., missing shared parameters, invalid settings). They should not be activated for transient/runtime exceptions. // Example: set warning only for actionable prerequisite failure var eval = MyPrereqEvaluator.Evaluate(uiapp, doc, tx, logger); if (eval.Kind == PrereqKind.Invalid) { foreach (var warningId in WarningIdsToSetOnFailure) warnings.SetWarning(warningId, true); return; } // Runtime exceptions propagate: Core shows the failure banner and skips the task for this document session (do NOT set warnings) updater.Run(); The warning IDs must be defined in the tool's settings pack and match entries in manifest.yml. Creating New Hook Types To add a new hook type (advanced): Prefer the existing lifecycle contract For attach/shutdown lifecycle work, implement IHookLifecycle and register the concrete type through ToolRegistry.RegisterHook<IHookLifecycle, TImplementation>(). Do not add a new hook contract for contextual ribbon or dialog suppression variants. Event-specific contracts require Core host support Add a new hook contract only when the Revit event needs a different dispatch shape than attach/shutdown lifecycle. The Core hook catalog must explicitly allow the contract and HookHost must own the subscription/detach path. Step 1: Define the Interface // In DBTools.Core/Tools/ public interface IDocumentClosingHookHandler { Task OnDocumentClosingAsync( UIControlledApplication application, DocumentClosingEventArgs args, CancellationToken ct); } Step 2: Add catalog support, resolution, and subscription public async Task AttachAsync(UIControlledApplication application, CancellationToken ct) { // ... existing code ... var closingHandlers = ResolveHandlers<IDocumentClosingHookHandler>(); if (closingHandlers.Count > 0) application.DocumentClosing += OnDocumentClosing; _closingHandlers = closingHandlers; } private async void OnDocumentClosing(object? sender, DocumentClosingEventArgs args) { if (_closingHandlers == null || _closingHandlers.Count == 0) return; try { await _executor.RunWithoutThrowingAsync( async () => { foreach (var handler in _closingHandlers) await handler.OnDocumentClosingAsync(_application!, args, CancellationToken.None); }, _logger, notifier: null, opts: new SafeExecuteOptions { /* ... */ }, ct: CancellationToken.None); } catch { /* Suppress to protect Revit */ } } Step 3: Add Detach Logic public void Detach() { // Unsubscribe direct host events, complete every lifecycle action, // aggregate contextual failures, then clear ownership. } Performance Considerations Don't Block the UI Thread Hooks run in response to Revit events. Blocking causes UI freezes: // BAD - blocks UI public Task ExecuteAsync(...) { Thread.Sleep(5000); // Never do this! return Task.CompletedTask; } // GOOD - async work public async Task ExecuteAsync(...) { await SomeAsyncOperation(); } Use SafeExecutor Options Wisely For frequent hooks like view activation, suppress banners: new SafeExecutionOptions("View activation") { BannerMode = SafeExecutionOptions.Mode.ErrorOnly // Only show errors } SafeExecutionOptions.LogFailure defaults to true. Disable it only for a lifecycle-owned background task whose already-published observer records the same fault after task observation; the task must still fail fast and remain observable. Ordinary hooks retain the default failure log. Filter Early with ShouldRunInternalAsync Avoid expensive work when the hook shouldn't run: protected override Task<bool> ShouldRunInternalAsync(...) { // Quick checks first var view = uiapp.ActiveUIDocument?.Document?.ActiveView; if (view == null) return Task.FromResult(false); if (view.ViewType != ViewType.FloorPlan) return Task.FromResult(false); // Only then check more expensive conditions return Task.FromResult(true); } Batch Operations in Transactions When modifying elements, batch changes in a single transaction: protected override Task ExecuteInternalAsync(...) { using var tx = new Transaction(doc, "Auto Update"); tx.Start(); foreach (var element in elementsToUpdate) UpdateElement(element); tx.Commit(); return Task.CompletedTask; } Real Examples ElevationTags Auto-Update The Elevation Tags tool uses a view-activated task to update tag values when entering floor plans: internal sealed class ViewActivatedTask : ViewActivationTask<ElevationTagsSettings> { public ViewActivatedTask( ISettingsProvider settings, SettingsSection<ElevationTagsSettings> settingsSection, ISettingsWarningService warnings, ElevationTagsUpdater updateService, IErrorNotifier notifier, ILogger<ViewActivatedTask> logger, IReadOnlyCollection<string> warningIds) : base(settings, settingsSection, warnings, notifier, logger, "structural.elevation_tags.updater", "Elevation Tags", warningIds) { _updateService = updateService; } protected override Task<bool> ShouldRunInternalAsync(...) { var view = uiapp.ActiveUIDocument?.Document?.ActiveView; return Task.FromResult( view?.ViewType == ViewType.FloorPlan || view?.ViewType == ViewType.CeilingPlan); } protected override Task ExecuteInternalAsync(...) { _updateService.Run(doc, uiapp, view, settings); return Task.CompletedTask; } } SGT Contextual Ribbon The Super Girt Tool injects an "Edit" button into the contextual "Modify | Structural Framing" tab: public sealed class ContextualRibbonInjector : ContextualRibbonInjector { public Task InitializeAsync(UIControlledApplication application, CancellationToken ct) { return _gate.RunAsync(app => { EnsureEditEventCreated(); // ExternalEvent.Create in API-safe context app.SelectionChanged += OnSelectionChanged; _subscribed = true; EnsureInjected(app); EvaluateAndToggle(app); }, ct); } private void EvaluateAndToggle(UIApplication uiapp) { var (hasGirts, systemIds) = EvaluateSelection(uiapp); UpdateSystemIds(systemIds); ToggleButtons(hasGirts, hasGirts); } private void EnsureInjected(UIApplication uiapp) { var targetTab = TryGetContextualModifyStructuralTab(ribbon); var panel = EnsurePanel(targetTab); var btn = BuildButton(); panel.Source.Items.Add(btn); } } AppHooksToolModule Registration The core hook module that wires up view-activated handling: public sealed class AppHooksToolModule : ToolModule { public override void RegisterServices(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { services.AddSingleton<ViewActivationHook>(); } public override void RegisterHooks(ToolRegistry registry, ToolManifest manifest) { registry.RegisterHook<ViewActivationHook, ViewActivationHook>(); } } Debugging Hooks Enable Debug Logging Hook handlers log at debug level. Enable in your development configuration: { "Serilog": { "MinimumLevel": { "Override": { "DBTools.App.Features.Hooks": "Debug" } } } } Common Issues Symptom Possible Cause Solution Hook never fires Not registered in RegisterHooks Verify RegisterHook<>() call Handler not resolved Service not registered Add AddSingleton<>() in RegisterServices UI thread deadlock Sync-waiting on async in hook Use async void for event handlers, never .Wait() Hook runs but no effect AdmitAsync returning null Check settings (AutoUpdateEnabled, HasWarning) Exception in hook Various Check logs; ISafeExecutor logs all errors See Also Creating a New Tool - Complete guide to building DBTools tools Architecture Overview - System architecture and component interactions Settings Packs - How tools integrate with the settings infrastructure

developer-guide/developing/modularity.ht.title: Leveraging DBTools Modularity | DB Tools
developer-guide/developing/modularity.ht.summary: Leveraging DBTools Modularity DBTools is designed as a modular Revit add-in platform where tools share common infrastructure while maintaining clear boundaries. This guide explains how to use DBTools.Core services and DBTools.Presentation WPF resources without crossing the stable/collectible boundary. Philosophy DBTools follows these modularity principles: Shared Infrastructure, Independent Tools - Core services are centralized; tools are self-contained Dependency Injection First - All services are resolved through DI, enabling testing and flexibility Contract-Driven - Interfaces define contracts; implementations can vary per context Error Handling at Boundaries - All entrypoints run inside ISafeExecutor Window-Scoped Theming - Each window owns its theme resources to avoid cross-add-in conflicts Composition Owns Concrete UI Services - Core window initialization attaches shared contracts, while App startup supplies concrete notification features such as WindowErrorNotifier; UI window error boundaries and logger-window error relay sinks depend on the UI-owned IWindowErrorLogSurface contract rather than the full logger-window shell implementation, WindowErrorBoundaryPresenter owns handled-error banner/log-surface presentation outside the dispatcher boundary host, and view-activated hooks consume IErrorNotifier from DI instead of constructing concrete notification feature types inside Core hook gates Two-Tier DI Architecture DBTools uses a two-tier dependency injection model: Tier Lifetime Purpose Examples Singleton Application lifetime Infrastructure services ISafeExecutor, IAlertService, ISettingsProvider, ToolRegistry Scoped Per-command lifetime Revit context services ITransactionRunner, IRevitCallGate, IRevitRunScope Shared Services from DBTools.Core ISafeExecutor The central error handling service. All tool entrypoints must execute within ISafeExecutor. public interface ISafeExecutor { Task RunAsync(Func<Task> action, ILogger logger, IErrorNotifier? notifier, SafeExecuteOptions opts, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<SafeExecutionResult> RunWithoutThrowingAsync(Func<Task> action, ILogger logger, IErrorNotifier? notifier, SafeExecuteOptions opts, CancellationToken ct = default); } What it provides: Correlation IDs for log tracing Execution timing Exception logging with full stack traces and inner exceptions Cancellation admission immediately before caller work, inside the existing cancellation boundary Diagnostic formatting through the internal SafeExecution/Runtime/ExceptionDiagnosticsLogger; SafeExecutor retains policy, notification, and propagation decisions User notification via banners Fatal-error surfacing through the execution-owned ISafeExecutionFailureSurface; App composition adapts the UI-owned log surface's show action without making Logging depend on SafeExecution Banner success/error presentation and notifier-failure logging inside the retained SafeExecutor execution boundary Explicit failure-policy split: RunAsync(...) rethrows, while RunWithoutThrowingAsync(...) is the named opt-in path for callers that intentionally suppress propagation after logging/notifying Source: src/DBTools.Core/SafeExecution/Runtime/SafeExecutor.cs:59-103 Source: src/DBTools.Core/SafeExecution/Runtime/ExceptionDiagnosticsLogger.cs:11-211 Usage in a command: // Commands automatically use ISafeExecutor via ToolCommand base class [Transaction(TransactionMode.Manual)] public sealed class GmCommand : ToolCommand { protected override Task RunAsync(ICommandContext context) { Guard.NotNull(context, nameof(context)); var uiapp = context.UIApplication ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("[SpecFail/GM/UIAppMissing] UIApplication is required."); var logger = context.Resolve<ILogger<GmCommand>>(); var loggerWindowManager = context.Resolve<ILoggerWindowHost>(); // Build a lightweight document fingerprint for resume staleness checks string? docKey = null; try { var doc = uiapp.ActiveUIDocument?.Document; if (doc != null) { var path = doc.PathName; var title = doc.Title; docKey = !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(path) ? path : title; } } catch (System.Exception ex) { logger.LogWarning("[GM] Failed to compute DocumentKey: {Message}", ex.Message); } // Launch GM UI ShellLauncher.Launch(context, docKey); loggerWindowManager.ShowIfDebugModeOrEnableForPendingError(); return Task.CompletedTask; } protected override SafeExecuteOptions CreateExecuteOptions(Autodesk.Revit.UI.ExternalCommandData commandData) { return new SafeExecuteOptions { Name = "Global Mapper", // Launching the GM window is not a "user-completed" operation; avoid a success banner on open. BannerMode = SafeExecuteOptions.Mode.ErrorOnly }; } } ITransactionRunner Unified API for executing Revit model modifications with automatic transaction management. public interface ITransactionRunner { Task RunInActiveDocumentAsync(string name, Action<RevitTransactionContext> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<T> RunInActiveDocumentAsync<T>(string name, Func<RevitTransactionContext, T> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task RunInDocumentAsync(Document doc, string name, Action<RevitTransactionContext> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<T> RunInDocumentAsync<T>(Document doc, string name, Func<RevitTransactionContext, T> action, CancellationToken ct = default); } Key behaviors: Auto-selects transaction type: SubTransaction if doc.IsModifiable, otherwise new Transaction Cross-document protection Failure handling with TransactionFailurePreprocessor Usage example: public class FoundationTypeOrganizer { private readonly ITransactionRunner _tx; public FoundationTypeOrganizer(ITransactionRunner tx, Document doc, ILogger logger) { _tx = tx; // ... } public async Task OrganizeAsync() { await _tx.RunInDocumentAsync(_doc, "Organize Foundation Types", tx => { var doc = tx.Document; // Modify document - transaction is automatic }); } } ITransactionGroupService Manages transaction groups for operations requiring multiple transactions to appear as a single undo item. public interface ITransactionGroupService { bool IsActive { get; } Task BeginAsync(string name, CancellationToken ct = default); Task FinalizeAsync(TransactionGroupFinalization finalization, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<bool> IsGroupHealthyAsync(CancellationToken ct = default); } Usage for batch operations: public class TdvService { private readonly ITransactionRunner _tx; private readonly ITransactionGroupService _group; public TdvService(IRevitCallGate gate, ITransactionRunner tx, ITransactionGroupService group, ILogger<TdvService> logger) { _tx = tx; _group = group; // ... } public async Task ApplyMultipleChangesAsync() { var commitGroup = true; await _group.BeginAsync("Batch Apply"); try { // Multiple transactions appear as one undo item await _tx.RunInActiveDocumentAsync("Step 1", tx => { /* ... */ }); await _tx.RunInActiveDocumentAsync("Step 2", tx => { /* ... */ }); await _tx.RunInActiveDocumentAsync("Step 3", tx => { /* ... */ }); } catch { commitGroup = false; throw; } finally { await _group.FinalizeAsync(commitGroup, CancellationToken.None); } } } IAlertService Service for showing alert dialogs with various body types. public interface IAlertService { AlertResult Show(AlertRequest request); bool Confirm(string message, string title = "DB Tools"); T? SelectSingle<T>(AlertSelectionRequest<T> request) where T : class; IReadOnlyList<T> SelectMultiple<T>(AlertSelectionRequest<T> request) where T : class; } Usage examples: // Simple confirmation var alerts = context.Resolve<IAlertService>(); if (alerts.Confirm("Delete 15 elements?", "Confirm Delete")) { // Proceed } // Single selection var selectedLevel = alerts.SelectSingle(new AlertSelectionRequest<Level>( levels, level => level.Name, "Select Level", "Target Level") { Message = "Choose the level to place elements on" }); // Multiple selection var selectedTypes = alerts.SelectMultiple(new AlertSelectionRequest<FamilySymbol>( familyTypes, t => t.Name, "Select Types", "Types to Process")); Selection dialog request construction and typed result extraction live behind the Core-owned selection dialog policy; concrete selection-list body composition is a Core alert-body factory responsibility, and consumers still use the IAlertService request-object API. ILogger DBTools uses Microsoft.Extensions.Logging with Serilog as the provider. // Resolve from DI var logger = context.Resolve<ILogger<MyService>>(); // Or use the context's logger var logger = context.Logger; // Structured logging logger.LogInformation("Processing {Count} elements in {Document}", elements.Count, doc.Title); logger.LogWarning("[GM] Failed to compute DocumentKey: {Message}", ex.Message); logger.LogError(ex, "[{Command}] execution failed.", GetType().Name); Important: Always use structured logging with named placeholders, not string interpolation. IRevitRunScope Represents a single Revit run scope (command, modeless session, or test). Owns UIApplication, the call gate, document access, and disposal; scoped transaction services are resolved from IAppRunScope or ICommandContext with Resolve<T>(). public interface IRevitRunScope : IDisposable { UIApplication UIApplication { get; } IRevitCallGate CallGate { get; } UIDocument GetActiveUiDocument(); Document GetActiveDocument(); Document GetVerifiedActiveDocument(Document expectedDocument, string? context = null); } The verification operation is current-state based: callers retain an expected document only as a session identity and receive the active document only after validity and DocumentSessionKey equality are established. Run Scope Profiles: Profile Use Case Description InlineUi Modal commands, daemon-hosted Revit automation Executes directly on Revit UI thread QueuedModeless Long-running/modeless tools Uses the App-owned ExternalEvent host ISettingsProvider Typed settings access with persistence. Each read combines application defaults and the current per-year file. public interface ISettingsProvider { TSettings Get<TSettings>(SettingsSection<TSettings> section) where TSettings : class, new(); Task CommitAsync(IReadOnlyCollection<SettingsSectionWrite> writes, CancellationToken ct = default); } Use SettingsSection<T>.CreateWrite(value) to build a typed batch. The provider commits the complete batch with one file swap, so consumers never observe a partially saved settings-window operation. Usage: // Via ISettingsProvider (singleton) var settings = context.Resolve<ISettingsProvider>(); var section = context.Resolve<SettingsSection<GmSettings>>(); var gmSettings = settings.Get(section); Shared UI from DBTools.Presentation BrushKeys All theme brushes are defined using ComponentResourceKey for reliable cross-template resolution: public static class BrushKeys { // Brand colors public static ComponentResourceKey Primary => new(typeof(BrushKeys), "Brush.Primary"); public static ComponentResourceKey Secondary => new(typeof(BrushKeys), "Brush.Secondary"); // Surface colors public static ComponentResourceKey Paper => new(typeof(BrushKeys), "Brush.Paper"); public static ComponentResourceKey Surface => new(typeof(BrushKeys), "Brush.Surface"); public static ComponentResourceKey CardSurface => new(typeof(BrushKeys), "Brush.CardSurface"); // Text colors (WCAG AA compliant) public static ComponentResourceKey Body => new(typeof(BrushKeys), "Brush.Body"); public static ComponentResourceKey TextSecondary => new(typeof(BrushKeys), "Brush.TextSecondary"); public static ComponentResourceKey TextMuted => new(typeof(BrushKeys), "Brush.TextMuted"); // Status colors public static ComponentResourceKey Success => new(typeof(BrushKeys), "Brush.Success"); public static ComponentResourceKey Warning => new(typeof(BrushKeys), "Brush.Warning"); public static ComponentResourceKey Error => new(typeof(BrushKeys), "Brush.Error"); // DataGrid specific public static ComponentResourceKey DataGridRowSelected => new(typeof(BrushKeys), "Brush.DataGrid.RowSelected"); public static ComponentResourceKey DataGridAccentStripe => new(typeof(BrushKeys), "Brush.DataGrid.AccentStripe"); // ... 130+ additional keys } Usage in XAML: <Window xmlns:theme="clr-namespace:DBTools.Presentation;assembly=DBTools.Presentation"> <Border Background="{DynamicResource {x:Static theme:ThemeBrushKeys.Surface}}"> <TextBlock Text="Hello" Foreground="{DynamicResource {x:Static theme:ThemeBrushKeys.Body}}"/> </Border> </Window> Design Tokens Standard spacing, sizing, and typography values for consistent layouts: <!-- Spacing --> <Thickness x:Key="Spacing4">4</Thickness> <Thickness x:Key="Spacing8">8</Thickness> <Thickness x:Key="Spacing16">16</Thickness> <!-- Padding --> <Thickness x:Key="Pad8">8</Thickness> <Thickness x:Key="Card.Padding">16,12</Thickness> <!-- Corner radius --> <CornerRadius x:Key="Radius4">4</CornerRadius> <CornerRadius x:Key="Radius8">8</CornerRadius> <!-- Typography --> <sys:Double x:Key="FontSize.Body">13</sys:Double> <sys:Double x:Key="FontSize.Title">16</sys:Double> <sys:Double x:Key="FontSize.Header">20</sys:Double> Tool-window sessions Tool UI uses raw embedded XAML without x:Class or code-behind. Its root is a stable view element such as Grid; ToolWindowHost supplies the modal or modeless shell. Core's ToolWindowFactory installs the theme, owner, icon, error boundary and progress lifecycle before parsing, then registers the session for normal close and generation retirement. using var xaml = new MemoryStream(ToolWindowXaml.ReadEmbeddedResource( typeof(MyToolWindowViewModel).Assembly, "DBTools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolWindow.xaml")); var session = factory.Create(ToolWindowKind.Modal, xaml, viewModel, new ToolWindowOptions { Title = "My Tool", Width = 800, Height = 600 }); _ = session.ShowDialog(); Use ToolWindowKind.Modeless and session.Show() for a modeless surface. Register payload event handlers and owned cleanup through the session. A custom shell initializer owns its cleanup handle and must register it with session.AddCleanup. DI Patterns Creating a Tool Module Every tool implements ToolModule to register its services: public sealed class GmToolModule : ToolModule { public override void RegisterServices(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { Guard.NotNull(services, nameof(services)); Guard.NotNull(manifest, nameof(manifest)); services.AddGm(); // Extension method for cleaner registration } } ToolModule Base Class public abstract class ToolModule { public virtual void RegisterSettings(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { } public virtual void RegisterServices(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { } public virtual void RegisterSettingsPacks(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { } public virtual void RegisterHooks(ToolRegistry registry, ToolManifest manifest) { } } After a module registers settings, services, settings packs, and hooks into temporary startup surfaces, Core validates that the manifest owns at least one concrete responsibility: ribbon tools, settings, settings packs, or hooks. Ribbon registration construction also belongs to Core once App startup resolves the concrete Revit command and availability types. Service Registration Patterns This abbreviated excerpt shows the current registration surface and omits repetitive scoped registrations with explicit markers. public static class ServiceCollectionExtensions { /// <summary> /// Registers all GM services. Prefer creating a DI scope per Revit command invocation. /// </summary> public static IServiceCollection AddGm(this IServiceCollection services) { Guard.NotNull(services, nameof(services)); AddMappingServices(services); AddDuplicatesServices(services); AddSharedParameterServices(services); AddCommitReviewServices(services); AddUsageServices(services); AddDeepScanServices(services); AddPreviewServices(services); AddCachingServices(services); AddShellServices(services); return services; } private static void AddMappingServices(IServiceCollection services) { services.AddScoped<IApplyWriter, MappingSymbolCreationWriter>(); // ... additional IApplyWriter registrations omitted ... services.AddScoped<IApplyWriter, TypeApplicationWriter>(); // ... style, shared-parameter, and saved-mapping registrations omitted ... services.AddScoped<RevitMappingPlanExecutor>(); services.AddScoped<MappingPlanVerifier>(); } // ... AddDuplicatesServices, AddSharedParameterServices, AddUsageServices, // AddDeepScanServices, AddPreviewServices, and AddCachingServices omitted ... private static void AddCommitReviewServices(IServiceCollection services) { services.AddScoped<CommitReviewApplyService>(); services.AddScoped<CommitReviewWindowService>(); // ... additional commit-review services omitted ... } private static void AddShellServices(IServiceCollection services) { services.AddScoped<IElementNameQuery, ElementNameQuery>(); // ... catalog/filter services omitted ... services.AddScoped<FamilyScanner, FamilyScanner>(); services.AddScoped<ShellContext>(); } } Resolving Services in Commands protected override async Task RunAsync(ICommandContext context) { Guard.NotNull(context, nameof(context)); var uiapp = context.UIApplication ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("[SpecFail/GM/UIAppMissing] UIApplication is required."); var logger = context.Resolve<ILogger<GmCommand>>(); var loggerWindowManager = context.Resolve<ILoggerWindowHost>(); // Build a lightweight document fingerprint for resume staleness checks string? docKey = null; try { var doc = uiapp.ActiveUIDocument?.Document; if (doc != null) { var path = doc.PathName; var title = doc.Title; docKey = !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(path) ? path : title; } } catch (System.Exception ex) { logger.LogWarning("[GM] Failed to compute DocumentKey: {Message}", ex.Message); } // Launch GM UI ShellLauncher.Launch(context, docKey); loggerWindowManager.ShowIfDebugModeOrEnableForPendingError(); await Task.CompletedTask.ConfigureAwait(false); } Best Practices 1. Always Use ISafeExecutor at Entrypoints // DO: Inherit from ToolCommand (uses ISafeExecutor internally) public sealed class MyCommand : ToolCommand { protected override async Task RunAsync(ICommandContext context) { // ISafeExecutor wraps this automatically } } // DON'T: Create IExternalCommand without error handling public class BadCommand : IExternalCommand { public Result Execute(...) { // No error handling - will crash Revit } } 2. Prefer Scoped Services for Revit-Dependent Code // DO: Scoped registration for services that need Revit context services.AddScoped<IElementNameQuery, ElementNameQuery>(); services.AddScoped<FamilyScanner, FamilyScanner>(); // DON'T: Singleton for services that capture Document references services.AddSingleton<IBadService, ServiceThatHoldsDocument>(); // Memory leak! 3. Use Transaction Services, Not Raw Transactions // DO: Use ITransactionRunner await _tx.RunInActiveDocumentAsync("Create Wall", tx => { Wall.Create(tx.Document, curve, levelId, false); }); // DON'T: Create raw Transaction objects using var tx = new Transaction(doc, "Create Wall"); tx.Start(); Wall.Create(doc, curve, levelId, false); tx.Commit(); // Manual error handling required 4. Reference Theme Brushes via BrushKeys <!-- DO: Use BrushKeys for reliable resolution --> <Border Background="{DynamicResource {x:Static theme:BrushKeys.Surface}}"/> <!-- DON'T: Use string keys (fragile) --> <Border Background="{DynamicResource Brush.Surface}"/> 5. Use the shared window lifecycle Compose raw views through ToolWindowFactory. Use session.ShowDialog() or session.Show() for presentation and session.AddCleanup for owned state. Settings, Alert, Logger and banners follow this lifecycle. Payload code supplies view models and raw resources; Presentation owns every shell and teardown. Anti-Patterns to Avoid 1. Service Locator Pattern // DON'T: Use AppRuntimeAccessor.Resolve outside of command constructors public class BadService { public void DoWork() { var alerts = AppRuntimeAccessor.Resolve<IAlertService>(); // Hidden dependency } } // DO: Inject via constructor public class GoodService { private readonly IAlertService _alerts; public GoodService(IAlertService alerts) { _alerts = alerts; } } 2. Silent Failures // DON'T: Swallow exceptions try { DoWork(); } catch { /* silent failure */ } // DON'T: Return defaults pretending success catch (Exception) { return new List<Element>(); } // DO: Let ISafeExecutor handle errors await executor.RunAsync(async () => { DoWork(); // Exception propagates to error handling }, logger, notifier); 3. Capturing Document References // DON'T: Hold Document references in singleton services public class BadService { private readonly Document _doc; // Will become stale! public BadService(Document doc) => _doc = doc; } // DO: Accept Document per-call public class GoodService { public void DoWork(Document doc) { // Fresh reference each call } } 4. Raw Console/MessageBox Output // DON'T: Use Console or MessageBox Console.WriteLine("Debug info"); MessageBox.Show("Error occurred"); // DO: Use logging and IAlertService _logger.LogDebug("Debug info"); _alerts.Show(new AlertRequest("Error", new MessageBodyViewModel("Error occurred"))); 5. Bypassing Theme System // DON'T: Use hard-coded colors <Border Background="#222228"/> // DO: Use theme brushes <Border Background="{DynamicResource {x:Static theme:BrushKeys.Surface}}"/> Related Documentation DBTools.Core Project - Complete Core API reference Theme System - Detailed theming documentation Architecture Overview - System-wide architecture Quick Reference Table Need Service Lifetime Error handling at entrypoints ISafeExecutor Singleton Model modifications ITransactionRunner Scoped Batch undo operations ITransactionGroupService Scoped User dialogs IAlertService Singleton Logging ILogger<T> Singleton Revit context IRevitRunScope Scoped Thread-safe API access IRevitCallGate Scoped Settings access ISettingsProvider Singleton Fresh settings reads ISettingsProvider Singleton

developer-guide/developing/new-tool-guid.title: Creating New Tools in DBTools | DB Tools
developer-guide/developing/new-tool-guid.summary:
Creating New Tools in DBTools This guide covers the complete process of creating a new tool for the DBTools Revit add-in platform. By the end, you'll understand the tool module system, manifest configuration, command implementation, and UI patterns. Overview DBTools uses a manifest-driven plugin architecture. Each tool: Lives in its own folder under src/Tools/ Declares metadata via manifest.yml Implements a ToolModule subclass for DI registration Provides one or more ToolCommand implementations when it exposes ribbon commands May instead be a service/settings module with settings packs or hooks and no ribbon command Optionally includes WPF UI, settings, and hooks Tool Module Lifecycle stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Discovered: Manifest scan at startup Discovered --> Instantiated: Reflection creates module Instantiated --> Registered: RegisterSettings()
RegisterServices()
RegisterHooks() Registered --> Active: Ribbon/settings composed Active --> Active: Commands or hooks executed Active --> [*]: OnShutdown note right of Discovered ToolManifestLoader scans embedded manifest.yml files end note note right of Registered DI container configured, hooks attached end note Assembly ownership: Every manifest root under src/Tools/ owns a project that declares true and ships as its own file-backed assembly beneath the product year's Tools/ directory, including service and settings modules without ribbon buttons. Manifests name the actual owning assembly, such as DBTools.TDV, DBTools.SGT, or DBTools.Settings; tool IDs are not assembly aliases. App discovers every manifest centrally and resolves its declared owner from /Tools/.dll in the active owning context. Prerequisites Before creating a new tool: Ensure you can build the solution: bash build.sh Use the singular desktop target map: net10.0-windows for Revit 2026.5+ and Revit 2027 Decide on a tool category: Common, Structural, Testing, Services, or new category Choose a unique tool ID (e.g., DBTools.MyTool) Step 1: Directory Structure Create your tool folder under the appropriate category: src/Tools/ Common/ # General-purpose tools GM/ # Global Mapper (complex example) ElevationTags/ # Simple example Structural/ # Structural engineering tools SGT/ # Super Girt Tool (complex example) FramingJoins/ # Simple example Services/ # Cross-tool services/settings modules DialogSuppression/ Experimental/ # In-development / not-yet-production tools Minimal Ribbon Tool Structure src/Tools/// Assets/ my_tool.png # 32x32 icon for ribbon (required) my_tool_16.png # 16x16 small icon (optional) Features/ MyToolCommand.cs # ToolCommand implementation manifest.yml # Tool metadata and ribbon config ToolModule.cs # DI registration DBTools..csproj # Project file (for IDE/tests) Use this shape when the manifest declares tool.ribbonTools. The command type named by each ribbon tool must extend ToolCommand; the icons named by iconBaseKey live under Assets/; and the project file provides IDE navigation and command/test isolation. Minimal Service/Settings Module Structure src/Tools/Services// manifest.yml # Tool metadata plus settings/settingsPacks or hooks ToolModule.cs # DI, settings pack, and hook registration Use this shape for modules that register shared services, hooks, settings, or settings packs without adding a ribbon button. These modules omit tool.ribbonTools, ToolCommand implementations, and ribbon icons. Add Settings/, Hooks/, or other source folders only when the module owns those concerns; add a .csproj only when the module needs independent IDE/test isolation. Complex Tool Structure (with UI) src/Tools/// Assets/ *.png # Icons Features/ MyToolCommand.cs # Simple tools can keep commands at the Features root / # Complex tools group files by feature slice MySliceService.cs MySliceModels.cs Shell/ ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs # DI extension methods colocated with shell wiring DesignTime/ MyWindowDesignTimeViewModel.cs Services/ # Optional shell-only coordinators/factories ViewModels/ MyWindowViewModel.cs Views/ MyWindow.xaml MyWindow.xaml.cs Shared/ Domain/ Models/ State/ # Optional cross-feature state Revit/ # Optional Revit-facing adapters/services Services/ Settings/ # Optional settings/options Tests/ # Owner test projects split by execution host DBTools..Pure.Tests.csproj DBTools..Local.Tests.csproj Properties/ # Optional designer metadata/resources DesignTimeResources.xaml # Optional, only if the tool needs a design-time resource dictionary manifest.yml ToolModule.cs DBTools..csproj Step 2: Project File (.csproj) Create a project file for a tool that owns an assembly. It participates in the product-output build and also enables: IntelliSense and navigation Per-tool test projects Design-time XAML preview Service/settings modules without ribbon commands may omit the project file unless they need independent IDE or test coverage boundaries. Minimal Project File $(DBT_RevitTargetFramework) $(DBT_DesktopRevitHostIdentity) latest enable enable DBTools.MyTool true true $(NoWarn);CS0618;MA0038;MA0048;MA0016;MA0051;MA0098;MA0004;CA1707;CA1725;CA1068;MSB3277 enable 6.1 Resources\\Icons\\%(Filename)%(Extension) For Tools with WPF UI Add the following to your .csproj: true If the tool includes Properties\DesignTimeResources.xaml, also add: Designer MSBuild:Compile true Step 3: manifest.yml (Complete Schema) The manifest file declares your tool's metadata, ribbon configuration, and optional settings. Complete Schema Reference # Required: Unique tool identifier id: DBTools.MyTool # Required: Actual owning assembly name (without .dll) assembly: DBTools.MyTool # Required: Fully-qualified type name of ToolModule subclass moduleType: DBTools.MyTool.MyToolToolModule # Required: Load order (lower = earlier). Use 0 unless you need ordering. order: 0 # Optional: Sandbox windows for design-time preview sandboxWindows: - id: DBTools.MyTool.Main displayName: "My Tool" group: "Common" # or "Structural", "Testing", "Services" xamlResource: "DBTools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolWindow.xaml" designTimeViewModelType: "DBTools.MyTool.App.DesignTime.MyToolWindowDesignTimeViewModel" designTimeViewModelAssembly: "DBTools.MyTool" designTimeViewModelVisibility: Public # Required: Tool configuration. A command-bearing ribbon module declares ribbonTools; # a service/settings module may provide only settings and settingsPacks. tool: # Optional: Settings configuration settings: configSection: Tools.MyTool # Section in settings.{YEAR}.json # Optional: Settings packs for Settings window settingsPacks: - key: common.my_tool title: "My Tool" warnings: - id: core.my_tool.warning title: "My Tool Disabled" message: "Tool is disabled due to a configuration issue." disableTools: - DBTools.MyToolCommand # Required for ribbon modules; omit for service/settings modules with no ribbon button. ribbonTools: - internalName: DBTools.MyToolCommand commandType: DBTools.MyTool.Features.MyToolCommand availabilityType: DBTools.MyTool.Features.MyToolCommand runProfile: InlineUi displayText: "My Tool" iconBaseKey: my_tool tooltip: "Launch My Tool" controlKind: PushButton order: 50 Manifest Properties Reference Property Required Description id Yes Unique identifier (e.g., DBTools.MyTool) assembly Yes Actual assembly name without .dll; every tool owner uses DBTools. moduleType No Full type name of ToolModule subclass when the tool has module-owned services, settings, settings packs, or hooks order Yes Load order (0 for most tools) panel Yes for moduleless ribbon tools Ribbon panel for manifests without moduleType sandboxWindows No Design-time preview windows tool.settings.configSection No settings.{YEAR}.json section for typed JSON settings tool.settingsPacks No Settings window configuration tool.ribbonTools No Ribbon button definitions. Required only for command-bearing ribbon modules; service/settings modules may omit it. Every manifest tool section must have at least one concrete responsibility: ribbon tools, settings, settings packs, or hooks registered by the module. Moduleless manifests must declare panel and at least one tool.ribbonTools entry, and cannot declare settings or settings packs. Hook-only modules may keep tool.ribbonTools empty, but they must register at least one hook during RegisterHooks(...). Ribbon Tool Properties Property Required Description internalName Yes Unique button identifier commandType Yes Full type name of command class availabilityType No Full type name of the concrete command, which also implements IExternalCommandAvailability runProfile No InlineUi (default) or QueuedModeless displayText Yes Button label (use \n for line breaks) iconBaseKey Yes Icon filename without extension tooltip Yes Button tooltip text controlKind Yes PushButton, SplitButtonItem, PulldownButtonItem, StackedButtonItem splitGroup No Group name for split/pulldown/stacked buttons order Yes Button order within panel groupDisplayText No Header text for pulldown groups groupTooltip No Tooltip for pulldown header groupIconBaseKey No Icon for pulldown header Entries that share a split or pulldown group form one ordered command sequence. The lowest-order entry is the split primary command and later entries are the dropdown commands. App planning and Revit construction consume that exact sequence; there is no second primary/dropdown list to keep synchronized. Example: Simple Tool id: DBTools.Structural.FramingJoins assembly: DBTools.FramingJoins order: 0 panel: Structural tool: ribbonTools: - internalName: DBTools.AllowJoinSelected commandType: DBTools.FramingJoins.App.Composition.AllowJoinSelectedCommand availabilityType: DBTools.FramingJoins.App.Composition.AllowJoinSelectedCommand runProfile: InlineUi displayText: "Allow Join" iconBaseKey: allow_join tooltip: "Allow structural framing joins for selected elements" controlKind: SplitButtonItem splitGroup: framing_joins order: 0 - internalName: DBTools.DisallowJoinSelected commandType: DBTools.FramingJoins.App.Composition.DisallowJoinSelectedCommand availabilityType: DBTools.FramingJoins.App.Composition.DisallowJoinSelectedCommand runProfile: InlineUi displayText: "Disallow Join" iconBaseKey: disallow_join tooltip: "Disallow structural framing joins for selected elements" controlKind: SplitButtonItem splitGroup: framing_joins order: 1 Example: Service/Settings Module id: DBTools.Services.DialogSuppression assembly: DBTools moduleType: DBTools.Services.DialogSuppression.Infrastructure.DialogSuppressionToolModule order: -1 panel: Services tool: settings: configSection: Tools.DialogSuppression settingsPacks: - key: services.dialog_suppression title: "Dialog Suppression" This module has no tool.ribbonTools section, so startup registers its settings/services without adding a ribbon button. Runtime explicitly allows modules with no ribbon tools when their tool: section exists for settings or settings packs. Example: Complex Tool with UI id: DBTools.GM assembly: DBTools.GM moduleType: DBTools.GM.App.Composition.Revit.GmToolModule order: 0 panel: Common sandboxWindows: - id: DBTools.GM.Main displayName: "Global Mapper" group: "Common" xamlResource: "DBTools.ToolViews.GM.GmWindow.xaml" designTimeViewModelType: "DBTools.GM.App.DesignTime.GmWindowDesignTimeViewModel" designTimeViewModelAssembly: "DBTools.GM" designTimeViewModelVisibility: Internal - id: DBTools.GM.CommitReview displayName: "Global Mapper - Commit Review" group: "Common" xamlResource: "DBTools.ToolViews.GM.GmCommitReviewWindow.xaml" designTimeViewModelType: "DBTools.GM.Features.CommitReview.DesignTime.GmCommitReviewWindowDesignTimeViewModel" designTimeViewModelAssembly: "DBTools.GM" designTimeViewModelVisibility: Internal tool: ribbonTools: - internalName: DBTools.GM commandType: DBTools.GM.App.Composition.Revit.GmCommand availabilityType: DBTools.GM.App.Composition.Revit.GmCommand runProfile: QueuedModeless displayText: "Global Mapper" iconBaseKey: gm tooltip: "Open Global Mapper" controlKind: PushButton order: 30 Step 4: ToolModule Class The ToolModule subclass is the manifest entry point. Keep it thin: validate inputs, bind settings/settings packs, and delegate feature or shell DI to Shell/ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs. Do not manually map manifest ribbon fields inside tool modules. App startup resolves the manifest command and optional availability types, then delegates registration construction to Core so panel mapping, execution defaults, control-kind mapping, and grouped-button metadata stay in the shared registry/ribbon contracts. Minimal Command Workflow Registration Simple inline command tools can register their command workflow dependency on the command itself. Framing Joins uses this path instead of a tool module: [Transaction(TransactionMode.Manual)] [CommandService(typeof(FramingJoinsWorkflow))] public sealed class AllowJoinSelectedCommand : ToolCommand { protected override async Task RunAsync(ICommandContext context) { Guard.NotNull(context, nameof(context)); var workflow = context.Resolve(); await workflow.ExecuteAsync(...).ConfigureAwait(false); } } With Service Registration using DBTools.Core.Tools; using DBTools.Core.Guarding.Domain; using DBTools.MyTool.Shell; using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection; namespace DBTools.MyTool; public sealed class MyToolToolModule : ToolModule { public override void RegisterServices(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { Guard.NotNull(services, nameof(services)); Guard.NotNull(manifest, nameof(manifest)); services.AddMyTool(); } } With Hooks using DBTools.Core.Tools; using DBTools.Core.Guarding.Domain; using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection; namespace DBTools.SGT; public sealed class SgtToolModule : ToolModule { public override void RegisterServices(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { Guard.NotNull(services, nameof(services)); Guard.NotNull(manifest, nameof(manifest)); services.AddSgt(); services.AddSingleton(); } public override void RegisterHooks(ToolRegistry registry, ToolManifest manifest) { Guard.NotNull(registry, nameof(registry)); Guard.NotNull(manifest, nameof(manifest)); // Register contextual ribbon lifecycle hook registry.RegisterHook(); } } ToolModule Virtual Methods Method Purpose RegisterSettings Register typed settings sections RegisterServices Register services for DI container RegisterSettingsPacks Register settings pack definitions RegisterHooks Register event hooks (ViewActivated, ContextualRibbon, DialogBoxShowing) Step 5: Command Implementation Command-bearing ribbon modules implement commands with ToolCommand (not IExternalCommand directly) to get automatic error handling, logging, and run scope management. Service/settings modules with no ribbon tools skip this step. Basic Command Structure using System; using System.Threading.Tasks; using Autodesk.Revit.Attributes; using DBTools.Core.Guarding.Domain; using DBTools.Core.Revit.Execution.Commands; using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging; namespace DBTools.MyTool.Features; [Transaction(TransactionMode.Manual)] public sealed class MyToolCommand : ToolCommand { protected override async Task RunAsync(ICommandContext context) { Guard.EnsureNotNull(context, nameof(context)); var logger = context.Logger; var doc = context.Document; var uidoc = context.UIDocument; logger.LogDebug("[MyTool] Starting execution"); // Your tool logic here await Task.CompletedTask.ConfigureAwait(false); } } With Transaction [Transaction(TransactionMode.Manual)] [CommandService(typeof(FramingJoinsWorkflow))] public sealed class AllowJoinSelectedCommand : ToolCommand { protected override async Task RunAsync(ICommandContext context) { Guard.NotNull(context, nameof(context)); var workflow = context.Resolve(); await workflow.ExecuteAsync( FramingJoinOperation.Allow, context.UIDocument, context.Document).ConfigureAwait(false); } } The workflow receives the scoped transaction runner, owner provider, and typed logger through constructor injection. The selected command profile has already created either InlineRevitCallGate or QueuedRevitCallGate for that scope, while the command passes only operation-specific inputs: public FramingJoinsWorkflow( ILoggerWindowHost loggerWindow, ITransactionRunner transactions, IWindowOwnerHandleProvider ownerHandleProvider, ILogger logger) { _loggerWindow = loggerWindow; _transactions = transactions; _ownerHandleProvider = ownerHandleProvider; _logger = logger; } await _transactions.RunInDocumentAsync(doc, $"DB Tools - {operationName} Join Selected", d => { modified = ExecuteCore(operation, framingTargets, _logger); }).ConfigureAwait(false); ICommandContext Properties Property Description UIApplication Revit UIApplication UIDocument Active UIDocument Document Active Document Logger ILogger for the command Resolve() Resolve service from DI Step 6: UI Implementation (MVVM Pattern) For tools with UI, follow the MVVM pattern with DBTools conventions. Raw XAML view template Embed the file with an explicit logical name such as DBTools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolWindow.xaml. It declares no tool CLR namespace, Window root, x:Class or event attribute. The manifest supplies its design-time model. Tool-window sessions Tool UI uses raw embedded XAML without x:Class or code-behind. Its root is a stable view element such as Grid; ToolWindowHost supplies the modal or modeless shell. Core's ToolWindowFactory installs the theme, owner, icon, error boundary and progress lifecycle before parsing, then registers the session for normal close and generation retirement. using var xaml = new MemoryStream(ToolWindowXaml.ReadEmbeddedResource( typeof(MyToolWindowViewModel).Assembly, "DBTools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolWindow.xaml")); var session = factory.Create(ToolWindowKind.Modal, xaml, viewModel, new ToolWindowOptions { Title = "My Tool", Width = 800, Height = 600 }); _ = session.ShowDialog(); Use ToolWindowKind.Modeless and session.Show() for a modeless surface. Register payload event handlers and owned cleanup through the session. A custom shell initializer owns its cleanup handle and must register it with session.AddCleanup. ViewModel Pattern Use CommunityToolkit.Mvvm for MVVM implementation: using CommunityToolkit.Mvvm.ComponentModel; using CommunityToolkit.Mvvm.Input; namespace DBTools.MyTool.Shell.ViewModels; public partial class MyToolWindowViewModel : ObservableObject { [ObservableProperty] private string _searchText = string.Empty; [ObservableProperty] private bool _isBusy; [RelayCommand] private async Task ExecuteAsync() { IsBusy = true; try { // Do work } finally { IsBusy = false; } } } Design-Time ViewModel Create a design-time ViewModel for XAML preview: using System.Windows.Input; using DBTools.Core.UI; namespace DBTools.MyTool.Shell.DesignTime; /// /// Design-time ViewModel for XAML Designer support. /// DO NOT instantiate at runtime. /// [System.ComponentModel.EditorBrowsable(System.ComponentModel.EditorBrowsableState.Never)] public sealed class MyToolDesignTimeViewModel { // Commands - use NoOpCommand for all public ICommand ExecuteCommand => NoOpCommand.Instance; public ICommand CloseCommand => NoOpCommand.Instance; // Properties with sample data public string SearchText { get; set; } = "Sample search"; public bool IsBusy => false; public MyToolDesignTimeViewModel() { // Initialize sample data for designer preview } } Step 7: Settings (Optional) Defining Settings Create a settings class: namespace DBTools.MyTool.Settings; public sealed class MyToolSettings { public bool EnableFeatureX { get; set; } = true; public int Threshold { get; set; } = 50; } Registering Settings In your ToolModule: public override void RegisterSettings( IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { Guard.NotNull(services, nameof(services)); Guard.NotNull(manifest, nameof(manifest)); services.AddSingleton(new SettingsSection( manifest.GetRequiredConfigSection(), MyToolSettingsJsonContext.Default.MyToolSettings)); } Using Settings public sealed class MyService { private readonly MyToolSettings _settings; public MyService(ISettingsProvider settings, SettingsSection section) { _settings = settings.Get(section); } } settings.{YEAR}.json Structure { "Tools.MyTool": { "EnableFeatureX": true, "Threshold": 75 } } Step 8: Hooks (Optional) Available Hook Contracts Contract Purpose ViewActivationHook Core-owned view-change dispatcher; tools plug in via IViewActivationTask IHookLifecycle Add application lifecycle hooks, including contextual ribbon tabs ViewActivated Hook For view-activated behavior, register an IViewActivationTask. The singleton ViewActivationHook is already provided by the app layer. using System; using System.Collections.Generic; using System.Threading; using System.Threading.Tasks; using DBTools.Core.Tools.Hooks.ViewActivation; using Autodesk.Revit.DB; using Autodesk.Revit.UI; using Autodesk.Revit.UI.Events; namespace DBTools.MyTool.Features.Hooks; public sealed class MyViewActivatedTask : IViewActivationTask { public string TaskId => "mytool.view-activated"; public string DisplayName => "My Tool View Activated"; public IReadOnlyCollection WarningIdsToSetOnFailure => Array.Empty(); // A non-null admission runs this attempt once; it captures the state its execution uses public Task AdmitAsync(UIApplication application, ViewActivatedEventArgs args, CancellationToken ct) { var view = args.CurrentActiveView; return Task.FromResult( view == null ? null : new ViewActivationAdmission(executionCt => ReactAsync(view, executionCt))); } private static Task ReactAsync(View view, CancellationToken ct) { // React to the admitted view return Task.CompletedTask; } } Register from your shell service collection extension: public static IServiceCollection AddMyTool(this IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { services.AddSingleton(); return services; } Step 9: Command-owned Availability Every ToolCommand implements IExternalCommandAvailability; its default predicate requires an open document. Set availabilityType to the same concrete command as commandType. Commands with another requirement override IsCommandAvailableCore and call CommandAvailability.HasActiveView, HasSelection, or HasStructuralFramingSelection. Step 10: Declare Assembly Ownership Set true in the tool's production .csproj under src/Tools///. Projects without WPF also set true to retain the existing content-version policy. Set manifest.yml's assembly and each design-time ViewModel assembly to the actual owner, such as DBTools.TDV. Embed icons, policies and raw XAML in that project. Preserve their logical resource names. Remove explicit App resource entries for the migrated tool. Reference the production project from Pure tests, Local tests and real consumers. Move required InternalsVisibleTo declarations to the tool project. ProductOutput.proj restores declared tool owners, builds their final images, and stages them beneath the selected year directory's Tools/ folder. App manifests remain embedded centrally, while ToolAssemblyResolver loads each declared owner by explicit path in the active owning context. The final tree contains the four top-level product DLLs plus the fourteen tool DLLs beneath Tools/. App embeds tool manifests for central discovery but compiles no source, XAML, or assets from src/Tools/. Runtime modules, commands, icons, settings, and raw XAML resolve from the manifest-declared owner. Tool XAML must continue to use framework and stable Presentation types. Every tool declares its own assembly, resources, and test references. No tool-specific product-output, Core, or App runtime logic is required. SGT, Settings, and DialogSuppression use assembly: DBTools.SGT, DBTools.Settings, and DBTools.DialogSuppression respectively. Step 11: Testing Setup Test Project Structure src/Tools///Tests/ DBTools..Pure.Tests.csproj # plain [Test] fixtures; no Revit host DBTools..Local.Tests.csproj # [RevitLocal] fixtures PureBehaviorTests.cs RevitHostedBehaviorTests.cs Support/ Do not create a consolidated unsuffixed tool test project. Owner tests follow the taxonomy in Test Pipeline: .Pure.Tests compiles plain off-Revit fixtures against a plain ProjectReference to the tool, .Local.Tests compiles local Revit-hosted fixtures, and DA coverage requires a separate WorkItem-backed [RevitDA] project. Its WorkItem tests run like the DA Sentinel: on the operator's host as an HTTP client with dotnet test, with APS_CLIENT_ID and APS_CLIENT_SECRET set, for 5–12 minutes of APS processing time per WorkItem (the account includes 300 free minutes a month). Sub-agents and the daemon never run them; see APS Design Automation Sentinel. A tool whose inward code should also run on Linux adopts the optional portable target described in the Test Pipeline and adds DBTools..Portable.Pure.Tests. Running Tests # Run a tool's pure lane through the repository wrapper ./test.sh test --tool MYTOOL --scope pure # Run a specific fixture through the repository wrapper ./test.sh test --tool MYTOOL --scope pure --fixture MyTestName Common Patterns and Best Practices 1. Service Extension Pattern Centralize DI registration in an extension method: // Shell/MyToolServiceCollectionExtensions.cs namespace DBTools.MyTool.Shell; public static class MyToolServiceCollectionExtensions { public static IServiceCollection AddMyTool(this IServiceCollection services) { Guard.NotNull(services, nameof(services)); services.AddScoped(); services.AddScoped(); return services; } } Then in ToolModule: services.AddMyTool(); 2. Error Handling Never swallow exceptions. Use ISafeExecutor for top-level error handling (provided by ToolCommand): // DON'T do this: try { DoWork(); } catch { } // Silent failure // DO this: // Exceptions propagate to ToolCommand's ISafeExecutor DoWork(); // Let exceptions propagate 3. Logging Use the injected logger, not Console.WriteLine: var logger = context.Logger; logger.LogDebug("[MyTool] Processing {Count} elements", count); logger.LogWarning("[MyTool] Skipped invalid element {Id}", elementId); logger.LogError(ex, "[MyTool] Failed to process"); 4. Transactions Always name transactions descriptively: await tx.RunAsync(doc, "DB Tools - My Tool Operation", d => { // Modifications here }).ConfigureAwait(false); 5. Icon Naming Main icon: my_tool.png (32x32) Small icon: my_tool_16.png (16x16, optional) Match the iconBaseKey in manifest (without extension) 6. Namespace Conventions Choose the namespace root from the live tool family instead of flattening every tool to the same prefix. Common and Testing tools currently use DBTools. roots such as DBTools.GM, DBTools.TDV, and DBTools.VTC; Structural tools use DBTools.Structural. roots such as DBTools.Structural.FramingJoins. Established tools keep their current root unless a deliberate source migration changes every project, manifest, and callsite together. # Root namespace .Features # Command entrypoints and feature-level APIs .Features. # Feature-slice services/models (Transfer, Library, Preview, etc.) .Shell # Shell wiring and DI extensions .Shell.Services # Optional shell-only coordinators/factories .Shell.Views # WPF windows and controls .Shell.ViewModels # Runtime ViewModels .Shell.DesignTime # Design-time ViewModels .Shared # Cross-feature shared types .Shared.Domain # Shared domain/value objects .Shared.Models # Shared DTOs/view models .Shared.State # Optional cross-feature state stores .Revit.Services # Optional Revit-facing adapters/services .Settings # Optional settings/options Avoid introducing retired namespace shapes in new scaffolds: Bootstrap, Features.Commands, Features.Logic, Shell.DI, and Shell.UI. Checklist: New Tool Completion Created directory structure under src/Tools/// Added manifest.yml with a unique id and either valid ribbonTools, settings/settings packs, or a hook registration contract Created ToolModule.cs extending ToolModule Implemented command(s) extending ToolCommand when the module declares ribbonTools Added icon(s) in Assets/ folder when the module declares ribbon tools Created .csproj file for command-bearing modules or modules that need independent IDE/test isolation Added every created production or test .csproj to DBTools.sln under its owning solution folder Build passes: bash build.sh Tool appears in Revit ribbon when the module declares ribbonTools Command executes successfully when the module declares ribbonTools (Optional) Created test project (Optional) Added UI with design-time preview Source: DBTools.sln:6 Source: build/Build.proj:1 Cross-References Architecture Overview Core Project Theme System Test Pipeline

developer-guide/developing/sandbox-integ.title: Sandbox Integration Guide | DB Tools
developer-guide/developing/sandbox-integ.summary: Sandbox Integration Guide The Sandbox previews tool windows and validates a staged product candidate without starting Revit. It runs one fresh process per candidate year. Candidate loading The BCL-only Sandbox entry validates a year directory before Core-backed logging, Presentation, or WPF startup: DBTools.addin DBTools.dll DBTools.Core.dll DBTools.Presentation.dll DBTools.HandyControl.dll Tools/DBTools.<Tool>.dll It checks the .addin, exact file set, PE identities, assembly locations, and supported year. It then loads the candidate's top-level product images and manifest-declared tool images from their actual paths in the default context. The entry uses a non-inlined boundary to start WPF after candidate loading and exits after validation. Do not add a Loader, Bootstrap, embedded payload, runtime manifest, or DBTools-owned load context to make Sandbox work. Register a window Declare the window in the tool's manifest.yml: sandboxWindows: - id: DBTools.MyTool.Main displayName: "My Tool" group: "Common" xamlResource: "DBTools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolView.xaml" windowKind: Modal designTimeViewModelType: "DBTools.MyTool.App.DesignTime.MyToolDesignTimeViewModel" designTimeViewModelAssembly: "DBTools.MyTool" designTimeViewModelVisibility: Public The xamlResource value must match the owning project's embedded logical name: <EmbeddedResource Include="App\Views\MyToolView.xaml"> <LogicalName>DBTools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolView.xaml</LogicalName> </EmbeddedResource> The required fields are `id`, `displayName`, `group`, `xamlResource`, `windowKind`, `designTimeViewModelType`, `designTimeViewModelAssembly`, and `designTimeViewModelVisibility`. Optional fields include width, height, minimum sizes, taskbar visibility, startup location, and tool-specific grouping metadata. Keep the manifest as the single owner of these values; do not infer a window type from a filename. For example, a tool with two raw views can declare separate stable ids while sharing one design-time state type: ```yaml sandboxWindows: - id: DBTools.MyTool.Main displayName: "My Tool" group: "Common" xamlResource: "DBTools.ToolViews.MyTool.MainView.xaml" windowKind: Modal width: 1200 height: 700 minWidth: 900 minHeight: 500 startupLocation: CenterScreen designTimeViewModelType: "DBTools.MyTool.App.DesignTime.MyToolDesignTimeViewModel" designTimeViewModelAssembly: "DBTools.MyTool" designTimeViewModelVisibility: Public Sandbox copies manifest values into local specifications and opens the raw view through `DBTools.Presentation.ToolWindows.ToolWindowHost`. It does not activate a candidate `Window` type by reflection. Raw views have no `x:Class`, code-behind, payload pack URI, event attribute, payload BAML, or implicit payload template. Use explicit templates, selectors, and display paths for bound content. ## Runtime ownership Presentation owns stable WPF shells, themes, resources, and `ToolWindowCallbackScope`. Core and tool assemblies remain candidate-owned and are loaded from the year tree. Sandbox does not invoke App's Revit startup and does not load Revit reference DLLs as executable product files. ## Archive and validation Distribution archives are year-keyed even though both years target the same TFM: ```text .artifacts/sandbox/<configuration>/<year>/<tfm>/ sandbox/<year>/<sanitized-tfm>/ Portable checks validate raw XAML, manifest ownership, metadata, and recursive file fingerprints. Native WPF layout, binding, theme, and window cleanup require the Windows acceptance process. A live daemon Dev Mode inject/reload remains a separate operational proof. Design-time ViewModels The manifest's designTimeViewModelType and designTimeViewModelAssembly are validated against the candidate tool image. The type must be public, concrete, and have a public parameterless constructor. Keep design-time construction independent of Revit documents, external events, network services, and production settings. public sealed class MyWindowDesignTimeViewModel { public MyWindowDesignTimeViewModel() { Rows = [new MyRow("Example", "Preview")]; } public IReadOnlyList<MyRow> Rows { get; } } Use explicit state and commands in the design-time graph. A small NoOpCommand is appropriate for a display-only action whose behavior is outside the validation surface; do not hide a production command failure behind a design-time double. If a design-time fixture needs an analyzer suppression, keep it on the narrow declaration and explain the actual WPF or generated-code reason. Raw XAML is the stable boundary. It must use the exact logical resource name, avoid x:Class, code-behind event attributes, payload CLR namespaces, inferred columns, and implicit payload templates. Bind visible text, headers, items, and tooltips explicitly. The stable Presentation host owns themes, resources, window lifecycle, and the callback scope; a tool owns its candidate view resource and design-time ViewModel. Local commands Build the candidate before running the Sandbox: ./build.sh AssembleDistributionCandidate -y 2026 ./build.sh AssembleDistributionCandidate -y 2027 Without --dist-dir, interactive validation opens the published Release tree. Pass --dist-dir to select a candidate: dotnet run --project src/DBTools.Sandbox/DBTools.Sandbox.csproj \ -- --dist-dir .artifacts/dist/candidate/2026 Headless validation avoids creating windows while preserving candidate checks: dotnet run --project src/DBTools.Sandbox/DBTools.Sandbox.csproj -- \ --headless --dist-dir .artifacts/dist/candidate/2026 \ --revit-reference-dir /path/to/Revit2026 The supported options are --dist-dir (or --dist-dir=<path>), --revit-reference-dir (required with --headless, rejected without it), and --headless. Blank values are rejected. An absent or ambiguous year directory fails before Core, Presentation, or WPF loads. Run one fresh process per candidate year; do not reuse a process after changing the candidate tree. Validation checks and troubleshooting The validation sequence is deliberately ordered: Parse the year and candidate directory. Validate .addin, required top-level files, recursive Tools/ files, PE identities, and supported target framework. Load candidate App/Core/Presentation/HandyControl and declared tool images from their actual default-context paths. Validate embedded manifests, raw XAML logical names, design-time ViewModels, and stable resource ownership. Construct native windows, exercise layout and interactions, capture binding errors, close windows, and verify Dispatcher cleanup. Common failures have direct owners: Failure Check Tool window resource missing Match xamlResource to the owning project's LogicalName. ViewModel cannot be created Make the declared type public, concrete, and parameterless. Binding errors Inspect the binding listener output and bind display state explicitly. Candidate file mismatch Rebuild the selected year and compare the recursive product listing. Revit reference mismatch Pass the matching installed year directory; reference files are metadata evidence. Window cleanup failure Close the window and allow its Dispatcher cleanup to complete before process exit. The Sandbox process does not prove Revit startup, daemon ProductLoadContext sharing, or Dev Mode reload behavior. Those remain separate coordinator-owned Windows/daemon proofs. Tool examples GM uses multiple sandboxWindows entries that point to raw logical resources and tool-owned design-time ViewModels. SGT follows the same pattern for its raw views. A new tool should copy the manifest shape, add explicit raw resources and ViewModels, and add the owning Pure validation fixture before requesting native evidence. See Sandbox Validator, Assembly Loading Contract, and Creating New Tools.

developer-guide/developing/settings-pack.title: Settings Packs | DB Tools
developer-guide/developing/settings-pack.summary: Settings Packs Settings Packs are the mechanism for tools to expose user-configurable options in the DBTools Settings window. This guide covers the complete settings lifecycle: from manifest declaration to runtime access and persistence. Overview What Are Settings Packs? A Settings Pack bundles together: Settings Model - A typed class holding the configuration values Settings Pack Context - A ViewModel that manages UI state and data binding Settings Pack View - A WPF UserControl rendered in the Settings window Warning Definitions - Optional conditions that can disable tool functionality Settings Packs appear as collapsible cards in the Settings window, organized by ribbon panel (Common, Structural, Testing). Why Use Settings Packs? Centralized configuration: Users manage all tool settings in one place Automatic persistence: Settings are saved to settings.{YEAR}.json with atomic writes Fresh reads: ISettingsProvider.Get(section) loads the current layered files Feature warnings: Link settings validation to tool availability Consistent UX: All tools share the same settings interface pattern Apply Timing The Settings window should describe when saved values take effect, not show a blanket restart warning. Ribbon visibility and similar shell-level flags can apply immediately after save. Tool settings typically apply on the next command run or next view-activation hook. RequiresRestart should be reserved for an explicitly documented pack-specific limitation, not shown globally. Architecture The Settings ribbon command resolves SettingsWindowFactory, which loads the embedded raw DBTools.Presentation.Settings.Views.SettingsWindow.xaml view through ToolWindowFactory and receives a registered modal IToolWindowSession. It calls session.ShowDialog(), so owner handling, reflection scope, normal-close cleanup, and generation-retirement teardown are owned by the same session lifecycle as other tool windows. The session change does not change pack loading, Save, Reset All, validation, warning, cancel, or success-banner behavior. Typed JSON settings in DBTools DBTools reads typed settings with source-generated System.Text.Json metadata and commits changes through a custom persistence layer: ┌─────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────┐ │ settings.{YEAR}.json │────>│ SettingsSectionReader│ │ (user data) │ │ (typed JSON read) │ └─────────────────────┘ └──────────┬───────────┘ │ ┌──────────▼───────────┐ │ ISettingsProvider │ │ (typed read/write) │ └──────────┬───────────┘ │ ┌─────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ ┌────────▼────────┐ ┌──────────▼──────────┐ ┌──────────▼──────────┐ │ Tool Command │ │ ViewActivatedTask │ │ Settings Window │ │ (read current) │ │ (check auto-update) │ │ (edit & save) │ └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────────┘ └──────────┬──────────┘ │ ┌──────────▼──────────┐ │ SettingsSectionWriter│ │ (one atomic batch) │ └──────────┬──────────┘ │ ┌──────────▼──────────┐ │ settings.{YEAR}.json │ │ (updated) │ └─────────────────────┘ Key Interfaces Interface Purpose SettingsSection<T> Typed persistence identity for one named JSON settings section ISettingsProvider Read typed sections and atomically commit one or more SettingsSectionWrite values SettingsSectionReader Merges app defaults and per-year overrides using generated JSON metadata ISettingsPackDefinition Heterogeneous catalog metadata plus creation of one context-bound runtime per row ISettingsPackRuntime Owns the exact pack context, typed section, bound warnings, lazy view, and current/default write staging ISettingsPackContext<T> ViewModel interface for settings UI ISettingsWarningDefinition Warning linked to settings validation Defining Settings in manifest.yml Settings packs are declared in the tool's manifest.yml under tool.settingsPacks: Schema tool: settings: configSection: "<section-name>" # Required: JSON key in settings.{YEAR}.json settingsPacks: - key: "<unique-pack-key>" # Required: Globally unique identifier title: "<display-title>" # Required: Shown in Settings window warnings: # Optional: Associated warnings - id: "<warning-id>" # Required: Unique warning identifier title: "<warning-title>" # Required: Warning card title message: "<warning-msg>" # Required: Explanation shown to user disableTools: # Optional: Tools disabled when warning active - "<tool-internal-name>" - "<another-tool>" Complete Example: FoundationTags id: DBTools.Structural.FoundationTags assembly: DBTools moduleType: DBTools.Structural.FoundationTags.FoundationTagsToolModule order: 0 tool: settings: configSection: Tools.FoundationTags settingsPacks: - key: structural.foundation_tags title: "Combined Foundation Tags" warnings: - id: core.structural.combined_tags title: "Combined Foundation Tags Disabled" message: "Combined foundation tag updates are disabled due to a warning. Clear the warning to re-enable." disableTools: - DBTools.UpdateCombinedFoundationTags - DBTools.MoveCombinedFoundationTags - DBTools.OrganizeFoundationTypes ribbonTools: # ... ribbon tool definitions Key Naming Conventions Property Convention Example configSection {Category}.{ToolName} Tools.FoundationTags key {category}.{feature} structural.foundation_tags warnings[].id core.{category}.{feature} core.structural.combined_tags Settings Model Classes Basic Settings Model A settings model is a POCO class with public properties: namespace DBTools.Structural.JoistGirderWeight.Settings; public sealed class JoistGirderWeightSettings : IAutoUpdateSettings { public bool AutoUpdateEnabled { get; set; } = true; public bool HasWarning { get; set; } } Settings DTO Type Contract Settings DTO graphs must end in built-in leaf types: booleans, strings, or doubles. Nullable values, collections, dictionaries, and nested DTOs are supported when all their keys, elements, and properties follow the same rule. Add-in enums and types or properties with a custom TypeConverter or JsonConverter are not allowed. Reads use SettingsSectionReader with each section's generated JSON metadata. It layers application defaults with per-year overrides, matches section and property names case-insensitively, and preserves the established scalar conversions. Only a missing file or missing parent directory is absent configuration; any other fault, such as a directory at the file path, propagates. Writes use the source-generated JsonTypeInfo<T> carried by SettingsSection<T>. Reads and commits share one JSON syntax (comments and trailing commas allowed) and case-insensitive section identity: a commit replaces a case-variant section in place, rejects case-variant duplicates in one batch, and does not keep comments. Section names are single JSON property names. They must be nonempty and cannot contain :; nested configuration paths are not supported. For properties with initialized defaults, use settable properties so absent keys retain their defaults. Cover these defaults and file compatibility through the real reader. Pure and Local test executables disable reflection-based JSON serialization through their runtime configuration. IAutoUpdateSettings Interface For tools with auto-update on view activation, implement IAutoUpdateSettings: namespace DBTools.Core.Settings.Domain; public interface IAutoUpdateSettings { bool AutoUpdateEnabled { get; set; } bool HasWarning { get; set; } } Complex Settings Model Settings can include collections, nested objects, and custom defaults: namespace DBTools.Structural.FoundationTags.Settings; public sealed class FoundationTagsSettings : IAutoUpdateSettings { public bool AutoUpdateEnabled { get; set; } = true; public bool HasWarning { get; set; } /// <summary> /// Regex patterns to match tag family names. /// </summary> public List<string> TagFamilyPatterns { get; set; } = new() { "^Combined Foundation Tag", "^DB Foundation Tag" }; /// <summary> /// Regex patterns to match pier family names. /// </summary> public List<string> PierFamilyPatterns { get; set; } = new() { "^Foundation Pier" }; /// <summary> /// Regex patterns to match footing family names. /// </summary> public List<string> FootingFamilyPatterns { get; set; } = new() { "^Footing-Rectangular$", "^Pile Cap-Rectangular$" }; } JSON Representation Settings are stored in settings.{YEAR}.json under the configSection key: { "Tools.FoundationTags": { "AutoUpdateEnabled": true, "HasWarning": false, "TagFamilyPatterns": [ "^Combined Foundation Tag", "^DB Foundation Tag" ], "PierFamilyPatterns": [ "^Foundation Pier" ], "FootingFamilyPatterns": [ "^Footing-Rectangular$", "^Pile Cap-Rectangular$" ] } } Registering Settings Settings registration happens in two phases within your ToolModule: Phase 1: RegisterSettings() Register the typed section used by the tool and its settings pack: public override void RegisterSettings( IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { Guard.NotNull(services, nameof(services)); Guard.NotNull(manifest, nameof(manifest)); var settingsSection = new SettingsSection<FoundationTagsSettings>( manifest.GetRequiredConfigSection(), FoundationTagsSettingsJsonContext.Default.FoundationTagsSettings); services.AddSingleton(settingsSection); } This registration: Reads the configSection from manifest (Tools.FoundationTags) Publishes one typed SettingsSection<FoundationTagsSettings> identity Lets consumers read the current layered files through ISettingsProvider.Get(settingsSection) Phase 2: RegisterSettingsPacks() Register the full settings pack definition with UI factory: public override void RegisterSettingsPacks(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { Guard.NotNull(services, nameof(services)); Guard.NotNull(manifest, nameof(manifest)); var settingsSection = new SettingsSection<FoundationTagsSettings>( manifest.GetRequiredConfigSection(), FoundationTagsSettingsJsonContext.Default.FoundationTagsSettings);
